title: Session 14 guided lab
text: Work in BIOS6301-mywork.Rproj. Copy one starter from the separate course clone into work/session14/: Quarto or R Markdown. Keep the course originals unchanged.

title: Session 14 guided lab
text:
Learning goals
Practice reproducible random draws, distinguish a population target from an estimate, and compare two procedures using a small simulation. Interpret Monte Carlo uncertainty with one proportion formula.

title: Session 14 guided lab
text:
Tasks following the lecture outline

Specify ADEMP — Let each outcome be SBP reduction: baseline minus 12-week SBP, in mmHg. Positive delta means greater mean reduction with treatment. Use independent normal control and treatment groups with SDs 12 and 4. Compare sizes 10/40 and 30/40 and true differences 0 and 6 (four scenarios). Define the estimand as the population mean difference, treatment minus control. Distinguish this target from the estimator and one sample estimate. Write the five ADEMP headings before running the study. Explain why normal reductions are a useful reference scenario, what prior or pilot evidence would support this model in a real project, and one reason to examine a skewed alternative. State the independence assumption and identify the means and SDs as teaching values.
Inspect one replicate — Generate one dataset. Inspect outcome ranges and group summaries to check the generator, allowing for sampling variation. Explain why simulated data cannot establish that real SBP reductions are normal. Compare Welch and pooled results on that same dataset. Verify the estimate direction, result names, and interval ordering. Exercise a failed constant-outcome sample.
Retain each method and replicate — Inspect the supplied run_study(s, B) function and run a pilot with B = 5. Identify where it generates one dataset, applies both methods, and retains results or errors. Check that five replicates produce ten rows. Both methods must use the same dataset in each replicate.
Run reproducible scenarios — Use B = 1000 for this teaching exercise. Assign each scenario a fixed seed and call set.seed() immediately before running that scenario. Insert an unrelated runif() call before the seed and verify that the scenario results stay unchanged. Do not reset the seed inside the replicate loop.
Summarize performance and failures — For each scenario and method report attempts, failures, bias, coverage, rejection rate, and MCSE for rejection. Use sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / B_valid), where B_valid counts successful replicates. Label performance summaries as conditional on success. Interpret rejection rates as type I error when delta = 0 and power when delta = 6.
Interpret the comparison — Compare null calibration, power, coverage, and failure counts across allocations. Draw one rejection-rate comparison with approximate Monte Carlo intervals. Explain why 5.2% from 1,000 replicates need not differ meaningfully from 5%, and why more replicates differ from more patients per trial.
Power for study planning — Use the delta = 6 results to compare Welch power for 10/40 and 30/40 patients. Report rejections, valid trials, power, MCSE, and an approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval. Explain why this interval concerns detection probability rather than the treatment effect. Distinguish power from coverage. Do the results support at least 80% power? Explain what increasing patient numbers changes and what increasing B changes.

title: Session 14 guided lab
text:
Exit evidence
Submit the source and rendered report with the requested results, checks, interpretation, and AI-use disclosure. Every result must identify its analysis sample or resampling unit. Use synthetic data supplied in the starter.

title: Session 14 guided lab
section: Warm-up: random draws and the normal distribution
text:
Warm-up: random draws and the normal distribution

Run two successive rnorm(3) calls after set.seed(42). Rerun the entire block. Which results repeat?
Save state_before <- .Random.seed, draw one value, and compare with identical(state_before, .Random.seed). Explain the generator’s changing bookmark.
Insert unused <- runif(1) between the two rnorm(3) calls. Explain why the second output changes even though unused is never used.
Call set.seed(99) immediately before the result you want to reproduce. Verify that earlier random work no longer changes that result. Explain why you should not put the same seed inside every replicate.
Evaluate dnorm(0), pnorm(1.96), qnorm(0.975), and rnorm(8). Match them to density height, left-tail area, cutoff value, and simulated observations. Which two functions reverse each other’s question? Why is dnorm(0) not the probability of observing exactly zero?

title: Session 14 guided lab
text:
Optional extensions

Extend the Welch power comparison to more sample sizes or a smaller effect (for example, 3 mmHg). Keep the test rule fixed and refine promising scenarios with more replicates.
Add dgm = "skewed" to the design using the supplied helper. Explain why it centers errors using the population mean rather than each sample mean. Keep the estimand unchanged.
Report empirical SE, mean model SE, RMSE, mean interval width, and MCSE for bias or coverage.
Plan B from a target MCSE using ceiling(p * (1 - p) / target^2). Try B = 4000 and explain why MCSE is about half its value at B = 1000.
Explore SimDesign::runSimulation() for running a larger study or rsimsum::simsum() for summarising saved results. No package installation is required for the core lab.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
The R programming sequence








Session
Main question
What you produce




11 · Functions
How do I express one operation clearly?
Functions with explicit contracts


12 · Reliability
How do I diagnose and prevent wrong results?
A repaired function and regression checks


13 · Iteration
How do I repeat a correct operation?
Named results, checked implementations, measured performance



The same numeric summaries and paired-change examples connect all three labs. Statistical methods in later sessions use these programming tools.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Distinguish if from ifelse() and say which one a given problem needs.
2 Read a function’s help page and write a function with explicit inputs and a return value.
3 Explain where R looks for a name, and why a function that reads a global variable is not reproducible.
4 Validate inputs with stopifnot(), stop(), and guard clauses.
5 Write a function that takes a data frame and a column name.
6 Refactor a copy-pasted script into functions, and verify the intended output is unchanged.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Session outline







Section
Focus




1. Conditions
Why branching is needed; scalar, vector, missing, and empty conditions


2. Why functions?
Repeated code and an input/output contract


3. Function basics
Read an interface; build, trace, and extend a summary function


4. Scope
Local names and hidden global dependencies


5. Validation
Guard clauses and predictable edge cases


6. Data-frame functions
Fixed, bare, and quoted column names


7. Refactoring and reuse
Compose helpers, compare results, and load saved functions


8. Exit check
Explain and apply the contract



The section numbers below follow this outline.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A calculation can run and still be wrong
text:
A calculation can run and still be wrong
A script receives four baseline readings but only two follow-up readings. It should flag the mismatch before calculating paired changes.

baseline <- c(150, 140, 160, 155)
followup <- c(138, 132)
followup - baseline

[1] -12  -8 -22 -23









Situation
What the script should do




Different numbers of readings
Flag the mismatch and skip the calculation


Equal numbers of already matched readings
Calculate follow-up minus baseline



R reused the two follow-up values and returned four changes without a warning. We need one decision about whether the calculation should run at all.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: More than two cases: else if

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A vector is not one decision
text:
A vector is not one decision

if (trial$sbp_0 > 140) "above cutoff" else "at or below cutoff"

Error in if (trial$sbp_0 > 140) "above cutoff" else "at or below cutoff": the condition has length > 1



head(trial$sbp_0 > 140)

[1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

length(trial$sbp_0 > 140)

[1] 60


There is one comparison per participant, but if requires one decision. The repair depends on the intended question: one label per participant, or one answer about the whole group? The cutoff is only a coding example.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
One label per participant: ifelse()

above <- trial$sbp_0 > 140
labels <- ifelse(above, "above cutoff", "at or below cutoff")
head(data.frame(sbp = trial$sbp_0, above, label = labels))

  sbp above              label
1 160  TRUE       above cutoff
2 162  TRUE       above cutoff
3 157  TRUE       above cutoff
4 157  TRUE       above cutoff
5 146  TRUE       above cutoff
6 127 FALSE at or below cutoff

length(labels)

[1] 60


ifelse() makes an elementwise choice: one comparison and one returned label per participant. This is the vectorized conditional introduced in Session 3.
It repairs the preceding code if the goal is a label for every row.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: One group decision: any() or all()

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Match the tool to the question
text:
Match the tool to the question



Intended result
Tool




One action based on a single condition
if (...) ... else ...


One label for each value
ifelse(test, yes, no)


One action if at least one value meets a rule
if (any(test)) ...


One action if every value meets a rule
if (all(test)) ...



An if expression can also supply a value for assignment:

label <- if (n_missing > 0) "missing outcomes present" else "no missing outcomes"
label

[1] "missing outcomes present"

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A missing condition is a separate problem

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Missing values in a group decision
text:
Missing values in a group decision

x <- c(120, NA, 155)
c(observed = sum(!is.na(x)),
  any_observed_above = any(x > 140, na.rm = TRUE),
  all_observed_above = all(x > 140, na.rm = TRUE))

          observed any_observed_above all_observed_above 
                 2                  1                  0 


na.rm = TRUE changes the question to the observed measurements. It does not show what the missing measurements would have been.
Without removal, a missing comparison can leave any() or all() unresolved. Report the observed count alongside a result that excludes missing values.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: An empty condition is a separate problem

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Scalar and elementwise operators








Need
Operators
Example




Combine checks for each value
&, |
!is.na(x) & x > 140


Combine single decisions
&&, ||
length(x) > 0 && all(is.finite(x))




candidate <- NA_real_
is.numeric(candidate) && length(candidate) == 1 &&
  !is.na(candidate) && candidate > 0

[1] FALSE


&& stops when the left check is false. Put shape and missingness checks before a comparison that assumes one observed value.

text:
Practice 1: choose and repair
For each task, choose a vectorized conditional or one if decision.

Label every change as "decrease", "no decrease", or "missing".
Stop if a required column is absent.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: Look at what you have been doing
text:
Look at what you have been doing
# session 6 — baseline SBP by arm
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_0), sd = sd(sbp_0))

# session 7 — the same, after the join
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_12), sd = sd(sbp_12))

# session 8 — weight, to annotate the figure
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight_kg), sd = sd(weight_kg))

# coursework — age, for the baseline table
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age), sd = sd(age))

Four blocks. One name differs.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
What copy-paste actually costs








Cost
What repeated copies make harder




Reading
A reader has to diff four blocks to find the one word that differs


Changing
If missing values arrive, update the missing-value policy in every copy; overlooking one gives inconsistent summaries


Naming
The block has no name, so you cannot say what it does, reuse it, or check it


Divergence
If one copy later adds round(..., digits = 2) and the others do not, the reporting rules diverge











The preceding code does not round any results. Rounding is an example of a future change that must be kept consistent across copies.





By the end of today that block is one line:
summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_0)

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
A contract before code
For a reusable summary, decide what the caller can rely on.







Part
Decision




Input
A numeric vector, possibly containing missing values


Options
Rounding precision and whether to remove missing values


Output
Named values with a documented meaning for n


Edge cases
What happens with no observations or the wrong input type?



Quick discussion: should n count all rows or observed measurements? What label would make that choice clear?

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Read the parts of a function call
text:
Read the parts of a function call
Before writing a function, read the interface of one you already use.

median_result <- stats::median(x = c(120, NA, 140), na.rm = TRUE)
median_result

[1] 130





Part
Meaning in this call




stats::
Select the function from the stats package namespace


median
Function name


x = c(120, NA, 140)
Supply the data argument


na.rm = TRUE
Supply an option controlling missing values


Returned value: 130
The result, saved in median_result by <-

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Package namespaces identify which function
A namespace holds a package’s objects and keeps its names separate from those in other packages. package::function selects an exported function.







Explicit name
Purpose




stats::median()
Compute a median


dplyr::filter()
Select rows of a data frame


stats::filter()
Filter a time series, for example with a moving average




The package must be installed. :: loads its namespace as needed.
You do not need to call library() first.
An explicit package name avoids confusion when packages share a function name.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Parameters define the interface; arguments fill it
text:
Parameters define the interface; arguments fill it
Parameters, or formal arguments, are the names in the definition. The help page’s Usage section shows them and their defaults:
median(x, na.rm = FALSE, ...)








Parameter
Meaning
Argument in our call




x
Data to summarize; no default
c(120, NA, 140)


na.rm
Remove missing values? Default: FALSE
TRUE


...
Further arguments for methods; unused by the default method
None supplied



The Arguments section explains accepted inputs. Omitting na.rm uses FALSE; supplying na.rm = TRUE overrides that default.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: The return value is an object you can use
text:
The return value is an object you can use
Our call returned one numeric value, 130. We saved it in median_result. The help page’s Value section describes the result’s type and length.

typeof(median_result)

[1] "double"

length(median_result)

[1] 1

median_result + 10

[1] 140


Returning makes an object available to the caller. Printing displays it. Assignment stores the result without automatically printing it.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Read the help page as a function contract
text:
Read the help page as a function contract
help("median", package = "stats")
# Alternatively: ?stats::median







Help section
Question it answers




Description
What does this function do?


Usage
How do I call it? Which defaults apply?


Arguments
What does each input mean and accept?


Value
What object comes back? What happens in edge cases?


Details
Which additional rules or methods matter?


Examples / See Also
How is it used? Which related functions may help?



Section names vary: some pages describe the return value under Details.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Check the contract before running the code
text:
Check the contract before running the code
Use Usage, Arguments, and Value in ?stats::median to predict:

Which call removes the missing value?
Does an empty input return an empty vector or one missing value?



stats::median(c(120, NA, 140))

[1] NA

stats::median(c(120, NA, 140), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 130

stats::median(numeric(0), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] NA


The results are NA, 130, and NA, each of length one. Now give your own function an equally clear input/output contract.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Start with a calculation you can check
text:
Start with a calculation you can check
For three measurements, work out the answer before writing a function: n = 3, mean 130, and sample SD 10.

example_sbp <- c(120, 130, 140)
summary_reference <- c(n = length(example_sbp),
                       mean = mean(example_sbp), sd = sd(example_sbp))
summary_reference

   n mean   sd 
   3  130   10 


The calculation is already useful. The next step is to make it work for a different numeric vector without editing its body.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Decide which parts belong in the interface
text:
Decide which parts belong in the interface








Choice
Our decision
Reason




Which measurements?
Required parameter x
The caller must choose the data


How much rounding?
Optional digits = 1
A common display choice, with an override


What comes back?
Named numeric vector: n, mean, sd
All three results are numeric


Which inputs initially?
Complete numeric vectors with at least two values
Establish a simple working version first



Replace every use of example_sbp in the calculation with x. Do not give x a default that silently selects a dataset from your workspace.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Your first function, from your own code

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Check the original case, then change the input
text:
Check the original case, then change the input

identical(sbp_summary(example_sbp), summary_reference)

[1] TRUE


Predict what changes when every measurement increases by 10.


rbind(original = sbp_summary(example_sbp),
      shifted = sbp_summary(example_sbp + 10))

         n mean sd
original 3  130 10
shifted  3  140 10


The mean increases by 10; the count and SD stay the same.
Matching one example is necessary. Changing the input checks whether the function actually uses the argument you give it.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A function wrapper can still use the wrong data
text:
A function wrapper can still use the wrong data
Which calculations below ignore the supplied x?

bad_summary <- function(x) {
  return(c(n = length(x), mean = mean(example_sbp), sd = sd(example_sbp)))
}



rbind(first = bad_summary(c(10, 20, 30)),
      second = bad_summary(c(100, 200, 300)))

       n mean sd
first  3  130 10
second 3  130 10




Only the count uses x. The mean and SD still read the external vector. Repair both references; expect means of 20 and 200 after the repair.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Call the same function with different inputs
text:
Call the same function with different inputs

sbp_summary(trial$sbp_0)

    n  mean    sd 
 60.0 149.5  11.9 

sbp_summary(trial$sbp_12)

    n  mean    sd 
 60.0 141.6  15.1 

sbp_summary(trial$weight_kg, digits = 2)

    n  mean    sd 
60.00 83.22 15.76 




Three calls, one definition. Here we deliberately add a digits argument and round the reported summaries; the earlier duplicated code did not round them.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
text:
Trace one function call
sbp_summary(c(120, 130, 140), digits = 1)

Bind x to the supplied vector and digits to 1 for this call.
Evaluate the function body using those local arguments.
Create local result: n = 3, mean = 130, and sd = 10.
return(round(result, digits)) sends the rounded result to the caller and ends the call.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Inspect the returned answer

answer <- sbp_summary(c(120, 130, 140), digits = 1)
answer

   n mean   sd 
   3  130   10 

answer["mean"]

mean 
 130 


Defining the function stores the recipe. Calling it runs the recipe.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Missing data requires an explicit design decision
text:
Missing data requires an explicit design decision
Suppose the new input is c(120, NA, 140). What should n mean?



Policy
Observed count
Reported mean
Reported SD




Keep missingness in the calculation
2
NA
NA


Summarize the observed measurements
2
130
About 14.1



We will define n as the observed count and add na_rm = TRUE as the default. The caller can choose FALSE to preserve missingness in mean and SD.
The count and the missing-data rule are separate decisions. State both.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
text:
Use or override a default

sbp_summary(trial_raw$sbp_12)

    n  mean    sd 
 57.0 141.3  15.3 

sbp_summary(trial_raw$sbp_12, na_rm = FALSE)

   n mean   sd 
  57   NA   NA 



A default is what the argument is when the caller says nothing. Choose the safe, common case — then let the caller override it.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
How R matches arguments
Three ways, tried in this order: exact name, then partial name, then position.

sbp_summary(trial$sbp_0, 2)                 # position

     n   mean     sd 
 60.00 149.47  11.85 

sbp_summary(digits = 2, x = trial$sbp_0)    # exact name — order stops mattering

     n   mean     sd 
 60.00 149.47  11.85 



Partial matching works, and is a trap:

report <- function(x, na_rm = FALSE, names = TRUE) return("ok")
report(1, n = TRUE)

Error in report(1, n = TRUE): argument 2 matches multiple formal arguments










House rule: data argument by position, everything else by full name. Partial names break the day somebody adds an argument.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: Choose a return shape for the next step
text:
Choose a return shape for the next step








Return shape
Useful when
Caller extracts a result with




One number
The next step needs only one statistic
Use the result directly


Named numeric vector
Several results share a numeric type
answer["mean"]


Named list
Results need different types or structures
answer$mean



Our sbp_summary() returns a named numeric vector. A future report might also need a text status or a table; that would justify a list.
Choose and document the shape before writing downstream code. Changing it later can break callers even if the numbers are unchanged.
c(mean = 130, status = "ok") makes both entries character. A list can retain the numeric mean and a character status separately.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Return several results in one list

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Use the returned components

description <- describe_measurements(c(120, NA, 140))
description$n_observed
description$n_missing
description$mean




Component
Value
Meaning




n_observed
2
Two measurements are available


n_missing
1
One measurement is missing


mean
130
Mean of 120 and 140; the missing value is excluded



description holds the list; $ selects a named component. Section 5 adds the policy for empty or entirely missing input.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Practice 2: one summary, four named results
text:
Practice 2: one summary, four named results
Write sbp_summary_missing(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE) for x <- c(120, NA, 140). Assume at least two observed numeric values.



Name
Meaning
Expected value




n
Observed count
2


n_missing
Missing count
1


mean
Mean of observed values
130


sd
Sample SD of observed values, rounded
14.1



Return one named numeric vector with these four components. Keep the counts unchanged when na_rm = FALSE; mean and SD then become NA. Use an explicit return() at the end.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Practice 2: build and return the summary
text:
Practice 2: build and return the summary

sbp_summary_missing <- function(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE) {
  counts <- c(n = sum(!is.na(x)), n_missing = sum(is.na(x)))
  estimates <- c(mean = mean(x, na.rm = na_rm),
                 sd = sd(x, na.rm = na_rm))
  return(c(counts, round(estimates, digits)))
}
answer <- sbp_summary_missing(c(120, NA, 140))
answer

        n n_missing      mean        sd 
      2.0       1.0     130.0      14.1 


The result always has four named numeric components in this example. Counts are separate from the estimates that need rounding.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Practice 2 extension: compute, then pass an argument
text:
Practice 2 extension: compute, then pass an argument

measurements <- c(10, NA, 14)
reference <- mean(measurements, na.rm = TRUE)
centered <- centre_values(measurements, centre = reference)
centered

[1] -2 NA  2

sum(centered, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0


The result is c(-2, NA, 2). The observed centered values sum to zero. The function still accepts one scalar center; the caller decides how to obtain it.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Extend the summary for a new reporting requirement
text:
Extend the summary for a new reporting requirement
A collaborator needs the missing count as well. Write sbp_summary_missing(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE).

Return a named numeric vector: n, n_missing, mean, sd.
Keep n as the observed count and preserve the existing missing-data option.
For c(120, NA, 140), expect c(2, 1, 130, 14.1) with those names.
Assume numeric input with at least two observed values for this first draft.

Which lines of the existing helper change? Which interface choices stay the same? Write your version before revealing the answer.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Use names to select the intended result
text:
Use names to select the intended result
Reorder the same four components. Which extraction still selects the mean?

reordered <- answer[c("mean", "sd", "n", "n_missing")]
rbind(
  by_name = c(original = answer[["mean"]],
              reordered = reordered[["mean"]]),
  by_position = c(original = answer[[3]],
                  reordered = reordered[[3]])
)

            original reordered
by_name          130       130
by_position      130         2


Both vectors have length 4. [["mean"]] gives 130 in either order; [[3]] gives 130 in the original order but 2 after reordering.
Names express what the caller wants; positions depend on the current order.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
What happens inside stays inside

centre_sbp <- function(x) {
  offset <- mean(x)      # local to this call
  return(x - offset)
}

centred <- centre_sbp(trial$sbp_0)
round(head(centred, 4), 1)

[1] 10.5 12.5  7.5  7.5

exists("offset", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)

[1] FALSE




Every call gets a fresh evaluation environment. Ordinary local assignments do not change objects in the global workspace.









<<- writes to the enclosing environment and defeats all of this. You will meet it in inherited code. Do not write it.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Forward additional arguments with ...
... collects arguments you did not name and passes them on:

mean_sbp <- function(x, ...) return(mean(x, ...))

mean_sbp(trial_raw$sbp_12)

[1] NA

mean_sbp(trial_raw$sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 141.3158

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Return a value without automatically printing it
text:
Return a value without automatically printing it
Use return(invisible(value)) to return a value without automatic printing. Explicit output such as cat() still appears:

report_n <- function(data) {
  cat("n =", nrow(data), "\n")
  return(invisible(nrow(data)))
}

report_n(trial)          # prints the message, not the value

n = 60 

n_rows <- report_n(trial)

n = 60 

n_rows

[1] 60

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Where R looks for a name
text:
Where R looks for a name





flowchart LR
  L["<b>1. Inside the call</b><br/>locals and arguments"] --> D["<b>2. Where the function<br/>was DEFINED</b><br/>usually the global env"]
  D --> P["<b>3. Attached packages</b><br/>dplyr, ggplot2, …"]
  P --> B["<b>4. base</b>"]
  B --> E["Error:<br/>object not found"]
  style L fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style D fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style E fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70













Step 2 is where the function was written, not where it was called from. That is what “lexical” means.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
The global that vanishes

threshold <- 140

is_high <- function(sbp) return(sbp > threshold)   # threshold is not an argument

sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))

[1] 50



It works. Now restart R — or hand the script to a colleague:

rm(threshold)
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))

Error in is_high(trial$sbp_0): object 'threshold' not found





This is the honest failure. It is annoying, and it tells you immediately.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A hidden input changes the answer
text:
A hidden input changes the answer
This version reads threshold from outside the function. It looks up that variable each time it is called; it does not keep its original value.

threshold <- 140
is_high <- function(sbp) return(sbp > threshold)
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))

[1] 50



A sensitivity analysis changes the external variable. The same call now uses that new value:

threshold <- 160        # for the sensitivity analysis
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))

[1] 8










The data and function definition are unchanged. The answer changes because threshold is a hidden input: the first call uses 140 and the second uses 160.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Everything comes in through an argument
text:
Everything comes in through an argument

# Flag patients above a systolic threshold. Threshold is an argument so the
# result depends only on what the caller passed.
is_high <- function(sbp, threshold = 140) {
  return(sbp > threshold)
}

sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))

[1] 50

sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0, threshold = 160))

[1] 8









The rule: a function’s return value should depend only on its arguments. Nothing else.






The sensitivity analysis is now a second call, visible on the page, instead of a reassignment fifty lines away.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Practice 3: find the hidden input
reference_mean <- 130
adjust <- function(x) return(x - reference_mean)
first <- adjust(c(120, 140))
reference_mean <- 150
second <- adjust(c(120, 140))

Predict first and second.
Rewrite adjust() so the reference value is a required argument.
Explain why restarting R exposes only some global-dependency problems.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: Fail loudly, or be wrong quietly
text:
Fail loudly, or be wrong quietly

mean_weight <- function(weight_kg) return(mean(weight_kg))

mean_weight(trial_raw$weight_kg)   # one weight is recorded as -99

[1] 80.275

mean_weight(trial$weight_kg)       # the same cohort, repaired

[1] 83.22




80.3 kg against 83.2 kg. Both are plausible. Only one is right, and the function had no opinion about which.









Important


A function that fails loudly on bad input is safer than one that returns a plausible wrong answer.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: Give failed checks a useful message

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
text:
How much validation is enough








Check
Because




Type and shape
is.numeric(), is.data.frame(), length(), column names present


Values that cannot be real
Negative weights, ages over 120, proportions above 1


What your code silently assumes
Sorted rows, one row per patient, non-empty groups






mean("a") warns and returns NA; it does not stop. Validate numeric input when a missing result would hide a data-type error.









Rule of thumb: validate what a collaborator’s file could plausibly get wrong. Two or three checks is usually right.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Specify the edge cases
Our safe_mean() contract accepts numeric vectors with finite values or NA/NaN. It returns one numeric value and ignores missing observations.



Input
Required behavior




c(2, 4, NA)
Return 3


numeric(0)
Return NA_real_


c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
Return NA_real_


"4", a matrix, or a data frame
Stop with a useful message


c(2, Inf)
Stop because infinity is outside this contract



NA_real_ explicitly creates numeric missingness. c(NA, NA) is logical, so use typed missing values when constructing a numeric teaching column.

title: Conditions and Functions
Conditions and Functions
section: Trace the branch that ends the call
text:
Trace the branch that ends the call
Follow safe_mean() from top to bottom. Stop tracing when a guard exits.



Input
First exit
Result
Does mean() run?




"4"
Type guard: stop()
Error
No


c(2, Inf)
Infinite-value guard: stop()
Error
No


c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
return(NA_real_)
One numeric NA
No


c(2, NA, 4)
Last expression
3
Yes



For numeric(0), the first two guards pass and all(is.na(x)) is TRUE. The early return supplies one numeric NA, not an empty vector.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Explain why the shorter version changes the contract
text:
Explain why the shorter version changes the contract

mean_shortcut <- function(x) return(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
mean_shortcut(numeric(0))

[1] NaN

safe_mean(numeric(0))

[1] NA


Both run. The first returns NaN; our helper returns NA_real_ by design.
Ask which behavior a report expects, and document it. A shorter implementation is useful only if it preserves the intended input and output rules.

Data argument first
When the column names are fixed, nothing special is needed:

# Add change from baseline; check the required columns before computing.
add_change <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data),
            all(c("sbp_0", "sbp_12") %in% names(data)))

  return(data |> mutate(change = sbp_12 - sbp_0))
}

trial_raw |> add_change() |> summarise(mean_change = mean(change, na.rm = TRUE))

  mean_change
1   -7.614035




Data first, so the function drops into a pipeline like any dplyr verb.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: A quoted column name with base R
text:
A quoted column name with base R

summarise_column <- function(data, column) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), is.character(column),
            length(column) == 1, !is.na(column),
            column %in% names(data))
  return(safe_mean(data[[column]]))
}
summarise_column(trial_raw, "sbp_12")

[1] 141.3158


data[[column]] looks up the value of column. data$column looks for a column literally named column.
Use {{ outcome }} for a bare-name dplyr interface and [[column]] for a quoted-name base R interface. State which interface the function expects.

section: Before: the script we all wrote
text:
Before: the script we all wrote
# baseline
tab_0 <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(sbp_0), 1), sd = round(sd(sbp_0), 1))

# 12 weeks
tab_12 <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(sbp_12), 1), sd = round(sd(sbp_12), 1))

# change — use the extract with missing outcomes
tab_ch <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(change, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            sd = round(sd(change), 1))     # <- na.rm missing here

ggplot(trial_raw, aes(arm, sbp_0)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(y = "SBP baseline")
ggplot(trial_raw, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(y = "SBP 12 wk")

Six blocks, two shapes, inconsistent missing-value rules. n = n() counts rows, including rows missing the outcome.

# One boxplot of an outcome by arm, labelled for a clinical reader.
plot_by_arm <- function(data, outcome, y_label) {

    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, width = 0.5) +

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Verify the refactor
A refactor preserves intended behavior. Fix a known bug separately, then compare the function with that corrected reference. Check.

old <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(sbp_0)),
            mean = round(mean(sbp_0), 1),
            sd = round(sd(sbp_0), 1))

new <- summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_0)

identical(old, new)

[1] TRUE

all.equal(old, new)

[1] TRUE

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Interpret the comparison

identical() checks exact equality. all.equal() returns TRUE or a description of differences. Use isTRUE(all.equal(old, new)) for a logical check.

title: Conditions and Functions
section: Compose two functions for paired measurements
text:
Compose two functions for paired measurements

classify_change <- function(change) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(change), is.null(dim(change)))
  out <- rep("missing", length(change))
  observed <- !is.na(change)
  out[observed & change < 0] <- "decrease"
  out[observed & change >= 0] <- "no decrease"
  return(out)
}
classify_change(c(-2, 1, NA, 0))

[1] "decrease"    "no decrease" "missing"     "no decrease"


This returns a character vector even for zero rows. It describes the sign of change, not whether a change is clinically meaningful.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
A reusable paired-change calculation

change_summary <- function(baseline, followup) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(baseline), is.null(dim(baseline)),
            is.numeric(followup), is.null(dim(followup)),
            length(baseline) == length(followup),
            !any(is.infinite(baseline)), !any(is.infinite(followup)))
  change <- followup - baseline
  return(data.frame(change = change, category = classify_change(change)))
}
change_summary(c(10, 8, NA, 12), c(8, 9, 7, 12))

  change    category
1     -2    decrease
2      1 no decrease
3     NA     missing
4      0 no decrease


Precondition: the two vectors refer to the same people in the same order. Equal lengths do not establish patient alignment; join by ID first when needed.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
Practice 5: verify the refactor
Before replacing the repeated code, write down the expected table.
baseline <- c(10, 8, NA, 12)
followup <- c(8, 9, 7, 12)
expected <- data.frame(
  change = c(-2, 1, NA, 0),
  category = c("decrease", "no decrease", "missing", "no decrease")
)

Compare change_summary(baseline, followup) with expected.
Try two empty numeric vectors. What are the output column types?
Try unequal lengths. Why should recycling be an error here?

text:
Practice 5: evidence before replacement

expected <- data.frame(
  change = c(-2, 1, NA, 0),
  category = c("decrease", "no decrease", "missing", "no decrease")
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  change_summary(c(10, 8, NA, 12), c(8, 9, 7, 12)), expected

'data.frame':   0 obs. of  2 variables:

Save a helper separately from the analysis
Keep reusable definitions in an .R file and analysis calls in your report:

Load the saved definition, then call it
In the saved report, with paths relative to its folder:
source("R/centre-values.R")
centre_values(c(10, NA, 14), centre = 12)
# [1] -2 NA  2

text:
Reuse should survive a fresh session

Copy the supplied R folder beside your report.
Put your other completed helpers in R/functions.R.
Add both source() calls to the report before the first function call.
Remove duplicate definitions from the report after checking equivalence.

title: Conditions and Functions
text:
House style for functions








Rule
In practice




Verbs for functions, nouns for objects
summarise_by_arm(), not arm_summary()


snake_case, no exceptions
plot_by_arm, not plotByArm


One job per function
If the name needs “and”, it is two functions


Make exits explicit
Use return(value) at every normal exit


Keep it focused
A long function is a reason to review its responsibilities


Data argument first
So it pipes


Validate inputs
Two or three checks, at the top


One line above saying what it does
What it takes, what it returns


Comments say why
The code already says what











All of this is in style-guide.md, §7. Code quality is graded on it.

Positron’s VS Code foundation
Positron builds on Code OSS, the open-source core of Visual Studio Code. Posit adds the R/Python Console, Variables, Plots, and Data Explorer.

VS Code serves a much broader developer community across many languages.
Its extension ecosystem offers a wide choice of AI assistants and advanced tools for debugging, Git, databases, testing, and remote development.
Positron can reuse many compatible extensions while providing a ready-made environment for data science.

Why this matters: a larger ecosystem means more options for extending your workflow. Availability and compatibility still depend on the specific tool.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
AI-assisted coding
Four parts, one workflow

Understand: how an LLM and a coding application work together.
Set up: choose a provider, mode, and permitted tools.

Verify: inspect the code, check the statistics, and disclose assistance.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
section: 1. Understand: the LLM and the application
text:
1. Understand: the LLM and the application
The AI model is usually a large language model (LLM), sometimes with image capabilities. It uses supplied context to generate responses, code, or tool requests.
The coding application lets you interact with the LLM. It gathers context, sends requests, displays responses, and can use tools to act on those responses.
R executes the R code. The LLM can propose a calculation without actually running it.
The same LLM can behave differently in applications with different context, tools, and permissions.

Models, applications, and tools in an agent workflow

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
section: What happens between typing and a result?
text:
What happens between typing and a result?







Step
Who does it?




You type, select code, or send a message
You provide an action or explicit request


Relevant code and instructions become model input
The application constructs a request


A continuation, explanation, edit, or tool request is generated
The LLM produces a response


Suggested text appears or a permitted tool runs
The application presents or acts on the response



You do not always type a question. The application can construct a request from what you type, select, or change.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Five interactions you may encounter








Interaction
What you do
What the application presents or does




Inline completion
Type code
Suggested continuation at the cursor


Next-edit suggestion
Change code
A predicted related edit


Chat / explanation
Ask a question
An answer or proposed code


Directed edit / inline chat
Request a specific change
An edit for review


Agent workflow
Request an outcome
Connected tool actions and results



The first two can start without an explicit user request. The last three respond to a request you express.

VS Code AI workflows · Completion and next-edit suggestions

Your action
Conceptual model request

Type write.csv(
“Given this code, what continuation is likely?”
An object, file path, and arguments


Change T1 to T001
“Given this edit and the nearby code, what related edit might follow?”
Change T2 to T002



The application displays the proposal for you to accept or dismiss.
A predicted edit is a guess about intent. Changing T1 does not establish that T2 should change too.

How inline suggestions use context

What you want back

Context: what information does AI receive?
Context is the information the application supplies for a model response. There are several ways information enters it:








Route
Example
What to check




Automatic context
Conversation, editor context, session metadata
Which features and settings are enabled?


You supply it
Paste an error, attach a plot, reference a file
Was it included, and was it truncated?


A tool retrieves it
Read a file, search code, inspect console output
Did a tool actually return the information?



Accessible is not the same as already read. An open tab or a named path does not prove the model has received the whole file.

In Posit Assistant
Ask mode
Regular agent work




Receive enabled session metadata (names/types)
Yes
Yes


Read/search files; inspect console history or plots
Available
Available


Edit files or execute R/Python

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
section: An agent works through a feedback loop
text:
An agent works through a feedback loop
An agent combines an LLM with tools and a feedback loop to pursue a task.
For “Fix the report and rerun it,” the workflow might be:

Read the report source and relevant input files.
Propose and apply a code change.
Run the report through an execution tool.
Read the error message or inspect the output.
Revise the code and check again.

The LLM proposes actions. The application runs permitted tools and returns their observations to the LLM.

Agent action-and-evaluation cycle

Depends on files and connections provided there


Typical workflow
Interactive work beside your editor

Workflow

What it may do

What happens

An automated reviewer allows or blocks actions

Four levels of explicit requests: the SBP example








Level
What you provide
What AI supplies

A fix or small change

text:
Level 1: revise existing code
The starter reads the CSV into trial and creates this plot object:
p <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
Debugging request: “I sourced this script, but the plot did not appear. Explain why and show the smallest fix.”
Editing request: “Color these points by treatment arm. Keep the axes.”
You provide the code and a specific change or problem.

section: Chat: where to ask and attach context
text:

Open Posit Assistant.
Enter /ask for a read-only discussion.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Level 1: discussion and directed editing
For an explanation: attach the code in Ask mode and ask why sourcing it shows no plot. Read the proposed fix and apply it yourself.
For an edit: request “Add arm colors and print the plot. Keep the variables unchanged.” In a workflow with editing tools, inspect the resulting code differences.
Both are level-1 requests. The difference is whether you want an answer or a change applied to the file.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Level 1: inspect the proposed change
p <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, color = arm)) +
  geom_point()
print(p)

print(p) displays the plot object when the script runs.
color = arm inside aes() maps treatment arm to colors.
Each point represents one patient’s baseline and week-12 SBP.
Three patients lack week-12 SBP. Account for their omitted points.

Check the explanation, the code change, and the result.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
section: Level 2: write code for a specified task
text:
Level 2: write code for a specified task

Using trial, make a scatterplot with baseline SBP on x and week-12 SBP on y. Color points by arm. Label both axes in mmHg and display the plot.

You have chosen the variables, plot type, grouping, and labels.
AI supplies the implementation. Chat can return code for you to run. An agent can write and run the script if asked.

From a specified plot to an analysis plan

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Level 4: review the proposed reasoning
A useful SBP plan should explain:

Whether it describes visit means, within-patient change, or both.
Why the chosen plots answer the question about change and arm differences.
How it preserves patient pairing across visits and handles missing SBP.
Whether descriptive summaries suffice or an inferential method is needed.

Visit means can involve different patients. A difference in visit means need not equal the mean paired change.
An agent can implement a reviewed plan. Successful execution does not validate its scientific reasoning.

4. Verify the work and its statistical meaning
Keep the same SBP data and inspect a plausible mistake.
The request: report the number of patients, observed week-12 SBP values, mean SBP, and SD by arm.
The trap: filtering missing SBP before counting changes the denominator.
We will predict the error, repair the code, check independently, and document the assistance.

title: Positron and AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Evaluating an AI coding workflow







Ask
Look for




What did it know?
The code, data, instructions, and context supplied


What did it do?
Suggested text, applied edits, or executed commands


What evidence supports the result?
Code differences, execution output, figures, and checks


Does it answer our question?
Correct quantities, pairing, missing-data handling, and interpretation



A successful run supports a claim about execution. Statistical validity requires additional reasoning.
Apply these questions to the week-12 SBP summary on the next slides.

# Using trial, report total n, observed n, mean and SD

# counting total n; omit them for the mean and SD.
These instructions can guide a completion or an explicit request. They specify the quantity you will verify.

trial |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_total = dplyr::n(),
    n_observed = sum(!is.na(sbp_12)),
    mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_sbp = sd(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = arm
  )
Both arms have 30 patients. Observed week-12 SBP counts are 28 Placebo and 29 Treatment.

title: Session 8 guided lab
text: Six questions, about 50–60 minutes. Work with a partner, take turns typing, and write your own short answers.

title: Session 8 guided lab
text:
Setup
Use the supplied synthetic marker data: 40 participants, 20 in each arm. One row is one participant. baseline and followup are marker measurements; change = followup - baseline. The marker has no specified clinical units or definition of improvement.
Work in BIOS6301-mywork.Rproj. Copy either the Quarto starter or R Markdown starter from the course materials to your personal work/session08/ folder. Choose one format. Run the supplied setup chunk before Q1.

title: Session 8 guided lab
text:
Q1. Base R boxplot
Create a boxplot of change by arm using participant.

Label the x-axis “Randomized arm” and the y-axis “Change in marker (follow-up minus baseline)”.
Overlay all 40 participant values with horizontal jitter. Keep their vertical values unchanged.
Add a dashed horizontal line at zero.

Answer: Which arm has the lower median change? What does a negative change mean?

title: Session 8 guided lab
section: Q2. The same boxplot with ggplot2
text:
Q2. The same boxplot with ggplot2
Create the same change-by-arm boxplot with ggplot2 and assign it to p.

Add geom_boxplot() and horizontally jittered participant points. Display each observation once.
Use the same axis labels and dashed zero line as Q1. Add the title “Marker change by randomized arm”.
Add a caption: “Synthetic data; one point per participant; 20 participants per arm.”

Answer: Do the two plots tell the same story? What do the points show that the boxes alone do not?

title: Session 8 guided lab
section: Q3. Save and check your figure
text:
Q3. Save and check your figure
Save p as change-by-arm.png and change-by-arm.pdf in an output/ folder.

Use 6 × 4 inches for both files and 300 DPI for the PNG.
Open both files. Check the labels, caption, and participant points. Make one improvement if needed and save again.

Answer: What are the PNG’s pixel dimensions? Why is a DPI setting unnecessary for the PDF’s vector lines and text?

title: Session 8 guided lab
text:
Q4. Base R histogram
Use hist() to draw a histogram of baseline for all 40 participants. Label the axes “Baseline marker” and “Number of participants”, and add a dashed vertical line at the sample mean.
Answer: Is the distribution roughly symmetric or noticeably skewed? What does the height of a bar represent?

title: Session 8 guided lab
text:
Q5. Baseline versus follow-up
Use ggplot2 to make a scatterplot of followup (y) versus baseline (x). Identify arm with both color and shape, label both axes, and add a dashed identity line (y = x). Save this plot as p_scatter.
Answer: What does a point below the line mean? Do all participants in the treated arm have lower follow-up values than baseline?

title: Session 8 guided lab
section: Q6. Compare distributions in separate panels
text:
Q6. Compare distributions in separate panels
Use ggplot2 to make histograms of followup, with one panel per arm. Use binwidth = 0.5, boundary = 0, and facet_wrap(~ arm). Keep the same x- and y-axis scales in both panels and label the axes.
Answer: Which arm’s follow-up distribution appears centered lower? Do the distributions overlap? Why keep the same bins and axis scales?

title: Session 8 guided lab
text:
Finish
Render or knit your completed report. Include the plots for Q1, Q2, Q4, Q5, and Q6, short answers to Q1–Q6, and the Q3 export code. Keep the PNG and PDF in output/ beside your report. Check that all plots appear in the HTML. Record one change made after opening the exported files, or state what you checked if no change was needed.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Why study data arrive in separate tables
text:
Why study data arrive in separate tables



File
One row represents
Typical identifier




Enrollment
A participant
Participant ID


Follow-up measurements
A participant at a visit
ID and visit


Site information
A study site
Site code



Different teams or systems may produce these files. A join connects related records using their identifiers.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Common reasons to join study data
text:
Common reasons to join study data

Add treatment assignment to each follow-up measurement.
Attach site names to a file containing only site codes.
Combine a baseline questionnaire with an outcome file.
Find enrolled participants who have no laboratory record.

Before choosing a function, decide which participants or measurements the result must retain.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Two tables from the same study
text:
Two tables from the same study


# A tibble: 4 x 2
  id    arm    
  <chr> <chr>  
1 P01   control
2 P02   treated
3 P03   treated
4 P04   control


# A tibble: 4 x 3
  id    marker_w0 marker_w4
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 P01         4.1       4.4
2 P02         5.2       4.7
3 P03         6         5.1
4 P05         4.8       4.9


Each table has one row per participant, but their participant lists differ.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Join keys
The by argument tells R which values identify a match.

patient_lookup |> count(id) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 0 x 2
# i 2 variables: id <chr>, n <int>

marker_wide |> count(id) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 0 x 2
# i 2 variables: id <chr>, n <int>


Zero rows here means no repeated IDs in that table.
A visit-level table can contain repeated IDs legitimately. Its row identifier would also need a visit variable.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Three joins for today’s work



Question
Function




Attach treatment to every measurement row
left_join()


Analyze only IDs represented in both files
inner_join()


List enrolled IDs with no lab record
anti_join()



left_join(x, y, by = "id") starts with x and matches its IDs against y.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: A left join, row by row
text:
A left join, row by row

course_joined <- marker_wide |>
  left_join(patient_lookup, by = "id")
course_joined

# A tibble: 4 x 4
  id    marker_w0 marker_w4 arm    
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  
1 P01         4.1       4.4 control
2 P02         5.2       4.7 treated
3 P03         6         5.1 treated
4 P05         4.8       4.9 <NA>   


P05 stays. Its arm is NA because the metadata table has no matching ID.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: The left table defines which records must stay
text:
The left table defines which records must stay
Suppose the question is: which enrolled participants have measurements?

patient_lookup |> left_join(marker_wide, by = "id")

# A tibble: 4 x 4
  id    arm     marker_w0 marker_w4
  <chr> <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 P01   control       4.1       4.4
2 P02   treated       5.2       4.7
3 P03   treated       6         5.1
4 P04   control      NA        NA  


P04 stays with missing measurements. P05 is outside this enrollment list.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: An inner join changes the retained participants
text:
An inner join changes the retained participants

marker_wide |> inner_join(patient_lookup, by = "id")

# A tibble: 3 x 4
  id    marker_w0 marker_w4 arm    
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  
1 P01         4.1       4.4 control
2 P02         5.2       4.7 treated
3 P03         6         5.1 treated


Three participants remain. P05 is absent.
Example: a planned analysis requires records from both the questionnaire and outcome files. An inner join restricts to their matching IDs. It does not guarantee that every variable in those records is observed.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Unmatched records in both directions

marker_wide |> anti_join(patient_lookup, by = "id")

# A tibble: 1 x 3
  id    marker_w0 marker_w4
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 P05         4.8       4.9

patient_lookup |> anti_join(marker_wide, by = "id")

# A tibble: 1 x 2
  id    arm    
  <chr> <chr>  
1 P04   control


The first result asks who lacks metadata. The second asks whose metadata has no measurements.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Joining records or stacking batches?







Files contain
Operation




Enrollment and lab results for overlapping participants
Join by the appropriate ID


The same lab columns for two different recruitment batches
Stack the rows with bind_rows()



A join matches records. Stacking adds observations with the same variables.
A worked bind_rows() example follows in the optional join block.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Duplicate lookup rows can repeat measurements
text:
Duplicate lookup rows can repeat measurements

extra_lookup <- tibble(
  id = c("P01", "P01"), arm = c("control", "treated")
)
marker_wide |> filter(id == "P01") |>
  left_join(extra_lookup, by = "id")

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  id    marker_w0 marker_w4 arm    
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  
1 P01         4.1       4.4 control
2 P01         4.1       4.4 treated


Which treatment label is correct? Resolve that from the data source. Keeping the first row would make an unsupported choice.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
A short join checklist

What does one row represent in each input?
Which columns identify the intended match?
Does the lookup have repeated keys?
How many rows remain, and which IDs failed to match?


c(before = nrow(marker_wide), after = nrow(course_joined))

before  after 
     4      4 


Here the lookup ID is unique, so four measurement rows stay four.

section: Optional examples: a larger synthetic study
text:
Optional examples: a larger synthetic study
The next slides use a separate synthetic dataset:

trial: 60 participants, one row per participant.
sites: one row per site, missing site 4 and including unused site 5.
labs: two visits per participant.
sites_dup: a conflicting extra record for site 2.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: Six joins, two kinds











Join
Keeps
Adds columns from y?




Mutating
left_join(x, y)
every row of x
yes



inner_join(x, y)
rows matched in both
yes



right_join(x, y)
every row of y
yes



full_join(x, y)
every row of either
yes


Filtering
semi_join(x, y)
rows of x with a match
no



anti_join(x, y)
rows of x without a match
no





The split is the useful thing here. A mutating join changes the columns and may change the rows. A filtering join changes only the rows — it is filter() with the condition stored in another table.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: Other joins in practice







Study task
Choice




Reconcile two participant lists and retain every ID from either source
full_join()


Keep cohort rows whose IDs appear in an eligibility list, without adding its columns
semi_join()


Preserve the second table in a join
right_join(), or swap inputs to left_join()



A full join can expose records that exist in only one source.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: The other three

c(left  = nrow(left_join(trial, sites, by = "site")),
  inner = nrow(inner_join(trial, sites, by = "site")),
  right = nrow(right_join(trial, sites, by = "site")),
  full  = nrow(full_join(trial, sites, by = "site")),
  semi  = nrow(semi_join(trial, sites, by = "site")),
  anti  = nrow(anti_join(trial, sites, by = "site")))

 left inner right  full  semi  anti 
   60    45    46    61    45    15 





full_join gives 61 — the 60 patients plus one all-NA patient row carrying site 5.
right_join(x, y) is left_join(y, x) with the columns in a different order. Use left_join and swap the arguments — then the table your analysis is about is always on the left.
semi_join gives 45 rows and the same columns as trial. Compare with inner_join, which gives 45 rows and two more columns.

text:

assay_demo <- tibble(id = c("P01", "P01", "P02"),
                     week = c(0L, 4L, 0L),
                     assay = c(10, 12, 20))
visit_demo |>
  left_join(assay_demo, by = c("id", "week"),

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Optional: What happens when week is omitted?
text:
Optional: What happens when week is omitted?

visit_demo |>
  left_join(assay_demo, by = "id",
            relationship = "one-to-one")

Error in `left_join()`:
! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
i Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.


Both tables contain repeated IDs for a valid reason. Correct the join key, rather than deleting valid visits.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Optional: Row counts in an equality join
text:
Optional: Row counts in an equality join
For each row of x, let m be its number of matches in y.



Join
Rows contributed by that row of x




inner_join()
m

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Optional: Relationships depend on both directions
text:
Optional: Relationships depend on both directions







Expected relationship
Match limit




one-to-one
Each row on either side matches at most one on the other


many-to-one
Each x row matches at most one y row


one-to-many
Each y row matches at most one x row


many-to-many
Multiple matches can occur in both directions



Many patients can share a site. A unique site lookup therefore supports a many-to-one patient-to-site join.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: Many-to-one: the safe case
sites has at most one row per site, so 60 rows in, 60 rows out.

nrow(trial)

[1] 60

nrow(left_join(trial, sites, by = "site"))

[1] 60



We are entitled to expect that only because we checked:

sites |> count(site) |> filter(n > 1)

[1] site n   
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)










A common lookup task is many-to-one: many patients, one lookup row each. When a join is supposed to be many-to-one and is not, you have found a data error — not a join problem.

    id     arm week creat
1 P001 Placebo    0  1.13
2 P001 Placebo   12  1.15
3 P002 Placebo    0  1.26
4 P002 Placebo   12  1.15




This is correct and often exactly what you want — the result’s grain is now one row per patient-visit. But every patient-level column is now repeated. A mean on this table weights patients by their visit counts. Here everyone has two visits, so it equals the patient-level mean.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Optional: Many-to-many: rows multiply by accident
text:
Optional: Many-to-many: rows multiply by accident
sites_dup contains two conflicting records for site 2 (240 versus 245 beds).

nrow(left_join(trial, sites_dup, by = "site"))

Warning in left_join(trial, sites_dup, by = "site"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and
`y`.
i Row 6 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
i Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
i If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.


[1] 78



Site 2 has 18 patients. 60 + 18 = 78.








Eighteen patients are now in the data twice. Patient counts are inflated and summaries or models can change — and the only visible symptom is a row count that nobody looked at.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: Predict, then check
Write the prediction into the code. It costs one line:

joined <- left_join(trial, sites, by = "site")
stopifnot(nrow(joined) == nrow(trial))



joined_bad <- left_join(trial, sites_dup, by = "site")
stopifnot(nrow(joined_bad) == nrow(trial))

Error: nrow(joined_bad) == nrow(trial) is not TRUE





stopifnot() is session 12 material — borrowed here as a one-liner. It does nothing when the condition holds and stops the render when it does not, which is exactly what you want from an assumption.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: The relationship argument
State what you believe, and let the join enforce it:

left_join(trial, sites_dup, by = "site", relationship = "many-to-one")

Error in `left_join()`:
! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
i Row 6 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.




Four values: "one-to-one", "one-to-many", "many-to-one", "many-to-many". The last one is not a safety rail — it is how you tell dplyr you meant it, and it silences the warning.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Optional: The unmatched argument

left_join(trial, sites, by = "site", unmatched = "error")

Error in `left_join()`:
! Each row of `y` must be matched by `x`.
i Row 4 of `y` was not matched.




Read the message carefully. For a left_join(), rows of x are never dropped — so unmatched= guards the only side that can lose rows: y. It just told us site 5 is unused.



To assert that every patient matched, use the diagnostic:

nrow(anti_join(trial, sites, by = "site")) == 0

[1] FALSE

Optional: merge() gotchas








Behaviour
Consequence




sort = TRUE by default
The result is reordered by the key. dplyr preserves x’s order


Omitted by
Matches all common column names; no common names gives a Cartesian product


Explicit by = NULL
Always requests a Cartesian product


Duplicated join keys
Can multiply rows; dplyr warns on unexpected many-to-many equality joins

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
What is tidyr?
tidyr helps organize data into a usable table:

Each variable has a column.
Each observation has a row.
Each cell holds one value.

Today: pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
Other tidyr tools split columns or make missing rows explicit. They are optional here.

section: When to change long measurements to wide
text:
When to change long measurements to wide
We have one measurement per participant-week, but want to:

Calculate week-4 minus baseline marker in one row.
Display baseline and follow-up values side by side.
Supply one row per participant to a model using separate visit predictors.

pivot_wider() makes a column for each requested week. Each participant-week cell needs one value or an explicit summary rule.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Long to wide with pivot_wider

marker_back <- marker_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = id,
    names_from = week,
    values_from = marker,
    names_prefix = "marker_w"
  )

id_cols identifies an output row. names_from supplies column names. values_from supplies cell contents.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data

The two pivots: main arguments








Role
pivot_longer()
pivot_wider()




Input
Wide table
Long table


Columns / row identity
cols = starts_with("marker_w") selects columns to gather
id_cols = id identifies each output row


Column names
names_to = "week" creates a column holding the old names
names_from = week uses values to build new column names


Measurements
values_to = "marker" names the new value column
values_from = marker supplies the output cell values


Prefix
names_prefix = "marker_w" removes this prefix
names_prefix = "marker_w" adds this prefix



In this example, longer repeats the unselected id column for each week. Wider uses id_cols (plural) to group those weeks into one row per ID.
