4 "p04 "  "control"  

" p01 " == "P01"

[1] FALSE


Our study’s documented ID convention is uppercase with no surrounding spaces. The raw export does not consistently follow it.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Spaces and capitalization

str_trim("  Repeat   visit ")

[1] "Repeat   visit"

str_squish("  Repeat   visit ")

[1] "Repeat visit"

str_to_lower("TREATED")

[1] "treated"

str_to_upper("p01")

[1] "P01"


str_trim() removes outer spaces. str_squish() also reduces internal whitespace to one space.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Cleaning inside mutate

patients_text <- raw_patients |>
  mutate(
    id = str_to_upper(str_trim(id)),
    arm = str_to_lower(str_squish(arm)),
    note = str_to_lower(str_squish(note))
  )

Keep raw_patients unchanged so the original values remain available.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
The cleaned text columns

patients_text |> select(id, arm, note)

# A tibble: 4 x 3
  id    arm     note         
  <chr> <chr>   <chr>        
1 P01   control first visit  
2 P02   treated repeat sample
3 P03   treated repeat visit 
4 P04   control first visit  


The IDs now match the study’s convention. Spacing and capitalization are consistent, while each participant keeps the same treatment category.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Detecting literal text

patients_text |>
  mutate(has_repeat = str_detect(note, fixed("repeat"))) |>
  select(id, note, has_repeat)

# A tibble: 4 x 3
  id    note          has_repeat
  <chr> <chr>         <lgl>     
1 P01   first visit   FALSE     
2 P02   repeat sample TRUE      
3 P03   repeat visit  TRUE      
4 P04   first visit   FALSE     


str_detect() returns TRUE/FALSE. fixed("repeat") requests a literal substring.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
A text condition inside filter

patients_text |>
  filter(str_detect(note, fixed("repeat"))) |>
  select(id, note)

# A tibble: 2 x 2
  id    note         
  <chr> <chr>        
1 P02   repeat sample
2 P03   repeat visit 


mutate() can retain the flag. filter() can retain just matching rows.
As in Session 6, filter() drops conditions that evaluate to NA.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Factor labels and level order
Session 4 introduced factor(), levels(), and relevel().
forcats provides functions for the same kinds of categorical-data tasks.

arm_factor <- factor(
  patients_text$arm, levels = c("treated", "control")
)
arm_factor

[1] control treated treated control
Levels: treated control


Each participant has a category. The factor also stores an order of levels.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
fct_relevel changes the level order

arm_ordered <- fct_relevel(arm_factor, "control")
levels(arm_ordered)

[1] "control" "treated"

as.character(arm_factor) == as.character(arm_ordered)

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE


The participant labels stay the same.
Under the usual treatment contrasts, the first level is the model reference.
For a full order: fct_relevel(x, "c", "b", "a").

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
fct_recode changes the labels

arm_labeled <- fct_recode(
  arm_ordered,
  Control = "control",
  Treatment = "treated"
)
arm_labeled

[1] Control   Treatment Treatment Control  
Levels: Control Treatment


The syntax is new_label = "old_label". This deliberately changes category labels, rather than only their order.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Factor operations inside mutate

patients_factor <- patients_text |>
  mutate(
    arm = fct_recode(arm,
      Control = "control", Treatment = "treated"),
    arm = fct_relevel(arm, "Control")
  )
patients_factor |> count(arm)

# A tibble: 2 x 2
  arm           n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Control       2
2 Treatment     2


fct_recode() can accept a character column and returns a factor.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Frequency order for a display

reported_site <- factor(c("East", "West", "West", "West", "East"))
levels(fct_infreq(reported_site))

[1] "West" "East"


fct_infreq() puts the most frequent level first.
Useful for displays. Use a deliberate scientific reference category for modeling.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Date parsers describe the input order
text:
Date parsers describe the input order

ymd("2026-10-18")

[1] "2026-10-18"

mdy("10/18/2026")

[1] "2026-10-18"

dmy("18/10/2026")

[1] "2026-10-18"


All three represent October 18, 2026.
Choose the parser using the source’s date convention.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: An ambiguous date still needs a decision
text:
An ambiguous date still needs a decision

mdy("03/04/2026")

[1] "2026-03-04"

dmy("03/04/2026")

[1] "2026-04-03"


Both conversions succeed, but they mean different days.
A parser cannot tell you which convention the data producer intended.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
section: Parsing a column and extracting components
text:
Parsing a column and extracting components

patients_clean <- patients_factor |>
  mutate(
    enrolled_date = ymd(enrolled),
    enrolled_year = year(enrolled_date),
    enrolled_month = month(enrolled_date)
  )

The original text column remains available for checking.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Dates and their components

patients_clean |>
  select(id, enrolled_date, enrolled_month)

# A tibble: 4 x 3
  id    enrolled_date enrolled_month
  <chr> <date>                 <dbl>
1 P01   2026-09-01                 9
2 P02   2026-09-03                 9
3 P03   2026-10-01                10
4 P04   2026-10-02                10


enrolled_date contains Date values. enrolled_month contains month numbers.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
One connected analysis

analysis <- marker_long |>
  left_join(
    patients_clean |> select(id, arm, enrolled_date),
    by = "id"
  )

The measurement table defines the rows. The cleaned metadata supplies each participant’s treatment label and enrollment date.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
The week-4 summary

analysis |> filter(week == 4) |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(mean_marker = mean(marker), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 3 x 2
  arm       mean_marker
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Control           4.4
2 Treatment         4.9
3 <NA>              4.9


P05 still has missing metadata. Keep that visible and investigate.

title: Joining, Reshaping, and Cleaning Data
text:
Summary

dplyr joins match records by keys.
tidyr pivots change how measurements occupy rows and columns.
stringr cleans and searches text.
forcats distinguishes relabeling from level ordering.
lubridate parses dates using a known input convention.

Optional examples appear beside their related topics earlier in the deck. Choose the data operation that answers the study question.

title: Session 6 guided lab
text:
Note



Suggested use: tasks 1–7 are the core analysis-table route. Additional practice repeats only the verbs and ideas introduced in Session 6; unfinished items may be completed after lab.
Choose one format and copy either starter/dplyr-lab.Rmd or starter/dplyr-lab.qmd to work/session06/. Knit the .Rmd file or Render the .qmd file.
Work in BIOS6301-mywork.Rproj. Paths under work/ below belong to your personal repository. Copy starters from the separate BIOS6301-materials clone, leaving the course originals unchanged.

title: Session 6 guided lab
section: Setup: install once, load in each session
text:
Setup: install once, load in each session
In the Console, check whether dplyr is installed:
requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)
If the result is FALSE, install it once:
install.packages("dplyr")
For today’s lab, dplyr is sufficient. Alternatively, install.packages("tidyverse") installs the broader collection. Do not put installation commands in a report that runs them every time it renders.
The starter already includes this line; keep it in the report:
library(dplyr)
Installation puts the package on your computer. Loading makes its functions available in the current R session, including the fresh session used to render your report. library(tidyverse) attaches the core packages; it is not required for this lab.

If a loading message says “masked”
A message that dplyr masks filter or lag is normally informational, not an installation failure. Another package has a function with the same name.
Use the explicit name when needed:
dplyr::filter(visit, week == 4)
Here, dplyr:: identifies which package’s function you want. Run this example after the starter has created visit. It does not install the package.


Pipe shortcut (optional)
In RStudio, choose Tools → Global Options → Code and enable Use native pipe operator if available. Then Ctrl+Shift+M (Windows) or Cmd+Shift+M (macOS) inserts |>. Typing it directly also works.

title: Session 6 guided lab
text:
Tasks

State what one row represents. Use count() and filter() to confirm that (id, week) is unique.
Keep all week-4 records, including missing marker values, in an object named analysis. State this inclusion rule in one sentence.
In analysis, create observed = !is.na(marker) and a marker_band category using case_when(): "missing" for NA, "high" for marker at least 5, and "lower" otherwise. Put missingness first.
Produce one row per arm with total n, observed n, mean, SD, and proportion observed (n_observed / n). Return an explicitly ungrouped result.
Center marker values within arm with grouped mutate(), then ungroup(). Confirm that the transformation did not change the row count.
Arrange by arm, then decreasing marker with desc(marker); missing marker values should be last within each arm. Select id, arm, week, marker, observed, marker_band, and the centered marker for review.
Verify the arm-specific observed counts with base R and explain the unit of observation in the analysis table and summary table.

title: Session 6 guided lab
text:
Additional practice: interrogate the pipeline

Recreate the week-4 analysis table with base R. Sort both versions by ID and inspect them side by side.
Produce a missingness table by arm and week with total rows, observed marker rows, missing rows, and proportion observed.
Use count() to tabulate marker_band within arm. Confirm that the explicit "missing" category appears.
Use select(id, arm, starts_with("marker"), observed) and then rename() to give marker the name marker_value. Alternatively, store those column names in a character vector and use all_of().
Use across(c(week, marker), function(x) sum(is.na(x))) inside summarise() to count missing values in those two columns. The equivalent \(x) shorthand from the slides is also acceptable.
Summarize by arm and week with .groups = "drop". State the row unit of the result and why dropping the grouping is useful.
Run the supplied line visit_with_duplicate <- rbind(visit, visit[1, ]) to append an identical row. Diagnose it with count() and remove it with distinct() only after confirming that the entire row is duplicated. Do not use distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE): the original data contain two legitimate visits for each participant.


Independent-practice check
The base-R and dplyr week-4 tables should agree after deliberate sorting. The grouped transformation must preserve all six week-4 rows.

text:
Exit evidence
Render the code, validation checks, table, cross-dialect verification, and prose.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Import a delimited file with read.csv(), and state rather than guess what type each column should be.
2 Convert missing-value codes to NA at import, and say why the door is the right place to do it.
3 Diagnose a file that is not what it claims to be — wrong delimiter, header junk, wrong encoding.
4 Read a selected Excel table, a compressed CSV, or a large text file.
5 Choose between write.csv() and saveRDS(), and explain when saving several objects or a workspace is useful.
6 Parse dates, do arithmetic on them, and rescue Excel serial numbers.
7 Recognise the import failures that produce a wrong answer rather than an error.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Roadmap for today




Block




1
Inspect a file and make a first import


2
Missing codes and simple checks


3
Worksheet examples: titles, tables, and headers


4
Excel, compressed files, and large CSV files


5
Save objects and record data checksums


6
Read and check dates


7
Practice and summary




Blocks 1–3 are one habit repeated: look, then state your intent, then verify.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
What read.csv() actually does





flowchart LR
  F["<b>bytes on disk</b><br/>trial_export.csv"] --> D["split into<br/>lines and fields<br/><i>sep, quote, dec</i>"]
  D --> E["decode characters<br/><i>fileEncoding</i>"]
  E --> H["header row?<br/><i>header, skip</i>"]
  H --> M["which text<br/>means missing?<br/><i>na.strings</i>"]
  M --> G["<b>guess a type<br/>per column</b><br/><i>colClasses</i>"]
  G --> DF["data.frame"]
  style F fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style G fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style DF fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff







Six decisions, and you made none of them. Each argument named under a box is a place where R chose for you — correctly most of the time, and silently either way.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Look at the file before you read it
text:
Look at the file before you read it

Before importing: What does -99 mean? Is the date month-first? Should 001 stay as text?

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: A quick look at a large text file
text:
A quick look at a large text file

writeLines(readLines("data/trial_export.csv", n = 3))

"id","arm","sex","wt","sbp12","creat","visit_0","visit_12","dob_ser"
"P001","Placebo","M",90,144,"1.29","01/15/2023","04/12/2023",27512
"P002","Placebo","M",67.8,156,"NA","05/31/2023","08/24/2023",23496


Read a few lines first. Check the separator, column names, and unusual values.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: State the types instead of guessing
text:
State the types instead of guessing

raw <- read.csv(
  "data/trial_export.csv",
  colClasses = c(id = "character", arm = "character", sex = "character",
                 wt = "numeric", sbp12 = "integer", creat = "character",
                 visit_0 = "character", visit_12 = "character",
                 dob_ser = "integer")
)
str(raw[, c("id", "arm", "sbp12")])

'data.frame':   60 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ id   : chr  "P001" "P002" "P003" "P004" ...
 $ arm  : chr  "Placebo" "Placebo" "Placebo" "Placebo" ...
 $ sbp12: int  144 156 156 163 140 125 153 149 -99 149 ...




colClasses makes expected types explicit. An incompatible value in a declared numeric column fails at import. Check column names and dimensions separately; type declarations do not validate the whole file structure.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
“Missing” is written a dozen ways









In the file
Comes from
Import default




NA
R, or a well-behaved export
NA ✓


empty field
Excel, REDCap, almost everything
NA if numeric, "" if character


.
SAS
text → column becomes character


-99, -999, 999, 9999
Fortran-era CRFs, SPSS conventions
a number ✗


NULL, N/A, #N/A, n/a
databases, Excel formulas
text → character ✗


Unknown, Not recorded, Missing
free-text data entry
text → character ✗


-1 for a count, 0 for a date
a field that “cannot be blank”
a number ✗





Session 3 showed you how to find these. Today they never get in.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: na.strings — do it at the door
text:
na.strings — do it at the door

clean <- read.csv("data/trial_export.csv",
                  na.strings = c("NA", "", "-99", "999"))
summary(clean$wt)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  51.30   78.22   83.95   84.15   90.67  120.20       4 

colSums(is.na(clean))

      id      arm      sex       wt    sbp12    creat  visit_0 visit_12 
       0        0        2        4        2        3        0        0 
 dob_ser 
       0

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
What na.strings cannot fix

str(clean$creat)

 chr [1:60] "1.29" NA "1.16" "0.83" "1.16" "0.58" "1.14" "0.8" "0.86" ...

clean$creat[c(2, 12)]

[1] NA      "<0.30"




The three "NA" records became NA. The two "<0.30" records did not, because "<0.30" is not a missing value — it is a measurement below the assay’s limit of detection, and throwing it away is a modelling decision, not a cleaning one.









The column is still character. One unhandled value is enough — session 3.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Then prove it

summary(clean[, c("wt", "sbp12")])

       wt             sbp12      
 Min.   : 51.30   Min.   : 99.0  
 1st Qu.: 78.22   1st Qu.:133.0  
 Median : 83.95   Median :142.5  
 Mean   : 84.15   Mean   :141.3  
 3rd Qu.: 90.67   3rd Qu.:151.0  
 Max.   :120.20   Max.   :184.0  
 NA's   :4        NA's   :2      

table(clean$sex, useNA = "ifany")


   F    M <NA> 
  31   27    2 




na.strings states an intention. These two lines are the evidence. An import is not finished until the ranges are plausible and the NA counts are ones you can explain.

Delimiters and the decimal comma

writeLines(readLines("data/site4_export.csv", n = 2))

id;wt;sbp12
P061;90,4;160

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Inspect the file before writing the import
text:
Inspect the file before writing the import

Where is the actual header? Where is the first observation?
Is there one table, or several tables on the same sheet?
Are units or descriptions placed under the column names?
Are headers repeated halfway down the file?
Are there totals, notes, blank separators, or hidden rows?
Which columns identify observations, and what are their units?

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: A title row is not a variable name
text:
A title row is not a variable name

Read A3:C5: column names plus observations. Exclude the title and total.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Tell R where the table starts and ends
text:
Tell R where the table starts and ends
For the worksheet on the previous slide:
d <- readxl::read_excel("clinic.xlsx", range = "A3:C5",
                       col_types = c("text", "numeric", "date"))
For a CSV export of the same layout:
d <- read.csv("clinic.csv", skip = 2, nrows = 2,
              colClasses = c(id = "character"))
The Excel example assumes date cells are stored as Excel dates. Recheck the range when a new file arrives.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Two tables on the same sheet
text:
Two tables on the same sheet

A shared row number does not mean these records belong together.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Import each table separately
participants <- readxl::read_excel("study.xlsx", range = "A1:B5",
                                 col_types = c("text", "numeric"))
sites <- readxl::read_excel("study.xlsx", range = "D1:E4")

Prefer one table per sheet when requesting a new export.
Preserve the original; document the selected ranges in code.
Combine tables using a meaningful key—not row position.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Mixed single and multiple header rows
text:
Mixed single and multiple header rows

Which header row should R use? Neither row alone identifies every variable.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Give every column one unambiguous name
text:
Give every column one unambiguous name

Keep the source. Assign names when reading its data rows:
d <- readxl::read_excel("visits.xlsx", skip = 2,
  col_names = c("id", "weight_0", "sbp_0", "weight_12", "sbp_12"),
  col_types = c("text", rep("numeric", 4)))

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Row numbers are not participant identifiers
text:
Row numbers are not participant identifiers
Repeated exports may produce X, X.1, or ...1 columns.
names(d)
head(d)
rownames(d)

Determine whether these are export counters or real identifiers.
Keep real IDs in an explicit column; preserve leading zeros as text.
Remove an extra column only after confirming its meaning.
Export with write.csv(d, "clean.csv", row.names = FALSE).

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Header junk, and names R rewrites
text:
Header junk, and names R rewrites

writeLines(readLines("data/redcap_export.csv", n = 4))

Study 42 - Blood Pressure Substudy
Exported 2024-03-04 09:12 by s.zhao

Patient ID,Weight (kg),SBP @ 12wk,% change

read.csv("data/redcap_export.csv")

[1] "Patient.ID"  "Weight..kg." "SBP...12wk"  "X..change"

[1] "Patient ID"  "Weight (kg)" "SBP @ 12wk"  "% change"

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Excel via readxl
library(readxl)

# What sheets are in here?
excel_sheets("data/study42.xlsx")
#> [1] "ReadMe"  "Enrolment"  "Labs"  "Sheet3"

labs <- read_excel(
  "data/study42.xlsx",
  sheet = "Labs",
  range = "A4:H210",              # skip the title block, stop before the totals
  col_types = c("text", "text", "date", rep("numeric", 5)),
  na = c("", "NA", "-99")
)







Excel workbooks are usable inputs when the sheet, range, types, and meaning are documented. The example above illustrates an import contract for a hypothetical workbook.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Highlighting and totals are not observations
text:
Highlighting and totals are not observations

If yellow means “exclude,” add an exclude column and a reason. Keep the mean row out of the participant data.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Names and types: inspect what actually arrived
text:
Names and types: inspect what actually arrived

Blank or duplicate column names may be repaired during import.
Names like Weight (kg) need careful access or documented renaming.
00123 can become 123 if the source treats an ID as numeric.
A displayed date or rounded value may hide a different stored value.

names(d)
anyDuplicated(names(d))
str(d)
# Preserve a source name, then rename deliberately:
d[["Weight (kg)"]]

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
readr::read_csv()
library(readr)
d <- read_csv("data/trial_export.csv")
#> Rows: 60 Columns: 9
#> -- Column specification ------------------------------------
#> chr (6): id, arm, sex, creat, visit_0, visit_12
#> dbl (3): wt, sbp12, dob_ser

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Declare column types and missing-value codes
text:
Declare column types and missing-value codes

That message is the best thing about it — the parser tells you what it decided, every time. Then you replace the guess with a contract:

d <- read_csv(
  "data/trial_export.csv",
  col_types = cols(id = col_character(), wt = col_double(),
                   visit_0 = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y")),
  na = c("", "NA", "-99")
)
# the base R way
read.csv("data/trial_export.csv", colClasses = c(id = "character"),
         na.strings = c("", "NA", "-99"))

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Compressed CSV files: .csv.gz
.gz means the file is compressed. It does not change the table’s meaning.
d <- read.csv("visits.csv.gz",
              colClasses = c(id = "character"))
R can read this directly; you do not need to unzip it first. Use the same checks for names, types, and missing values.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Large CSV files: data.table::fread()
# install.packages("data.table")  # once
d <- data.table::fread("large_visits.csv",
  colClasses = c(id = "character"),
  data.table = FALSE)
str(d)

A useful fast reader for large CSV/TSV files—not Excel workbooks.
data.table = FALSE returns the familiar data frame.
Faster reading does not replace checking the result.

text:
What CSV cannot carry

small <- data.frame(mrn = c("0042", "0007"),
                    visit = as.Date(c("2024-01-03", "2024-02-11")),
                    arm = factor(c("Placebo", "Treatment")))
write.csv(small, "data/small.csv", row.names = FALSE)
str(read.csv("data/small.csv"))

'data.frame':   2 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ mrn  : int  42 7
 $ visit: chr  "2024-01-03" "2024-02-11"
 $ arm  : chr  "Placebo" "Treatment"




Three columns in, three columns wrecked. A CSV holds text, and nothing else — no types, no factor levels, no attributes. write.csv() then read.csv() is a round trip through a format that cannot represent what you had.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Save a workspace when there is a reason
text:
Save a workspace when there is a reason

Useful when several related objects are needed to resume an analysis.
Especially helpful after expensive calculations or when preserving a result checkpoint together with its intermediate objects.
Save deliberately to a named file; document what it contains and when to load it.
Keep the generating code, input data, and software-version information too.

A workspace snapshot preserves R objects—not the entire computing environment. It supports reproducibility; it does not establish it by itself.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Several objects: save and restore explicitly
text:
Several objects: save and restore explicitly
# Illustrative objects from a completed analysis:
save(clean_data, fitted_model, results,
     file = "analysis-checkpoint.RData")

# Later, in a fresh R session:
load("analysis-checkpoint.RData")

save() stores selected objects under their current names.
save.image("workspace-checkpoint.RData") stores the global workspace.
load() restores saved names and can overwrite existing objects.
Record sessionInfo() in the report to document R and package versions.

Which exact data file produced this report?

1 trial_export.csv 6d06f10032c2327361a9a00e091ce6eb


Put this chunk in the .Rmd or .qmd report before importing the file. The rendered table records a fingerprint of the input file’s contents.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
section: Use the checksum as a record, not a data-quality test
text:
Use the checksum as a record, not a data-quality test

Different MD5 values mean the file contents differ.
The same MD5 is strong practical evidence of unchanged bytes for routine version checking, not a security guarantee.
A filename change alone does not change the checksum.
Formatting, line endings, or workbook metadata can change it even when the analytical values appear unchanged.
A checksum neither validates the data nor replaces keeping the original file.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
A date is a number

d <- as.Date("2024-03-04")
class(d)

[1] "Date"

as.numeric(d)

[1] 19786

d + 84

[1] "2024-05-27"




A Date is days since 1970-01-01, stored as a number and printed as a date. That is why d + 84 works and why d1 - d2 gives you an interval.









A character column that looks like a date supports none of this. "2024-03-04" + 84 is an error, and "03/04/2024" < "12/31/2023" is TRUE.

Code
Means
Matches




%Y / %y
year, 4-digit / 2-digit
2024 / 24

month, as a number
03

month name, short / full
Mar / March

%b and %B are locale-dependent. A French export gives you mars, and your parse returns NA.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
3/4/24

x <- c("3/4/24", "12/31/23", "7/15/24")
as.Date(x, format = "%m/%d/%y")

[1] "2024-03-04" "2023-12-31" "2024-07-15"

as.Date(x, format = "%d/%m/%y")

[1] "2024-04-03" NA           NA          




The first value parsed both ways, silently, into different dates. The other two failed loudly under the wrong format — because 31 and 15 cannot be months.









A day-first file read as month-first is wrong on every date where both parts are ≤ 12 — about a third of the year — and correct-looking everywhere else.

Reference: SPSS and Stata via haven
library(haven)

d <- read_sav("data/study42.sav")     # SPSS   .sav
d <- read_dta("data/study42.dta")     # Stata  .dta
d <- read_xpt("data/adsl.xpt")        # SAS transport  .xpt

[1] 27512 23496 22594

             origin = "1899-12-30"), 3)

[1] "1975-04-28" "1964-04-29" "1961-11-09"







Workbook
Serial 1 is
origin =




Windows Excel, and everything modern
1900-01-01
"1899-12-30"


Legacy Mac Excel (pre-2011)
1904-01-02

Use the wrong one and every date lands four years and a day out — plausibly, and with no warning.

title: Getting Data In: Files, Import Checks, Dates
text:
Reference: Times, and time zones

t1 <- as.POSIXct("2024-03-04 14:30:00", tz = "America/Chicago")
as.numeric(t1)                                     # seconds since 1970

[1] 1709584200

format(t1, tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)

[1] "2024-03-04 20:30:00 UTC"

difftime(as.POSIXct("2024-03-04 14:30:00", tz = "UTC"), t1, units = "hours")

Time difference of -6 hours




POSIXct is seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC. A time with no tz uses your machine’s zone — so the same code gives different answers on different laptops.







Always name the zone. "America/Chicago", not "CST".

text:
Reference: lubridate, the friendlier version
library(lubridate)

ymd("2024-03-04");  mdy("03/04/2024");  dmy("4 March 2024")   # named parsers
year(d); month(d); day(d); wday(d, label = TRUE)              # components
d + days(84);  d %m+% months(3)                               # safe arithmetic
interval(dob, visit) / years(1)                               # exact age
with_tz(t1, "UTC");  force_tz(t1, "UTC")                      # two different jobs


# the base R way
as.Date("03/04/2024", format = "%m/%d/%Y")
as.numeric(format(d, "%Y"))



mdy() versus dmy() puts the ambiguity in the function name, where a reader can see it. That is the real gain, not the typing.

Note



Suggested use: complete the eight core tasks first. Additional practice provides a second pass through the same containers, indexing, factor, ordering, and grouped-summary concepts; unfinished items may be completed independently.

title: Session 4 guided lab
text:
Tasks

State the unit of observation. Use table() to confirm that there is one row for every (id, week) combination.
Compare visit["marker"], visit[["marker"]], and visit$marker using class(), typeof(), and length().
Convert visit$grade to a factor with the protocol levels mild, moderate, severe, and life-threatening, in that order. Use levels() and table() to show that an unobserved protocol category is still retained.
Safely reverse the complete grade-level order by rebuilding the factor from its character labels. Verify that the observed labels did not change. Then make a separate copy and try the tempting but incorrect levels(x) <- ... approach; display several rows and explain what it changed.
Select week-4 observations without removing rows that have missing markers. Add observed and marker_at_least_5 without overwriting supplied columns.
Use table() and tapply() to report, separately by arm, total n, observed n, and mean observed marker.
Inspect the supplied participant-by-week marker matrix. Select week 4 using drop = FALSE and explain why its dimensions are preserved.
Apply the five-check routine from class: str(), dim(), summary(), table(..., useNA = "ifany"), and colSums(is.na(...)).

title: Session 4 guided lab
section: Additional practice: repeat the base-R workflow
text:
Additional practice: repeat the base-R workflow

Store visit, week4, the arm means, and marker_matrix in a named list. Extract the arm means with [, [[, and $; describe the resulting structures.
Convert visit$arm to a factor whose first level is control, then use relevel() to make treated the reference. Verify that the observed labels remain unchanged while the level order changes.
Subset the relevelled factor to treated observations, then use droplevels() and compare the levels before and after dropping the unused level.
Select one row from week4 and one column from marker_matrix, both with drop = FALSE. Report their classes and dimensions.
Sort week4 first by arm and then by decreasing marker, keeping all columns together so that each row remains one participant record.
Calculate the arm-specific observed mean once with tapply() and once with aggregate(). State what rows with missing marker contribute to each result.
Make a copy with one impossible marker value of -10. Use summary() to find the problem, repair the copy, and confirm the original object was unchanged.


Independent-practice check
Your results should show how the choice among [, [[, and $ changes the returned structure, how drop = FALSE preserves dimensions, and why safe factor reordering differs from assigning new text directly to levels().

Exit evidence
Render the row/key statement, structure comparisons, factor levels and label comparison, analysis table, summary, matrix dimensions, and five-check output.

What biostatisticians use R to do



Import and validate study data
Reshape and derive analysis variables
Summarize cohorts and missingness
Fit statistical models



Create publication-quality graphics
Run simulation and resampling studies
Automate repeated analyses
Produce reproducible reports









R is both a statistical language and a computing environment. The same language carries an analysis from raw data to a report that can be rerun.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: An R session is a running process
text:
An R session is a running process
The current session contains temporary state:



Objects held in memory
Attached packages
Options and locale



Current working directory
Open connections
Random-number-generator state



Saved .R, .Rmd, .qmd, and data files remain after the session ends. Objects that exist only in memory do not.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: Inspect the workspace before trusting it
text:
Inspect the workspace before trusting it
age <- c(54, 61, 72)
arm <- c("A", "B", "A")

ls()          # names of objects in the current environment
class(age)    # the object's user-facing class
typeof(age)   # how R stores it
str(age)      # compact structure and a preview

The Environment pane is a convenient view. These functions are the reproducible, scriptable view.

Remove an object—or restart the process
rm(arm)              # remove one named object
ls()

rm(list = ls())      # remove all visible objects

rm(list = ls()) does not reset attached packages, options, connections, the working directory, or every other form of session state.






Use targeted rm() while exploring. Use Session → Restart R when testing whether an analysis really starts cleanly.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
There are no scalars
R has no single-number type. 42 is a vector of length one.

length(42)

[1] 1

length("hello")

[1] 1

x <- c(4, 9, 16)
sqrt(x)

[1] 2 3 4









sqrt(x) did not loop. The function applied to the whole vector at once. That is what “vectorized” means, and it is why R code for data analysis contains so few loops.

text:
Four types you will actually use










Type
Looks like
typeof()
Holds




logical
TRUE, FALSE, NA
"logical"
Conditions, flags, filters


integer
1L, 1:10
"integer"
Counts, indices, IDs


double
1, 3.14, 1e-8
"double"
Everything measured


character
"F", "P001"
"character"
Labels, IDs, free text






c(typeof(TRUE), typeof(1L), typeof(1), typeof("F"))

[1] "logical"   "integer"   "double"    "character"





There are two more — complex and raw. You will not meet them this term.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Integer or double?

typeof(3)

[1] "double"

typeof(3L)

[1] "integer"

typeof(1:3)

[1] "integer"




.Machine$integer.max + 1L

Warning in .Machine$integer.max + 1L: NAs produced by integer overflow


[1] NA










Use doubles. Write 3, not 3L. Integers matter in three places: memory for very large data, 1:n sequences, and reading someone else’s code.

Function
Answers with

class()
"numeric", "character", "data.frame"

"double", "integer", "list"

NA, NaN, Inf, NULL











Means
Comes from
Test with

Not available — a value exists, we do not know it
Missing data
is.na()


NaN
Not a number — the arithmetic is undefined
0/0, log(-1)
is.nan()

Infinite — too big, or divided by zero

c(1 / 0, -1 / 0, 0 / 0)

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
NA is contagious

creat <- as.numeric(creat_raw)
mean(creat)

[1] NA




mean(creat, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0.9385455

sum(is.na(creat))

[1] 5










na.rm = TRUE is not a fix. It is a decision — to analyse a different set of patients than the one you enrolled. Report how many you dropped.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
NA == NA is not TRUE

NA == NA

[1] NA

creat[7] == NA

[1] NA



Two unknown values. Are they equal? Unknowable. So R returns NA.

is.na(creat[7])

[1] TRUE





NA & FALSE

[1] FALSE

NA | TRUE

[1] TRUE

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
One vector, one type
An atomic vector holds one type. Combine types and R does not complain — it picks the type that can hold everything.







flowchart LR
  L["<b>logical</b><br/>TRUE FALSE"] --> I["<b>integer</b><br/>1L 2L"]
  I --> D["<b>double</b><br/>1.5 3.14"]
  D --> C["<b>character</b><br/>"a" "1.5""]
  style L fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style I fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style D fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style C fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff









Coercion runs left to right only. One character element and the whole vector is character. There is no way back that R will find for you.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
c(1, 2, "3")

c(1, 2, "3")

[1] "1" "2" "3"




typeof(c(TRUE, 1L))

[1] "integer"

typeof(c(1L, 1.5))

[1] "double"

typeof(c(1.5, "a"))

[1] "character"










No error. No warning. No message. The quotes in the output are the only evidence anything happened.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Where this actually bites
Three cells in a creatinine column hold the text "NA". Two hold "<0.30".

str(creat_raw)

 chr [1:60] "1.49" "0.54" "0.7" "1.27" "0.64" "1.11" "NA" "1.39" "0.75" "1" ...

creat_raw[c(7, 12)]

[1] "NA"    "<0.30"

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: Two failures from a text column
text:
Two failures from a text column

mean(creat_raw)

Warning in mean.default(creat_raw): argument is not numeric or logical:
returning NA


[1] NA




sum(creat_raw > 1.2)

[1] 14





Nine patients have a creatinine above 1.2. The count says fourteen: as text, both "NA" and "<0.30" sort above "1.2".

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
as.numeric() and what it costs

creat <- as.numeric(creat_raw)

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

sum(is.na(creat))

[1] 5




R warned. But look at the count: five NAs, from three "NA" cells and two "<0.30" cells. The warning does not say which.




creat_raw[is.na(creat)]

[1] "NA"    "<0.30" "NA"    "NA"    "<0.30"








After every coercion: print the values that became NA. One line, and it turns a warning into information.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: The one coercion that is a gift
text:
The one coercion that is a gift
TRUE is 1 and FALSE is 0, so arithmetic on logicals is counting.

sum(arm == "Treatment")

[1] 30

mean(sex == "F")

[1] 0.5166667




sum(is.na(creat))

[1] 5

round(100 * mean(sbp_0 > 140), 1)

[1] 78.3





sum() of a logical is how many. mean() of a logical is what proportion. You will use both constantly.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Sentinel values
The source system codes “not recorded” as -99.

mean(weight_kg)

[1] 68.72667




range(weight_kg)

[1] -99.0 114.4

weight_kg[weight_kg == -99] <- NA
mean(weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 80.70714










The first number is a plausible adult weight. It is wrong, and nothing warned you. No coercion, no error, no NA — a valid mean of invalid numbers.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Names
A vector’s elements can carry names, and names are a way to index.

sbp <- c(P001 = 152, P002 = 138, P003 = 161, P004 = 144)
names(sbp)

[1] "P001" "P002" "P003" "P004"

sbp["P003"]

P003 
 161

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: Look up several names—or a missing name
text:
Look up several names—or a missing name

sbp[c("P001", "P004")]

P001 P004 
 152  144 

sbp["P999"]

<NA> 
  NA 




A name that does not exist gives NA, not an error. Silent again.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Four ways to subset




By
Looks like
Returns




Position
x[c(1, 3)]
Elements 1 and 3


Negation
x[-1]
Everything except element 1


Logical
x[x > 140]
Elements where the condition is TRUE


Name
x["P003"]
The element called P003






One operator, [, and four meanings, decided by what type you put inside it.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Position, and negation

sbp_0[1:3]

[1] 160 163 154

sbp_0[c(1, 60)]

[1] 160 160




length(sbp_0[-1])

[1] 59

length(sbp_0[-(1:10)])

[1] 50





sbp_0[c(-1, 2)]

Error in sbp_0[c(-1, 2)]: only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
The workhorse: logical subsetting

high <- sbp_0 > 160
head(high, 8)

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

length(sbp_0[high])

[1] 13




mean(sbp_12[arm == "Treatment"])

[1] 133.9

mean(sbp_12[arm == "Placebo"])

[1] 147.2





arm == "Treatment" is a logical vector of length 60, used as a mask over a different vector of length 60. This one line is the base-R equivalent of filter() plus summarise().

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
x[NA], x[FALSE], x[0]

x <- c(a = 10, b = 20, c = 30)
x[NA]

<NA> <NA> <NA> 
  NA   NA   NA 

x[FALSE]

named numeric(0)




x[0]

named numeric(0)

x[10]

<NA> 
  NA 










x[NA] returns three NAs — the logical NA is recycled to length 3. x[FALSE] returns nothing at all. These are different failures with very different symptoms.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Subsetting on the left of <-

w <- c(78.2, -99, 91.5, -99, 84.0)
w[w == -99] <- NA
w

[1] 78.2   NA 91.5   NA 84.0




sbp_flag <- rep("normal", 5)
sbp_flag[c(152, 138, 161, 144, 130) > 140] <- "high"
sbp_flag

[1] "high"   "normal" "high"   "high"   "normal"





The same four ways of subsetting work on the left-hand side. This is how you repair a column in place.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
which()
which() converts a logical vector into positions.

which(sbp_0 > 175)

[1] 46

id[which(sbp_0 > 175)]

[1] "P046"




which.max(sbp_0)

[1] 46

id[which.max(sbp_0)]

[1] "P046"





which() silently drops NAs. That is convenient, and it is a difference from logical subsetting you must know about.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: %in%: the one that never returns NA
text:
%in%: the one that never returns NA

c(1, NA, 3) == 1

[1]  TRUE    NA FALSE

c(1, NA, 3) %in% 1

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE




sites <- c("VUMC", "MCV", "typo", NA)
sites %in% c("VUMC", "MCV")

[1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE










Use %in% for set membership, == for a single comparison. %in% always returns TRUE or FALSE — never NA — which makes it safe inside [.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
The rule
When two vectors have different lengths, R repeats the shorter one to match.

c(10, 20, 30) + 1

[1] 11 21 31

sbp_0[1:4] * 2

[1] 320 326 308 300




You have been relying on this since your first line of R. x * 2 is a length-60 vector plus a length-one vector, recycled sixty times.




c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: When it divides evenly, R says nothing
text:
When it divides evenly, R says nothing
Two arms, sixty patients. You want a per-arm baseline correction.

correction <- c(2, 5)             # Placebo, Treatment
adjusted <- sbp_0 - correction
adjusted[1:6]

[1] 158 158 152 145 153 144




Intended: subtract 2 from the 30 placebo patients, 5 from the 30 treatment patients. Actual: alternating 2, 5, 2, 5 down all sixty rows.









60 is a multiple of 2, so no warning. Every patient got a number. Half of them got the wrong one.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: When it does not, R warns
text:
When it does not, R warns

c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)

Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20): longer object length is not a multiple of
shorter object length


[1] 11 22 13




longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length — a warning, not an error. The result is still returned and assigned.









This warning is one of the most valuable messages R produces. If you have warning: false in your YAML and have never read your warnings once, you will never see it.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: ifelse() is a function. if is not.
text:
ifelse() is a function. if is not.










ifelse(test, yes, no)
if (cond) ... else ...




Is a
vectorized function
control-flow keyword


Test length
Any — one answer per element
Exactly one TRUE or FALSE


Returns
A vector as long as test
Whatever the chosen branch returns


Used for
Deriving a variable from a column
Choosing what a script does


Taught in
Today
Session 11











They look alike, share four letters, and do unrelated jobs. Today we use ifelse(). if does not appear on any slide in this session.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
ifelse()

bp_group <- ifelse(sbp_0 > 140, "high", "normal")
head(bp_group, 6)

[1] "high" "high" "high" "high" "high" "high"

table(bp_group)

bp_group
  high normal 
    47     13 




adjusted <- sbp_0 - ifelse(arm == "Treatment", 5, 2)
adjusted[c(1, 2, 31, 32)]

[1] 158 161 150 130





The second line is the recycling bug from block 5, fixed — because the condition is length 60, so the answer is length 60.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Three ways ifelse() surprises you

ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE, NA), "yes", "no")

[1] "yes" "no"  NA   




ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(1, 2, 3), 0)

[1] 1 0





ifelse(c(FALSE, TRUE), 1, "x")

[1] "x" "1"





NA in the test gives NA out · the result is as long as the test, not the branches · and the branches are coerced to one type.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: Everything today was a silent wrong answer
text:
Everything today was a silent wrong answer
Session 1: the two ways an analysis fails. It won’t run — annoying, honest. It runs and is wrong — dangerous.









Today’s bug
What R said
What you got




c(1, 2, "3")
Nothing
A character vector


creat_raw > 1.2
Nothing
14 patients above 1.2. There are 9


"<0.30" coerced
A warning you will skim
Two patients silently missing


mean(weight_kg) with -99
Nothing
A plausible, wrong mean


sbp_0 - c(2, 5)
Nothing
Half the cohort mis-adjusted


x["P999"]
Nothing
NA where you expected a value


ifelse(cond, 1, "x")
Nothing
Numbers turned into text











Seven bugs. One warning between them. This is why class(), str(), range(), and length() are habits and not commands.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Summary

Atomic vectors have one type and R coerces toward a common type.
NA propagates; test it with is.na() rather than equality.
Logical indexing expresses inclusion rules directly.
Recycling can return plausible results without an error.
ifelse() is vectorized classification; scalar control flow arrives in Session 11.


Next connection: Session 4 combines vectors into matrices, lists, factors, and data frames.

Important

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
1. Verify Git
The following commands are one-time setup checks, not syntax to memorize.
Open RStudio, select the Terminal tab, and run:
git --version
Copy the output. If the command is not recognized, install the current version of Git and restart RStudio.
On Windows, use the regular Git for Windows Setup installer and accept its default credential-helper option. Do not choose Portable Git for the standard course setup: portable or application-bundled Git copies may omit GCM or may not configure it for the Windows account.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
2. Configure your commit identity
First, check whether Git already has an identity for you:
git config user.name
git config user.email
If both values are present and correct, do not change them. Students with previous Git experience may already have appropriate settings.
If either value is missing or incorrect, set the default identity for new commits on this computer:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "EMAIL_ASSOCIATED_WITH_GITHUB"
Then verify the effective values:
git config user.name
git config user.email






Important



This is not your GitHub username, password, or login.

user.name is normally your human-readable name.
user.email is recorded in every new commit together with your name.
GitHub can connect the commit to your account when the email is verified on that account. You may instead use the private noreply address shown under GitHub → Settings → Emails.
GitHub authentication is a separate browser sign-in covered in Step 4.

Never place a password or access token in user.name or user.email.


The --global option makes these values the default for repositories used by your computer account. A repository-specific setting can override them later. Changing the setting affects future commits; it does not rewrite earlier commits.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
3. Verify RStudio can find Git
In RStudio, open Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN.
Confirm that:

Enable version control interface for RStudio projects is checked; and
a path appears beside Git executable.


The exact Git path depends on the operating system. The SSH-key field can remain empty because BIOS6301 uses HTTPS. Image source: Posit RStudio User Guide.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
section: 4. Prepare and check HTTPS browser authentication
text:
4. Prepare and check HTTPS browser authentication
This course uses HTTPS repository URLs. GitHub does not accept an ordinary account password for Git pushes. A credential helper will authenticate through GitHub in a browser and store the resulting credential securely.
You need one of the following methods, not both.

Method A: Git Credential Manager
Current Git for Windows includes Git Credential Manager (GCM), but GCM is not included with every Git installation on every operating system. Check for it:
git credential-manager --version
A successful check prints a version number. Blank output is not success. If a version is displayed, authenticate in a browser before class:
git credential-manager github login --username YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME --browser
git credential-manager github list
The second command should list the GitHub account saved by GCM. Do not display, copy, or submit any token.
If git credential-manager is unavailable on Windows, update Git using the official Git for Windows installer and keep its default Git Credential Manager option. This includes cases where the command prints nothing. Alternatively, keep the portable Git copy and use Method B.


Method B: GitHub CLI
GitHub CLI is a supported alternative on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Install GitHub CLI and verify:
gh --version
Then authenticate through the browser and configure Git to use that login:
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web
gh auth setup-git
gh auth status --active --hostname github.com
When asked whether Git should use your GitHub credentials, answer Yes. The final command should display the active GitHub username and report that the account is logged in. Do not use the --show-token option.






Note



There is no HTTPS username-and-password test analogous to ssh -T git@github.com. That command tests an SSH key, while this course uses HTTPS. Browser login followed by the GCM account list or gh auth status is the appropriate preparation check. The first Push to your private repository in the supervised lab remains the final end-to-end test.


If neither method is ready, bring the error message to class. You can still complete local Git work, but the course’s browser-based private Push/Pull workflow is not ready until an HTTPS credential helper is configured.

GitHub’s new-repository form with the repository-name field highlighted

Choose a license: None

Initialize it with a README and the R .gitignore template. This creates an initial branch. We will clone it as a separate project; no course history or instructor remote is needed. If it is already empty, add README.md on GitHub before cloning.
Have its HTTPS URL available:
https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git

GitHub repository header with the Settings tab highlighted


Then:

In the left sidebar under Access, select Collaborators.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub

7. Test access to the private repository
After creating the private repository, run this read-only command with your username substituted:
git ls-remote https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git
Copy the command from the code block and replace only YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME. The URL must be plain text: do not include Markdown brackets or parentheses such as [https://...](https://...).
This may open the browser sign-in prepared in Step 4. A successful check should list the repository’s branch and commit identifier. No authentication error means that Git can read the private repository using the configured HTTPS helper. This command does not modify or clone the repository.






Warning



If the Terminal asks for Username and Password instead of opening a browser, press Ctrl+C. Do not enter your GitHub password: GitHub does not accept account passwords for Git operations. Return to Step 4, complete either the GCM browser login or the GitHub CLI browser login, and then retry this command.


This is the closest useful HTTPS preparation test for this course. It tests the actual private repository rather than a public URL, which would not require authentication. The supervised first Push remains the test of write access.

# BIOS6301 Session 1: a small reproducible analysis

clinic <- data.frame(
  patient_id = 1:6,
  group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"),
  age = c(52, 61, 47, 70, 58, 64),
  marker = c(8.2, 7.5, 9.1, 6.8, 7.9, 7.2)

title: Homework 2: Data dictionary
text:
Study and file layout
The intended observation unit is one participant, with baseline and follow-up measurements in separate columns. The study has 24 participants, with IDs "001" through "024". The export includes one accidentally repeated record. Identify it by inspecting the data; do not remove records merely because an ID appears more than once.
The first two lines are descriptive notes. The third line contains column names; all later lines are records. There are no totals or footer rows. The delimiter is a comma, the decimal mark is a period, and dates use year-month-day.








Variable
Meaning
Import type and rules




id
Participant identifier
Character; preserve all three digits


arm
Study arm
Character initially; control or treated


age
Age at baseline, in years
Numeric; complete


sbp_baseline
Baseline systolic blood pressure, mmHg
Numeric after applying the missing-value rules


sbp_followup
Follow-up systolic blood pressure, mmHg
Numeric after applying the missing-value rules


date_baseline
Baseline visit date
Character; no date calculation required here


date_followup
Follow-up visit date
Character; no date calculation required here

title: Homework 2: Data dictionary
text:
Missing-value rules
In the blood-pressure columns, . and NM both mean not measured. Treat both as NA; neither means zero. They do not occur in other columns. A visit date can be recorded even when blood pressure was not measured.
There are no intentionally invalid dates or undocumented numeric corrections. Do not infer or invent missing measurements.

title: Homework 2: Data dictionary
text:
Analysis definitions

Include all unique participants; there is no age restriction.
change = sbp_followup - sbp_baseline, in mmHg.
Change is observed only when both measurements are available.
Negative change indicates a decrease; zero indicates no change.
Calculate means among participants with observed change. Keep participants with missing change in the analysis table and the total participant counts.

These data were constructed for the course, not sampled from a real study. Arm comparisons are descriptive exercises, not evidence of treatment efficacy.

Study vectors
The starter supplies four parallel vectors from a small, synthetic blood pressure study:
patient_id <- sprintf("P%02d", 1:12)
arm <- rep(c("control", "treated"), 6)
baseline_sbp_text <- c(
  "142", "138", "not recorded", "151", "133", "145",
  "128", "160", "139", "147", "136", "154"
)
week4_sbp_raw <- c(140, 128, 131, 143, 129, 136, 126, 18, 135, 139, NA, 142)
Each position refers to the same patient across all four vectors. The value "not recorded" represents a missing baseline measurement. Patient P08’s week-4 value was entered as 18; source verification established that it should be 148.

Install in this order
Use only the official links below. You do not need GitHub Desktop or a separate Git graphical interface. RStudio may offer to install the rmarkdown package the first time you Knit an .Rmd file; accept that prompt.

1. Install R
R is the program that performs the calculations. Choose your operating system from the official R download page:

Windows: Download R for Windows
macOS: Download R for macOS

Accept the standard installation options. If R is already installed, you do not need to reinstall it merely to complete this diagnostic.


2. Install RStudio Desktop
RStudio is the interface we will use during the opening sessions. Download the free, open-source edition from the official RStudio Desktop download page.
Install R before RStudio. Then start RStudio once and confirm that the Console opens without an error.


3. Verify document rendering
R Markdown and Quarto both turn a source document containing prose and R code into an HTML report. You may use either format for this diagnostic. RStudio uses Knit for .Rmd and Render for .qmd. If RStudio cannot render a .qmd file, use the official Quarto installation page and then restart RStudio.


4. Install Git using the course recommendation
Git records versions of analytical source files. We will use command-line Git through RStudio’s Terminal tab; we will not require GitHub Desktop.

Windows

Download Git for Windows.
Choose the standard 64-bit installer unless you know that your computer uses Windows on ARM.
Accept the installer defaults, including Git Credential Manager. It will provide browser-based GitHub authentication later in the course.
Completely close and reopen RStudio after installation.



macOS

Open Terminal.
Run:
git --version
If macOS offers to install the Command Line Developer Tools, accept the installation. If no prompt appears and Git is unavailable, run:
xcode-select --install

See the official Git installation instructions for macOS.


Linux
Use the Git package supplied by your Linux distribution. See the official Git installation page.



5. Verify Git inside RStudio
After restarting RStudio, select Tools → Terminal → New Terminal and run:
git --version
A successful result begins with git version. You do not need to create a GitHub account or configure GitHub authentication yet; that will happen before Session 2.






TipIf your computer requires administrator approval



Do not download an installer from an unofficial mirror. Submit the error or permission message and contact the course TA while there is still time to resolve the installation.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: R and RStudio are not the same
text:
R and RStudio are not the same


R

The statistical programming language
Performs calculations
Stores objects in a running R session
Can run without RStudio


RStudio

An integrated development environment, or IDE
Provides an editor, Console, plots, Help, projects, and Git tools
Sends instructions to R
Does not replace R









If RStudio opens but R is not installed or configured, the interface exists but there is no R engine available to execute your code.

section: R Markdown is the practical starting point
text:
R Markdown is the practical starting point
You will meet .Rmd constantly—in existing analyses, package vignettes, collaborators’ reports, and online examples. It remains a supported and widely used format for R-based reporting.







An R Markdown document combines narrative, executable R code, and computed results in one inspectable source file.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Anatomy of an .Rmd
---
title: "Baseline summary"
output: html_document
---

The report contains **prose** and computed results.

```{r summary, echo=FALSE}
clinic <- read.csv("data/clinic_summary.csv")
mean(clinic$age)
```

YAML configures the output; Markdown explains; R chunks compute.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
What .Rmd adds to an .R script







.R script
.Rmd document




R code and comments
Explanatory Markdown plus executable R chunks


Results appear in Console or plot device
Results are placed into a rendered report


Usually one stream of commands
Organized into named analytical sections


Excellent for reusable functions and pipelines
Excellent for an analysis narrative and report




These formats complement one another. A report may source() functions from an .R file while keeping the statistical explanation in .Rmd.

title: "Synthetic clinic summary"
author: "Student name"
date: "2026-11-02"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
---


YAML is between the opening and closing --- lines.
R Markdown uses the output: key.
Indentation expresses nesting; spaces after colons matter.
Start with HTML because it requires no LaTeX installation.

Apply the same document model in .qmd
These ideas do not change:

Markdown provides headings, prose, lists, and links.

knitr executes R chunks from top to bottom.
Inline R inserts calculated values into prose.
Source remains separate from generated output.
A complete render should not depend on objects left in the Environment pane.


Quarto changes selected authoring and publishing syntax; it does not change the R language or the logic of the analysis.

What rendering requires

Two things follow from this picture, and both matter:

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Inline code
Write this in your prose:
Mean baseline SBP was `r round(mean(trial$sbp_0), 1)` mmHg
in `r nrow(trial)` patients.

And it renders as:

Mean baseline SBP was 149.9 mmHg in 60 patients.









Important


This is the feature that removes an entire class of error. A number typed into prose by hand becomes wrong the moment the data changes — and nothing will tell you. A number computed inline cannot.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
A case worth knowing
Duke University, 2006–2011. Papers claimed that gene-expression signatures could predict which chemotherapy a patient would respond to. Three clinical trials enrolled patients on the strength of the work.

When Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes tried to reproduce the analyses, they reported problems including shifted gene indices, reversed sensitive/resistant labels, and analyses that could not be reconstructed from the stated methods.


The trials were suspended and stopped; multiple papers were retracted. The case contributed to a major review of how omics-based tests enter clinical use.
Detailed analysis: Baggerly & Coombes (2009). Timeline and policy review: Institute of Medicine (2012).

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Three words that get confused









Term
Means
Needs




Reproducible
Same data, same code → same result
Organized source and documented inputs


Replicable
New data, same question → same conclusion
A new study


Generalizable
The conclusion holds beyond the sample
Theory and external validity





Only the first is directly under the analyst’s control, and it is the minimum needed for someone else to evaluate the computation.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
The two ways analyses fail


It will not run
Missing files, unavailable data mounts, uninstalled packages, or undocumented manual steps.
Annoying, but visible.

It runs and is wrong
Wrong file silently read, stale object left in memory, or a result edited by hand.
Dangerous, because it looks finished.








A saved script and a document rendered from its source make the second class of failure easier to detect.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: Projects give the analysis a stable home
text:
Projects give the analysis a stable home
Use File → New Project → New Directory → New Project and create session01-lab.
session01-lab/
├── session01-lab.Rproj
├── analysis.R
├── report.Rmd
└── report.qmd


Opening the project establishes a predictable project root.
Relative paths are interpreted from that project context.
The project folder becomes a natural Git repository in Session 2.
Source files and input data remain distinct from generated output.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Paths are a design choice


Data inside the project
clinic <- read.csv(
  "data/clinic_summary.csv"
)
Relative paths are convenient for course-sized, shareable data.

Large or protected data elsewhere
data_root <- "D:/shared/study123"
clinic <- readRDS(file.path(
  data_root, "derived/cohort.rds"
))
An absolute root is often correct on a server, cluster, or shared drive.


setwd() is legitimate when the working directory is chosen deliberately. For collaboration, define a machine-specific location once and document the required drive, mount, or environment.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Restarting R tests saved source
rm(list = ls())
This removes objects, but loaded packages, changed options, working-directory changes, and other process state can remain.







Tip


Use Session → Restart R for a genuinely fresh process, then source the .R script or render the complete document from the project.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: The standing rule of this course
text:
The standing rule of this course






Every submission must render from a clean session in its documented computing environment.







Before you submit, every time:

Restart R — Ctrl-Shift-F10Ctrl-Shift-F10
Render the whole document from scratch
Confirm the output is what you expect — not just that it succeeded
Confirm every external data location is defined once and documented
Confirm there is no install.packages() or hidden manual step in the report




Rendering already uses a fresh session, so a document that renders is close to verified. Restarting first catches the remaining case: a file that quietly depends on something you did in the console.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Summary

Reproducibility is a statistical concern, not end-of-project clerical work.
R Markdown and Quarto both keep prose, code, and computed results together.
Use relative paths for project data; use documented absolute roots for large or protected data stored elsewhere.
This course begins from .Rmd literacy and focuses new work on .qmd.
Inline values and generated tables prevent copy-and-paste drift.
A clean-session render tests whether the source is complete.


Next connection: Session 2 adds Git and GitHub so analytical changes become inspectable and recoverable.

title: Session 2: Version control in RStudio
text:
Learning goals
By the end of the session, students should be able to:

Read file status in RStudio’s Git pane.
Distinguish saved edits, staged changes, local commits, and pushed commits.
Clone the public course repository through RStudio.
Clone an independent private repository using HTTPS browser authentication.
Invite the instructor and TA to the private repository for grading access.
Inspect line-level changes before staging their current versions.
Complete the everyday edit–review–stage–commit–push cycle through RStudio.
Use .gitignore appropriately.
Choose the correct project for course Pull versus personal Commit and Push.
Stop safely when a conflict, rejected push, or destructive choice appears.
Keep restricted data and credentials out of repositories.
