title: Visualization
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Read base-R plotting code and produce a fast diagnostic panel with it.
2 Name the components of the grammar of graphics and map an existing figure onto them.
3 Build a plot in layers — distributions, comparisons, relationships, and uncertainty.
4 Control facets, scales, transformations, and position adjustments.
5 Choose color mappings and palettes that match the data, and preserve group information with shapes, labels, or panels.
6 Critique a figure against explicit criteria — including your own.
7 Export a publication figure reproducibly at a stated size and resolution.

title: Visualization
text:
Roadmap for today







Block
Main question




1 · Base R
How do plotting commands build a figure?


2–4 · ggplot2 layers
Which marks answer our statistical question?


5 · Repeated visits and facets
How do we show people over time and compare subsets?


6 · Scales and color
How should values, groups, and axes be represented?


7 · Figure critique
What could a reader misunderstand, and how can we repair it?


8 · Export
How do we save a readable, reproducible figure?



Question pauses: predict, discuss, then reveal the answer. The optional geom catalogue is a reference within this deck.

title: Visualization
text:
The teaching data
All observations in this session are synthetic.





id
arm
age
sbp_0
sbp_12




P001
Placebo
47
160
144


P002
Placebo
59
162
156


P003
Placebo
61
157
156


P004
Placebo
48
157
163






One row represents one participant.
sbp_0 and sbp_12 are systolic blood pressure at baseline and week 12, in mmHg.
trial_long has one row per participant per visit, as in Session 7.

title: Visualization
section: A plot starts with a question
text:
A plot starts with a question







Question
Useful starting plot




What values and unusual observations occur?
Histogram or dot plot


How do participant values differ by arm?
Boxplot with individual points


How does baseline relate to follow-up?
Scatterplot


How does one participant change over time?
Connected points, grouped by ID


How many participants come from each site?
Bar chart of counts



The same plotting function may answer different questions. Labels and the observation unit tell the reader which question you mean.

title: Visualization
section: A labelled scatterplot in base R
text:
A labelled scatterplot in base R

plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
     ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
     main = "Baseline and follow-up",
     pch = 19, col = "steelblue")








plot(x, y) puts the first numeric vector on x and the second on y.

title: Visualization
text:
Common base R plotting arguments








Argument
Meaning
Example




pch
Point symbol
pch = 19 for a filled circle


col
Colour
col = "steelblue"


cex
Symbol/text size multiplier
cex = 1.3


lty, lwd
Line pattern and width
lty = 2, lwd = 2


xlab, ylab, main
Axis labels and title
ylab = "SBP (mmHg)"


xlim, ylim
Display limits
ylim = c(90, 190)



Use ?plot.default and ?par to look up options as needed.

title: Visualization
section: Which participant has lower follow-up SBP?
text:
Which participant has lower follow-up SBP?
THINK, THEN VOTE
The scatterplot has baseline SBP on x and week-12 SBP on y.
Imagine a line where y = x.
A. A point above the line
B. A point below the line
C. A point on the line

B. Below the line, week-12 SBP is lower than baseline.
On the line, the two measurements are equal.

title: Visualization
text:
Adding a reference line

plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
     xlim = c(90, 190), ylim = c(90, 190), pch = 19)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")








a is the intercept and b is the slope. Below the line, follow-up is lower than baseline. This line represents equality, not a fitted regression.

title: Visualization
section: Colours and a legend by treatment arm
text:
Colours and a legend by treatment arm

plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12, pch = 19,
     col = arm_col[trial$arm],
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
legend("topleft", legend = names(arm_col),
       col = arm_col, pch = 19, bty = "n")








arm_col is a named vector: c(Placebo = "#D55E00", Treatment = "#0072B2"). Indexing it by arm assigns the same colour consistently.

title: Visualization
text:
New plot or added marks?



Creates a new plot
Adds to the current plot




plot()
points()


hist()
lines()


boxplot()
abline()


barplot()
text(), legend()



For example, points(x, y, col = "red") adds observations to existing axes. Calling plot(x, y) again normally starts a new plot.

title: Visualization
text:
Connected measurements from one participant

weeks <- c(0, 6, 12)
values <- c(trial$sbp_0[1], trial$sbp_6[1], trial$sbp_12[1])
plot(weeks, values, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Week", ylab = "SBP (mmHg)", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = weeks)








type = "p" draws points, "l" draws lines, and "b" draws both. Base R connects points in supplied order, so arrange time first.

title: Visualization
text:
Histogram bins change the picture

saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$sbp_0, breaks = seq(80, 210, 5),
     main = "5-mmHg bins", xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)")
hist(trial$sbp_0, breaks = seq(80, 220, 20),
     main = "20-mmHg bins", xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)")







par(saved_par)

A vector in breaks specifies bin boundaries. A single number requests an approximate number of bins. A pattern should not depend on one convenient choice.

title: Visualization
text:
Different bins, different participants?
THINK, THEN COMPARE
The previous slide showed the same baseline SBP values in 5-mmHg and 20-mmHg bins.
Did the participants change, or did the grouping of values change?
Tell your neighbor one pattern that could look different.

The observations stayed the same. Only the bin boundaries changed.
Apparent peaks and gaps can change. Check more than one reasonable bin width.

title: Visualization
text:
Boxplots with participant-level values

boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, outline = FALSE,
        ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)", xlab = "")
stripchart(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial,
           vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = "steelblue", add = TRUE)









outline = FALSE hides the boxplot’s outlier symbols. Box borders and whiskers remain.
stripchart() then draws all observations, including values beyond the whiskers.
Together, these calls show each observation once, without duplicate outlier symbols.

title: Visualization
section: Bar charts use counts or summaries
text:
Bar charts use counts or summaries

site_counts <- table(trial$site_f)
barplot(site_counts, col = "steelblue",
        xlab = "Recruiting site", ylab = "Number of participants")








table() calculates the counts. barplot() draws their heights. A histogram instead bins a numeric variable such as blood pressure.

title: Visualization
text:
Optional: two distribution diagnostics








Plot
What it shows
How to read it




Empirical CDF (ECDF)
The observed cumulative distribution
At a given SBP, read the proportion of participants at or below it


Normal Q–Q plot
Sample quantiles against theoretical normal quantiles
Points near a straight line suggest an approximately normal distribution




The ECDF uses every observation, with no histogram bins.
In a normal Q–Q plot, systematic curvature or tail departures suggest departures from normality.

title: Visualization
section: Optional: ECDF and normal Q–Q examples
text:
Optional: ECDF and normal Q–Q examples

saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(ecdf(trial$sbp_0), main = "Cumulative proportion",
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Proportion at or below x")
qqnorm(trial$sbp_0, main = "Normal Q-Q plot")
qqline(trial$sbp_0, col = "steelblue")







par(saved_par)

Left: proportion at or below each SBP value. Right: sample versus normal quantiles.
A roughly straight Q–Q pattern supports approximate normality. This is a visual assessment, without a p-value.

title: Visualization
text:
Multiple panels and graphics state
saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # one row, two columns
hist(trial$sbp_0)
hist(trial$sbp_12)
par(saved_par)                    # restore changed settings

par() affects the current graphics device.
Restore settings after the multi-panel display.
If separate panels need direct comparison, choose common axis limits.
par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) resets the layout, but does not reset every other option.

title: Visualization
text:
Raster and vector figures









PNG: raster image
PDF: vector graphics




Stores
A grid of coloured pixels
Drawing instructions for lines, shapes, and text


When enlarged
Individual pixels can become visible
Vector elements remain sharp as they scale


Size settings
Width, height, and pixel density
Physical page width and height



A PDF has no single overall DPI for its vector elements.
A PDF can also contain raster images. Those images retain their pixel-resolution limits.

title: Visualization
text:
Resolution: pixels and physical size
DPI means dots per inch. For raster export, R uses this setting as pixels per inch (PPI).
Pixel width = width in inches × DPI



A 6 × 4 inch PNG
Pixel dimensions




150 DPI
900 × 600 pixels


300 DPI
1800 × 1200 pixels


600 DPI
3600 × 2400 pixels



At fixed physical size, higher DPI creates more pixels. At fixed pixel dimensions, changing DPI changes the physical size, without adding detail.

title: Visualization
text:
Saving a base R figure
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
png("output/base-sbp.png", width = 6, height = 4,
    units = "in", res = 300)
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
dev.off()
The file device receives drawing commands until dev.off() closes it. This PNG has 1800 × 1200 pixels: 6 × 4 inches at res = 300.
For a 6 × 4 inch vector PDF, open pdf("output/base-sbp.pdf", width = 6, height = 4) instead. No res or dpi argument.

title: Visualization
text:
Base graphics in four functions

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$sbp_0, main = "hist", xlab = "SBP baseline")
boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, main = "boxplot", xlab = "")
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12, main = "plot", xlab = "Week 0",
     ylab = "Week 12")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) splits the device into a 1 × 3 grid. It is device state: it stays set until you change it back.

title: Visualization
text:
A quick panel of distributions

par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$age,       main = "age")
hist(trial$weight_kg, main = "weight_kg")
hist(trial$sbp_0,     main = "sbp_0")
hist(trial$crp,       main = "crp")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Four columns on one screen. You are not making a figure — you are checking that the file is what you think it is. crp is right-skewed and you now know it before you fit anything.

title: Visualization
text:
Two plotting workflows

Base graphics: draw to a graphics device, then add points, lines, or labels. Many functions share options such as col, xlab, and ylim.
ggplot2: build a plot object, then add or change layers and scales. Grouping, legends, and facets follow shared rules.
Both can produce reproducible, publication-quality figures. Choose the workflow that makes your analysis easy to understand and maintain.

title: Visualization
text:
Our ggplot2 route
We will keep returning to the same synthetic blood-pressure study.

Build a plot: baseline versus follow-up.
Choose displays: distributions and arm comparisons.
Add summaries: means, intervals, and fitted trends.
Show repeated visits: one line per participant.
Refine and export: scales, labels, accessibility, and file size.

title: Visualization
text:
A plot is a specification
Question: How does baseline blood pressure relate to week 12?

Data: one row per participant.
x: baseline SBP.
y: week 12 SBP.
Marks: one point per participant.

ggplot(trial, aes(x = sbp_0, y = sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
We describe the data and its visual mappings, then choose how to draw it.

title: Visualization
text:
Seven components, plus a theme
The first four determine the data shown in a layer.



Component
In our study




Data
Participant records in trial


Aesthetics
aes(x = sbp_0, y = sbp_12)


Geom
geom_point() draws each participant


Stat
Points use raw values; a histogram counts bins



Most early examples need only data, mappings, and a geom.

title: Visualization
text:
Scales, coordinates, facets, and theme
The remaining components control how the plot appears.








Component
Role
Example




Scales
Translate values to positions or colours
Logarithmic y axis


Coordinates
Define the plotting space and view
Zoom into a region


Facets
Repeat a plot for subsets
One panel per site


Theme
Style non-data elements
Fonts and grid lines



We will add these after the basic plot answers the scientific question.

title: Visualization
text:
What will this code draw?
THINK, THEN VOTE
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12))
A. A scatterplot with participant points
B. Axes without participant points
C. An error

B. Data and mappings establish the axes.
Adding geom_point() draws the participant marks.

title: Visualization
section: A first ggplot: axes, then points
text:
A first ggplot: axes, then points



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12))










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()









Data and mappings establish the axes. The geom adds visible marks.

title: Visualization
section: The pipe and the plus sign have different jobs
text:
The pipe and the plus sign have different jobs
trial |>
  filter(site == 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")

|> passes the filtered data into ggplot().
+ adds plotting components to the ggplot object.
Put + at the end of a line when continuing the expression.
ggplot(...) |> geom_point() does not mean “add a point layer.”

title: Visualization
section: A ggplot object can be revised
text:
A ggplot object can be revised

p_scatter <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
p_scatter + labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
                 y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








p_scatter + ... displays a revised plot. To keep that version, assign it: p_scatter <- p_scatter + labs(...).

title: Visualization
text:
Will these points be blue?
THINK, THEN VOTE
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))
A. Yes, because the code says “blue”
B. It maps a category named “blue”
C. It cannot run

B. Inside aes(), “blue” becomes a category mapped through a colour scale.
For fixed blue points: geom_point(colour = "blue").

title: Visualization
section: aes() means map. Outside means set
text:
aes() means map. Outside means set



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  colour = arm)) +
  geom_point()










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue")










Inside aes(): colour carries information, and you get a legend. Outside: colour is fixed, and this setting does not create a mapped legend.

title: Visualization
text:
Colour, fill, and shape

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, fill = arm)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, colour = "black", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arm_col) +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








For shapes 21–25, fill controls the interior and colour controls the border. For most other point shapes, use colour. For bars, fill colours the interior.

title: Visualization
text:
Questions that need different displays

Distribution: What baseline values occur?
Comparison: How do week-12 values differ between arms?
Counts: How many participants belong to each category?

We will keep the study data, but change the variables and marks.

title: Visualization
text:
Choosing a geom
A geom is a layer’s drawing method: points, lines, bars, text, or another mark. Some geoms also compute a default summary before drawing.







Your data/question
Start with




Two numeric measurements per person
geom_point()


One numeric variable’s distribution
geom_histogram()


A numeric outcome across groups
geom_boxplot() plus points


Counts of records by category
geom_bar()


Heights already calculated in a table
geom_col()


Repeated measurements within a person
geom_line() with group = id

title: Visualization
text:
Optional: complete ggplot2 geom catalogue
The next slides list the exported geom_*() functions in the ggplot2 version used to render this deck, including aliases and older interfaces.

They are a lookup reference, not a memorization requirement.
Extension-package geoms, such as ggrepel::geom_text_repel(), are separate.
stat_*(), scales, and themes are different function families.

Skip the catalogue and continue to distributions
Official ggplot2 function reference

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: points and labels





Function
Purpose




geom_point()
One mark at each x/y location


geom_jitter()
Points with position offsets to reveal overlap


geom_count()
Point area represents the number at an x/y location


geom_rug()
Small marks along the plot margins


geom_text()
Text from a label variable


geom_label()
Text with a background box

title: Visualization
text:
Geom examples: points and jitter









Points show a relationship between two measurements. Jitter separates overlapping observations within categories. Both show individual participants.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: connected observations





Function
Purpose




geom_line()
Connect observations in x order within each group


geom_path()
Connect observations in their row order


geom_step()
Connect observations using steps


geom_segment()
Separate segments, with start and end coordinates


geom_curve()
Curved connections between endpoints


geom_spoke()
Segments specified by angle and length





Connecting observations implies a relationship or order. It is usually inappropriate to connect unrelated participants just because their rows are adjacent.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom examples: line and step









A line connects measured summaries. A step can represent a dose held constant until the next change. The right-hand schedule is a separate synthetic example.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: distributions





Function
Purpose




geom_histogram()
Counts or densities in numeric bins


geom_freqpoly()
A line through binned frequencies


geom_density()
A smooth estimate of a one-variable density


geom_dotplot()
Stacked dots in bins


geom_boxplot()
Median, quartiles, whiskers, and extreme points


geom_violin()
A mirrored density for each group


geom_qq()
Sample quantiles against reference quantiles


geom_qq_line()
A reference line for a Q-Q display

title: Visualization
text:
Geom examples: distribution summaries









The histogram groups observations into numeric bins. A violin describes a smoothed distribution, while the overlaid box marks its quartiles and median.

title: Visualization
section: Geom reference: bars and filled regions
text:
Geom reference: bars and filled regions





Function
Purpose




geom_bar()
Count records by category by default


geom_col()
Draw supplied y values as bar heights


geom_area()
Filled region to a baseline, stacked by default


geom_ribbon()
Region between supplied ymin and ymax


geom_rect()
Rectangles defined by boundary coordinates


geom_tile()
Rectangles defined by centres and dimensions


geom_raster()
Efficient equal-sized rectangular cells

title: Visualization
section: Geom examples: bars and a ribbon
text:
Geom examples: bars and a ribbon









Bars show counts. The ribbon fills a supplied lower-to-upper range, here approximate 95% intervals for the treatment-arm mean at each visit.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: intervals









Function
Purpose




geom_pointrange()
Point estimate and interval


geom_linerange()
Interval alone


geom_errorbar()
Interval with end caps


geom_crossbar()
Central value across an interval box


geom_errorbarh()
Older horizontal error-bar interface (deprecated)





For new horizontal error bars, use geom_errorbar(orientation = "y") with xmin and xmax. The plotting function does not determine whether your interval means SD, SE, or a confidence interval.

title: Visualization
section: Geom examples: two ways to draw an interval
text:
Geom examples: two ways to draw an interval









These show the same means and approximate 95% confidence intervals. Pointrange draws both marks; errorbar supplies the interval with end caps.

title: Visualization
section: Geom reference: fits and reference lines
text:
Geom reference: fits and reference lines









Function
Purpose




geom_smooth()
Fitted trend with an optional uncertainty band


geom_quantile()
Conditional quantile regression lines


geom_function()
Evaluate and draw a supplied function


geom_abline()
Lines specified by intercept and slope


geom_hline()
Horizontal reference lines


geom_vline()
Vertical reference lines


geom_blank()
Invisible layer, useful for establishing scale ranges

title: Visualization
section: Geom examples: fitted and reference lines
text:
Geom examples: fitted and reference lines









The fitted line summarizes a relationship in the data. The identity line marks equality between visits and needs no fitted model.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: two-dimensional patterns









Function
Purpose




geom_bin_2d()
Counts in rectangular x/y bins


geom_hex()
Counts in hexagonal x/y bins


geom_density_2d()
Contours of an estimated x/y density


geom_density_2d_filled()
Filled regions of an estimated x/y density


geom_contour()
Contour lines for supplied grid values z


geom_contour_filled()
Filled contour regions for supplied grid values z





geom_hex() needs the hexbin package. Counts, estimated densities, and supplied surface values answer different questions.

title: Visualization
section: Geom examples: binned counts and contours
text:
Geom examples: binned counts and contours









Left: counts of participants in x/y bins. Right: equal-value lines from R’s built-in volcano elevation grid. Contours require surface values, not just x/y pairs.

title: Visualization
text:
Geom reference: maps and shapes





Function
Purpose




geom_polygon()
Closed shapes from ordered vertices


geom_map()
Values joined to a separate map polygon table


geom_sf()
Geometry from an sf spatial object


geom_sf_text()
Text located using sf geometry


geom_sf_label()
Boxed text located using sf geometry





The geom_sf*() functions use the sf package and spatial data structures. Spatial analysis is outside this session’s core material.

title: Visualization
section: Geom example: regions defined by vertices
text:
Geom example: regions defined by vertices









Each group supplies one shape’s vertices in boundary order. Real geographic work commonly uses geom_sf() with spatial geometry instead of hand-entered vertices.

title: Visualization
section: Geom reference: aliases and package version
text:
Geom reference: aliases and package version





Function
Purpose




geom_bin2d()
Alias of geom_bin_2d

Alias of geom_density_2d

Alias of geom_density_2d_filled





This deck lists 53 exported names, including aliases, for ggplot2 4.0.0.
Use ?geom_point or the official reference for arguments. Newer releases may add functions. There is no need to install an extension package just to complete the core examples.

title: Visualization
text:
Back to the study: distributions
The catalogue shows the range of available marks. Now we use a small set to answer the study questions.
First question: What is the distribution of baseline SBP?
Compare a histogram’s bins with a density curve’s smoothing.

title: Visualization
text:
Distributions: histogram and density



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 8,
                 fill = "grey35")










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey80")

title: Visualization
text:
Choose the distribution summary deliberately

binwidth = 8 uses 8-mmHg bins. bins = 30 asks for a number of bins. Either choice needs checking: try alternatives and see whether the pattern persists.
The base R way: hist(trial$sbp_0) · plot(density(trial$sbp_0))

title: Visualization
text:
Distributions compared: boxplot and violin



ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5)










ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey85")










A boxplot shows the median, quartiles, whiskers, and possible outlying points. A violin shows an estimated density. Neither displays the sample size by default.
The base R way: boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)

title: Visualization
section: Show the data, not only the summary
text:
Show the data, not only the summary

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.7, size = 2)









outlier.shape = NA stops the boxplot drawing outliers that geom_jitter() already drew. Two marks for one observation is a real error, not a style choice.

title: Visualization
text:
Sixty participants, fewer visible dots?
THINK, THEN VOTE
Our scatterplot contains 60 participants.
Could it show fewer than 60 separately visible dots?
A. Yes, observations can overlap
B. No, R always separates the points
C. Only if some participants were removed

A. Multiple observations can occupy the same or nearby plotting positions.
Transparency or suitable jitter can help reveal overlap.

title: Visualization
text:
Overlap can hide observations

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12,
                                        height = 0, seed = 6301),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








Horizontal jitter separates tied marks. height = 0 preserves the measured outcome, and seed makes the offsets repeatable. Alpha reduces visual overlap.

title: Visualization
text:
Counts versus a precomputed table





arm
n




Placebo
30


Treatment
30





# One row per participant: let the geom count
ggplot(trial, aes(arm)) + geom_bar()

# One row per arm: heights are already calculated
ggplot(counts, aes(arm, n)) + geom_col()
Both give the same counts here. A mean or percentage already stored in y usually calls for geom_col(), not the default geom_bar() statistic.

title: Visualization
text:
Comparisons: bars, and position adjustments

ggplot(trial, aes(site_f, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")












position =
Shows
Good for




"stack" (default)
Counts, one bar per group
Totals


"dodge"
Counts, side by side
Comparing subgroups


"fill"
Proportions, all bars to 1
Composition — but hides n

title: Visualization
text:
Participant values and group summaries
Question: What is the average week-12 SBP in each arm, and how uncertain is it?

Keep the participant-level data visible.
Calculate an arm-level summary table.
Draw a summary layer from that table.
State what its interval means.

The raw data and summary layers have different observation units.

title: Visualization
section: What do these error bars tell us?
text:
What do these error bars tell us?
THINK, THEN VOTE
A caption says: “Mean week-12 SBP with a 95% confidence interval for each arm mean.”
A. The interval contains 95% of participant SBP values
B. It describes uncertainty about each arm’s population mean
C. It shows the minimum and maximum SBP

B. A confidence interval for a mean concerns that population mean.
The individual points show participant-level variation.

title: Visualization
text:
What do the intervals mean?







Interval
Describes




Mean ± SD
Spread of individual measurements around their mean


Mean ± SE
Estimated sampling variability of the mean


Confidence interval
Uncertainty about a population parameter under a model


Prediction interval
Uncertainty about a new individual observation



The same geom_errorbar() can draw any of these. Its inputs do not tell the reader which one you intended. State the meaning and method in the caption.
The earlier mean ± 1.96 * SE examples use an approximate 95% confidence interval. The longitudinal ribbon gives intervals at each visit, not a model of change.

title: Visualization
section: Uncertainty: an estimate needs an interval
text:
Uncertainty: an estimate needs an interval

by_arm <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12),
            se = sd(sbp_12) / sqrt(n()))

ggplot(by_arm, aes(arm, mean_sbp)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se))

title: Visualization
section: A layer can use its own data
text:
A layer can use its own data

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0,
                                        seed = 6301), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = by_arm, aes(x = arm, y = mean_sbp),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 5,
             colour = "#0072B2")








Grey points use participant data. Blue diamonds use the summary table. inherit.aes = FALSE makes the summary layer use only its own mappings.

title: Visualization
text:
Relationships: points and a smooth

ggplot(trial, aes(age, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, alpha = 0.15)









method = "lm" specifies a linear fit. With method = NULL, ggplot2 chooses loess or GAM according to the largest group’s size. The band describes uncertainty in the fitted mean, not a prediction interval for an individual.

title: Visualization
text:
Layer-specific mappings

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = arm)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col)








Colour belongs only to the points here. The smooth uses all participants together. Putting colour = arm in the global aes() would fit one line per arm.

title: Visualization
section: A new question needs a different data shape
text:
A new question needs a different data shape
Question: How does blood pressure change over the three visits?

One row in trial: one participant, with visits in separate columns.
One row in trial_long: one participant at one visit.
Individual lines need id, week, and sbp.
Group-average lines need an arm-by-week summary.

Session 7’s wide-to-long reshape makes these plots easier to specify.

title: Visualization
text:
Did reshaping triple our study?
THINK, THEN COMPARE
There are 60 participants and three visits per participant: weeks 0, 6, and 12.
After reshaping to long form:

How many rows do we have?
How many participants do we have?
Which variable keeps each person’s line together?


180 rows, 60 participants, and group = id for individual trajectories.
One long-table row represents one participant at one visit.

title: Visualization
section: Plotting repeated visits uses the long table
text:
Plotting repeated visits uses the long table
trial_long <- trial |>
  select(id, arm, sbp_0, sbp_6, sbp_12) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(starts_with("sbp_"),
                     names_to = "week", names_prefix = "sbp_",
                     values_to = "sbp") |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week))





id
arm
week
sbp




P001
Placebo
0
160


P001
Placebo
6
146


P001
Placebo
12
144





The first participant contributes three rows. Their shared id tells the plot which measurements belong together.

title: Visualization
text:
One line per participant

p_lines <- ggplot(trial_long,
                  aes(week, sbp, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "SBP (mmHg)")
p_lines








group = id connects each participant’s own measurements. The lines overlap: how could we compare the two arms without hiding individual trajectories?

title: Visualization
text:
Faceting: when and why
Faceting repeats the same plot for subsets of the data in labelled panels.







Use facets when you want to…
Why panels help




Compare arms, sites, or other groups
Each subset has its own space


See patterns hidden by overlapping marks
Groups no longer cover one another


Apply the same display to several groups
One specification controls every panel



Keep a shared scale when comparing levels or spread. Use a single panel when direct overlap is the main question and only a few groups need distinguishing.

title: Visualization
text:
facet_wrap(): one panel per group

p_lines + facet_wrap(~ arm, nrow = 1)









~ arm assigns each observation to its arm’s panel.
nrow = 1 places the two panels in a row.
The default scales = "fixed" keeps the axes comparable.

title: Visualization
text:
facet_grid(): rows and columns

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(arm ~ site_f) +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








arm ~ site_f means rows = arm, columns = site. Read across a row to compare sites; down a column to compare arms within a site.

title: Visualization
text:
Fixed and free facet scales






















scales = "free_y" lets each panel choose its y range. This can reveal detail within a panel, but the same vertical position can represent different values.

title: Visualization
section: Which facet scale fits the question?
text:
Which facet scale fits the question?
CHOOSE AND EXPLAIN
“Is week 12 SBP generally higher at one site than another?”
Would you choose fixed y scales or free y scales across the site panels?

Fixed scales. The question compares levels across sites; equal heights should represent equal SBP values.

title: Visualization
text:
Mean trajectories and their uncertainty

by_week <- trial_long |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarise(m = mean(sbp),
            se = sd(sbp) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")
ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se,
                  ymax = m + 1.96 * se),
              fill = "grey75") +
  geom_line() + facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)")








The ribbon shows approximate pointwise 95% confidence intervals for each arm mean, not the range containing 95% of participants.

title: Visualization
text:
What does a scale control?
aes() maps a variable to an aesthetic. A scale controls how that variable is represented and labelled.



Function
Controls




scale_x_continuous()
Numeric x-axis ticks and labels


scale_x_discrete()
Category order and labels


scale_y_log10()
A logarithmic y-axis


scale_color_manual()
Colors assigned to categories


scale_fill_viridis_c()
A continuous fill-color gradient



Read the name as scale → aesthetic → type. color and colour are aliases.

title: Visualization
text:
scale_x_continuous(): meaningful tick marks

p_visit <- ggplot(filter(by_week, arm == "Placebo"),
                  aes(week, m)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)", title = "Placebo arm")
p_visit +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Study visit",
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12),
    labels = c("Baseline", "Week 6", "Week 12"))








breaks chooses tick locations; labels supplies the text at those ticks. These settings do not add, remove, or move observations.

title: Visualization
text:
Axis settings do different jobs








Argument
Job
Example




name
Axis title
"Week 12 SBP (mmHg)"


breaks
Tick positions
seq(100, 180, 20)


labels
Tick text or formatting
scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)


limits
Permitted values on the scale
c(120, 160)



scale_y_continuous(
  name = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
  breaks = seq(100, 180, 20),
  labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1))
Limits are not just tick settings: they can exclude values before a statistical layer is calculated. We will compare this with coordinate zoom.

title: Visualization
text:
scale_x_discrete(): category order and labels

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = c("Treatment", "Placebo"),
    labels = c(Treatment = "Active treatment",
               Placebo = "Placebo")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








Use a discrete scale for categories. Named labels match the actual data values. Include all intended categories in limits; omitted categories are excluded.

title: Visualization
section: Log scales: equal ratios, equal distances
text:
Log scales: equal ratios, equal distances
Use a log scale for positive values spanning a wide range, especially when ratios are more informative than absolute differences.



Values
Linear axis
Log10 axis




1 → 10
Increase of 9
One tenfold step


10 → 100
Increase of 90
One tenfold step



scale_y_log10() spaces values by their logarithms and labels ticks in the original units. There is no general scale_log10() call: choose x or y.
Check first: zero and negative values have no finite real log10 value. Do not add an arbitrary constant just to make the plot run.

title: Visualization
section: scale_y_log10(): see the same positive data
text:
scale_y_log10(): see the same positive data






















p_crp + scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30))
The same values are shown. Low values are easier to distinguish; large values occupy less space. Tick labels still show CRP, not log10(CRP).

title: Visualization
section: Will these give the same boxplot?
text:
Will these give the same boxplot?
PREDICT, THEN DISCUSS
p_box <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()
# A
p_box + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(120, 160))
# B
p_box + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(120, 160))
Which keeps all observations in the boxplot calculation?

A. Coordinate zoom changes the visible window after calculation. In B, out-of-range values become missing first, so the boxplot can change.

title: Visualization
section: Zoom and scale limits give different summaries
text:
Zoom and scale limits give different summaries






















Compare the median and box edges, not just the frame. Use coord_cartesian() for a closer view; filter explicitly when exclusion is part of the analysis and explain the criterion.

title: Visualization
section: Color: what information should it carry?
text:
Color: what information should it carry?
Color can identify a group, show an ordered magnitude, or emphasize a selected feature. Decide its job before choosing a palette.








Data meaning
Palette idea
Example




Unordered categories
Distinct hues
Placebo and treatment


Low to high
Sequential gradient
Age or mean SBP


Below/above a reference
Diverging gradient
Negative/positive change



Hue distinguishes colors; lightness runs from dark to light. Use axes for the primary numerical comparison when precise reading matters.

title: Visualization
section: color and fill control different parts
text:
color and fill control different parts

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12, fill = arm)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "grey25") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
       fill = "Randomized arm")









fill = arm inside aes() maps arm to the box interiors.
color = "grey25" outside aes() gives every box the same border color.
For ordinary points and lines, use color; filled point shapes 21–25 also use fill.

title: Visualization
text:
scale_color_manual(): name the category colors

arm_colors <- c(Placebo = "#D55E00",
                Treatment = "#0072B2")
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  color = arm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = arm_colors,
    name = "Randomized arm") +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








The names in values match data values. Reuse the same mapping across figures so “Treatment” does not change color between slides.

title: Visualization
section: scale_fill_manual(): the same groups, filled marks
text:
scale_fill_manual(): the same groups, filled marks

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12, fill = arm)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = arm_colors,
    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








Choose the scale that matches the mapped aesthetic: fill → scale_fill_*(). Here the x-axis already identifies each arm, so the fill legend is redundant.

title: Visualization
text:
Continuous color: scale_color_viridis_c()

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  color = age)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Age (years)") +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








The color bar represents a numeric range. _c means continuous; _d means discrete. Use a continuous gradient for age, not a separate color per year.

title: Visualization
text:
Continuous fill: a site-by-arm heatmap

site_summary <- trial |>
  group_by(site_f, arm) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12),
            .groups = "drop")
ggplot(site_summary,
       aes(arm, site_f, fill = mean_sbp)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Mean SBP\n(mmHg)") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)








scale_fill_viridis_c() controls the tile interiors. A heatmap shows patterns across combinations; use a dot plot or numeric labels for precise comparisons.

title: Visualization
text:
Diverging color: a meaningful midpoint

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  color = sbp_12 - sbp_0)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "grey90",
    high = "#B35806", midpoint = 0,
    name = "Change\n(mmHg)") +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








Zero means no change. Two color directions distinguish decreases from increases. A midpoint needs a scientific meaning, not just visual symmetry.

title: Visualization
text:
What survives a grayscale printout?
CHOOSE A REPAIR
A scatterplot uses color alone to identify treatment arms. Some readers cannot distinguish those hues, and a grayscale printout loses the distinction.
What would preserve the arm information?

Add point shape, direct labels, or separate labelled panels. A suitable palette helps; an additional encoding preserves group identity.

title: Visualization
text:
Accessible color: palette plus shape

ggplot(trial,
       aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
           color = arm, shape = arm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = arm_colors,
    name = "Randomized arm") +
  labs(shape = "Randomized arm",
       x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")








The blue/orange pair comes from the Okabe–Ito palette. Shape supplies a second cue. Check the plot at its final size and without color.

title: Visualization
section: A figure review starts with the question
text:
A figure review starts with the question
Question: how does week 12 SBP differ between the randomized arms?



Check
Ask the reader




Comparison
What quantity, groups, and time point are shown?


Evidence
Are marks participants, summaries, or both?


Scale
Does the axis support the intended comparison?


Uncertainty
What do the intervals represent?


Readability
Can you identify groups, units, and sample size?



Give feedback as: “This choice could suggest …; I would change ….”

title: Visualization
section: Critique: what could a reader misunderstand?
text:
Critique: what could a reader misunderstand?









Think, then compare with a neighbor. Name two specific problems and explain the impression each could create.

title: Visualization
section: Diagnose the choice, then choose a repair
text:
Diagnose the choice, then choose a repair








Choice in the figure
What it hides or suggests
Repair




Bars clipped above zero
Exaggerated length comparison
Start bars at zero, or use points


Only two arm means
Within-arm variation is invisible
Show participant values


No defined intervals
Precision cannot be assessed
Add and define mean confidence intervals


“SBP results” / “SBP”
Summary, visit, and units unclear
Name all three


Duplicate fill legend
Extra lookup without new information
Use the labelled x positions



The repair follows the reading task—not a rule that every plot needs every layer.

title: Visualization
section: Revised figure: individuals and defined summaries
text:
Revised figure: individuals and defined summaries









Read it: compare the arm means, then the spread and overlap of participants. The intervals describe each mean; they are not intervals for individual SBP.

title: Visualization
section: Build the revision in two layers
text:
Build the revision in two layers
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 8),
    alpha = 0.55, color = "grey45") +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = by_arm,
    aes(y = mean_sbp, ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
        ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se),
    color = "#0072B2")

First layer: 60 participant rows, with horizontal jitter only.
Second layer: two summary rows, one mean and interval per arm.
Labels and caption explain what each layer represents.

title: Visualization
section: Does every y-axis need to start at zero?
text:
Does every y-axis need to start at zero?
COMPARE ENCODINGS
The revised SBP plot has a y-axis above zero. Is that necessarily misleading?

No. Points encode position on a labelled axis, so a focused range can help. Bars encode length from a baseline; cutting off zero distorts that length.

Choose a range that preserves relevant variation and reference values. For change, zero is often an important no-change reference.

title: Visualization
text:
Labels explain the measurement
labs(
  title = "Week 12 SBP by randomized arm",
  subtitle = "Synthetic data; 30 participants per arm",
  x = NULL,
  y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
  caption = "Grey points: participants. Blue: mean and approximate 95% CI.")
Title: comparison and time point. Axes: variable and units. Caption: marks, summaries, and interval meaning.
A descriptive title reports what is displayed. Avoid a causal or clinical claim that the plotted analysis does not establish.

title: Visualization
section: Direct labels for a few lines
text:
Direct labels for a few lines

ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, color = arm)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(data = filter(by_week, week == 12),
            aes(x = 12.5, label = arm),
            hjust = 0, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = arm_colors,
                     guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 18)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)")








Labels at the line ends remove repeated legend lookup. They work well for a few separated lines; a legend or facets may be clearer when labels collide.

title: Visualization
section: Themes: make the data easy to see
text:
Themes: make the data easy to see






















theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
Both themes are valid. Keep guides that help readers estimate values; remove clutter without removing units, labels, or useful reference lines.

title: Visualization
text:
Choosing an alternative display








Reading task
A useful choice
Why




Rank category counts precisely
Sorted bars or dots
Positions/lengths share an axis


Show a few parts of a whole
Bars, or a clearly labelled pie
State the denominator


Compare trends in different outcomes
Separate panels with a shared time axis
Each outcome keeps its units



A second y-axis is appropriate for a defined one-to-one conversion of the same quantity. Arbitrarily rescaling two outcomes can change their apparent alignment.

title: Visualization
section: Can your revision answer these questions?
text:
Can your revision answer these questions?
READ AS A NEW VIEWER

What does one mark represent?
Which groups and measurement are being compared?
What does the interval or reference line mean?
What conclusion is supported—and what is still uncertain?


If the figure cannot answer one of these, revise the relevant layer, label, scale, or caption before changing decorative details.

title: Visualization
section: Plot debugging: connect the symptom to the cause
text:
Plot debugging: connect the symptom to the cause







Symptom
Check




Legend says “blue”
Was a constant placed inside aes()?


A fill scale changes nothing
Is the geom using color instead of fill?


Group colors change between figures
Are manual colors named consistently?


Panel patterns look identical
Are facet axes fixed or free? Read the ticks


A summary changes after axis limits
Did scale limits remove observations?


“Removed rows” warning
Inspect missing, nonfinite, and out-of-range values



Run the plot one layer at a time. Read warnings before hiding them with na.rm = TRUE.

title: Visualization
section: Finish it: labs() and a theme
text:
Finish it: labs() and a theme

p_final <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.45, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = by_arm,
                  aes(y = mean_sbp,
                      ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se),
                  colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SBP at 12 weeks (mmHg)",
       caption = "Points: participants; mean and approximate 95% CI.\nn = 30 per arm.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
p_final

title: Visualization
text:
Same code, different-sized figures?
THINK, THEN VOTE
Two collaborators run:
ggsave("figure.png", plot = p_final)
Their RStudio plot panes have different dimensions.
Could the saved figures have different dimensions too?

Yes. Without explicit width and height, the export can use the current graphics device’s size.
Specify width, height, and units; choose DPI for a raster export.

title: Visualization
section: ggsave(), with the arguments filled in
text:
ggsave(), with the arguments filled in
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/fig-sbp-arm.png",
  plot     = p_final,
  width    = 6.5,     # inches - the column width of your journal
  height   = 4, units = "in",
  dpi      = 300,     # pixels per inch for this raster PNG
  bg       = "white"
)

title: Visualization
text:
Why explicit export settings matter








Argument
Leave it out and you get




width, height
The last size of your plot pane. Irreproducible by construction


dpi
PNG pixel density defaults to 300; it does not set vector PDF sharpness


bg
Background comes from the plot theme and may be transparent


.pdf / .svg extension
Vector marks scale without pixelation; embedded raster layers still have finite resolution

title: Visualization
text:
PNG versus PDF with ggsave()
# Raster: 6 x 4 inches at 300 DPI = 1800 x 1200 pixels
ggsave("output/figure.png", plot = p_final,
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# Vector: 6 x 4 inch page; no raster DPI is needed
ggsave("output/figure.pdf", plot = p_final,
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
For PDF at a fixed size in inches, changing dpi does not sharpen vector lines or text.
With units = "px", ggsave() uses dpi to convert pixel dimensions to physical size, even for PDF. Prefer inches or cm for vector exports.

title: Visualization
section: Why the plot pane is not a workflow
text:
Why the plot pane is not a workflow


Export → paste
Right-click, copy, paste into Word.
Nothing records what produced it. The data changes, the figure does not, and no warning appears anywhere.

ggsave() in the document
The figure is regenerated when its code executes during rendering.
The script records the data and plotting steps. Check data versions and caching settings so the figure stays aligned with the analysis.








A pasted figure is the same class of error as a number typed by hand — and it is harder to spot, because a stale figure still looks like a figure.

title: Visualization
text:
patchwork: several panels, one figure
library(patchwork)

p_box  <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()
p_scat <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) + geom_point()
p_time <- ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm)) + geom_line()

(p_box | p_scat) / p_time +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

| side by side · / stacked · plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") labels the panels A, B, C the way a journal wants them.
Optional extension package: install.packages("patchwork") if needed.

A ggplot is a specification of mappings, layers, scales, coordinates, facets, and theme.
Mapping a variable differs from setting a display property.
Show distributions and uncertainty rather than only summary bars.
Exported dimensions, labels, accessibility, and reproducibility are part of the figure.

title: Session 9 · Positron and AI-assisted coding
text:
Before class

What is Positron?
Positron is an integrated development environment (IDE) from Posit, the company behind RStudio. It gives you a place to edit code, run R or Python, and inspect results. R is still the language and interpreter that execute your R code. Positron uses an installed copy of R, so keep your existing R installation.
Your R syntax and source files carry over. In Positron, the Editor corresponds to RStudio’s Source pane, Variables to Environment, and Explorer to Files. The slides include annotated screenshots and a complete panel comparison. Positron opens a folder as a workspace and builds on Code OSS, the open-source core of VS Code. This connects it to a broad developer ecosystem of AI and advanced development tools. Keep your .Rproj file for use in RStudio.
Many VS Code extensions work in Positron, but Microsoft restricts direct use of its Marketplace. Use Positron’s Extensions view, whose default gallery serves the Open VSX catalog through Posit Public Package Manager. An extension’s license and technical requirements still determine whether it can run in Positron. See the extension guide.
Read more in Posit’s R guide and RStudio migration guide.


Install Positron

Download Positron for your computer. On a Mac, choose Apple Silicon or Intel to match your processor.
Open the download and follow the installation prompts. On macOS, drag Positron into Applications.

Keep your existing R and RStudio installations. We will introduce Positron and connect Copilot together in class.


Apply for GitHub student benefits

Sign in with the GitHub account you use for BIOS6301. Add and verify your student email in GitHub email settings.
Open Education benefits, select Start an application, and apply as a student. Provide your school information and any requested proof of current enrollment, such as a class schedule or dated student ID.
After approval, return to Education benefits and follow the prompts to activate the free Copilot Student benefit.

See GitHub’s student application guide for application details.

title: Session 9 guided lab
text:
1. Set up

Open your BIOS6301-mywork folder in Positron. From the separate course materials folder, copy the Quarto starter and sbp-demo.csv into work/session09/. If you prefer R Markdown, use the Rmd starter instead. Choose one document format.
Select your R interpreter. The lab uses the familiar ggplot2 and dplyr packages. Install either if missing before continuing.

If not already connected, open the Command Palette and run Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers. Select GitHub Copilot, sign in, and open Posit Assistant. Confirm the provider and selected model. Keep the usual Normal approval setting.

The CSV contains the same 60 synthetic patients used in class: id, arm, sbp_0, sbp_6, and sbp_12. Each row is one patient. SBP is in mmHg. Keep the original CSV unchanged.

title: Session 9 guided lab
text:
2. Discuss in Ask mode
Read the starter’s two candidates. Before asking AI, write one sentence predicting what the summary’s n counts after missing SBP rows are removed.
Select Ask (/ask). Use @ to reference your copied document and CSV, then send:

Read these two files. Explain which columns represent baseline and week-12 SBP. Explain why assigning the plot to p does not explicitly display it. Does the prepared summary report all patients or only patients with observed week-12 SBP? Suggest the smallest corrections. Do not change files.

Record whether the explanation agrees with your prediction and how the assistant obtained the column names.






Note



Reading a CSV does not require running R. Ask can read its header and values with a file tool. It cannot run names(trial) or other R code to inspect a live object. Automatic session context supplies object names/types, not their values. If needed, run an R check yourself and paste its output. A saved CSV can differ from an object you have transformed in memory.

title: Session 9 guided lab
text:
3. Request a bounded revision
Save your prediction. Leave Ask using /normal, then send this implementation plan in Posit Assistant:

In my copied lab document, fill only the Revised plot and Corrected summary sections. Plot sbp_0 on x and sbp_12 on y, color by arm, label both axes in mmHg, and explicitly print the plot. Use complete pairs for the plot only. Summarize week-12 SBP by arm as n_total, n_observed, mean_sbp, and sd_sbp. Count all patients in n_total and use observed SBP for the mean and SD. Keep the CSV, original candidates, my prediction, verification code, and disclosure unchanged. Render or knit the document if the tools are available; otherwise tell me what to run. Report what you actually changed and ran.

Inspect the file differences before accepting the result. Check that the agent changed only the intended sections. If something is wrong, request one focused correction and inspect again. An agent’s statement that it ran the report is not enough: look for the command result or render it yourself.
This implements a supplied plan, matching level 3 in the lecture. Adding arm colors alone is a level-1 edit. The same interface can handle either scope.

title: Session 9 guided lab
text:
4. Verify and explain
Run the starter’s supplied base-R checks yourself and compare them with the revised analysis. Check the rendered output as well as the code.

Plot: baseline on x, week 12 on y, labels in mmHg, and arm colors. There are 57 complete pairs and 3 omitted patients. Points can overlap, so use the count rather than trying to count visible dots.
Summary: two rows, one per arm. Total counts are 30 and 30. Observed week-12 counts are 28 Placebo and 29 Treatment.
Meaning: excluding a missing week-12 value from a mean must not exclude that patient from the total count. Explain this in your own words.

Save and render/knit the document from the beginning. Keep one source document and its HTML report, containing your prediction, the preserved candidates, revised plot and summary, verification results, and a short disclosure. Record Posit Assistant, GitHub Copilot as provider, and the displayed model name if available. Describe your own review and corrections.

Inline completion, next-edit suggestions, and the full three-visit implementation remain lecture demonstrations. The demo script and reference script are optional follow-up materials. Custom functions and edge-case testing are not part of this core lab.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
The question behind this session

When would Python help our research, and how can we transfer our R data-analysis reasoning while checking differences in behavior?

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Learning goals

Explain when Python can help a research project.
Run a versionable Python script in Positron.
Recognize lists, NumPy arrays, and pandas DataFrames.
Translate selection, transformation, and grouped summaries.
Compare missing-value and indexing behavior with R.
Verify equivalent R and Python results.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Goal 1 · When Python helps
Explain when Python can help a research project.

A research package or collaborator’s model already uses Python.
The team’s data-processing workflow uses Python tools.
A suitable library provides the numerical or GPU operations we need.


Which part of the research task would Python help us do?

R remains our main analysis language. We choose tools for the task.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Large data: when a different workflow helps
text:
Large data: when a different workflow helps

You have 200 GB of visit records, 16 GB of RAM, and need the mean of one marker. What must stay in memory?


pd.read_csv(..., usecols=["marker"]) keeps only the required column.
Add chunksize=100_000 to process one batch at a time.
pd.read_parquet(..., columns=["marker"]) can read selected columns from a column-oriented file.

These can use less memory than loading the whole table with read.csv(). R also has chunked readers and Arrow. The workflow creates the advantage.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Large data: a mean without loading every row
text:
Large data: a mean without loading every row
Illustration for a separate CSV containing a numeric marker column:
import pandas as pd

total, observed = 0.0, 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv("visits.csv", usecols=["marker"],
                         chunksize=100_000):
    total += chunk["marker"].sum()
    observed += chunk["marker"].count()
mean_marker = total / observed if observed else float("nan")
Keep a batch and two running totals in memory. Combine sums and counts, not batch means when observed batch sizes differ.
When useful: a full import exceeds RAM, but each batch fits.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Reading and saving: compare the functions
text:
Reading and saving: compare the functions



Task
Python
R alternatives




Read CSV
pd.read_csv()
read.csv() / data.table::fread()


Save CSV
df.to_csv()
write.csv() / data.table::fwrite()


Read Parquet
pd.read_parquet()
arrow::read_parquet()


Save Parquet
df.to_parquet()
arrow::write_parquet()



For CSV, compare pd.read_csv(..., engine="c") or engine="pyarrow" against both R readers. A win over base read.csv() does not establish a win over fread().
Match the file, selected columns, types, and compression before timing.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Columns and means: compare equivalent operations
text:
Columns and means: compare equivalent operations



Task
Python / pandas
R




Add y = 2 * x
df.assign(y=2*df["x"])
transform(df, y=2*x)


Mean, omit missing
df["x"].mean()
mean(df$x, na.rm=TRUE)



For a data.table DT, DT[, y := 2*x] adds the column by reference.

NumPy/pandas vector operations can beat an R loop that updates one row at a time.
R’s vectorized operations and data.table are the relevant optimized comparisons.
For custom repeated calculations, Python’s @numba.njit can compile a loop. Compare with R’s compiled options, such as Rcpp, too.

No universal winner: measure the actual operation and peak memory.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Machine learning with scikit-learn
Example: predict a binary follow-up outcome from baseline measurements.







Part of the analysis
scikit-learn tools




Prepare predictors
SimpleImputer, StandardScaler


Fit a prediction model
LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier


Combine the steps
make_pipeline()


Evaluate on held-out folds
cross_validate()



Models share a fit(X, y) / predict(X_new) interface. Python is useful when the research team’s models and preprocessing use this API.
R counterparts: mlr3 (successor to mlr), tidymodels, and caret also support model fitting, resampling, and tuning.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: A scikit-learn pipeline in a research study
text:
A scikit-learn pipeline in a research study
Illustration: X has numeric predictors, y has 0/1 outcomes, and each row is an independent participant.
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

model = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(), StandardScaler(),
                      LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
scores = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
The pipeline learns preprocessing within each training fold. scores["test_score"] contains the five held-out ROC AUC values.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Deep learning: why Python is useful
text:
Deep learning: why Python is useful

A collaborator shares a Python neural-network model for research on medical images. What would we need to understand to use their code?


Images contain arrays of pixel values that become model inputs.
Libraries such as PyTorch provide tensors and tools for training models.
A tensor is a multidimensional array used for data and model parameters.
Python knowledge helps us read and adapt the collaborator’s workflow.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: GPUs: why they help deep learning
text:
GPUs: why they help deep learning

Training repeatedly performs matrix operations on data and model parameters.
A GPU can perform many numerical operations in parallel.
Python libraries send supported operations to the GPU. Python syntax alone does not provide the acceleration.
Benefits depend on the workload. Data transfers and limited GPU memory also matter.

For this session: understand the use case. No GPU or extra software is required.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Research software: single-cell biology








Research task
Python software
Example API




Quality control and clustering of single-cell RNA-seq
Scanpy
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics() / sc.tl.leiden()


Model and integrate single-cell expression across batches
scvi-tools
scvi.model.SCVI



Why learn Python here? A collaborator shares an AnnData object and a Scanpy/scvi-tools workflow. Python lets you inspect the data, adjust the analysis, and reuse that implementation.
Goal 1 check: name a package, the research task it supports, and why you would use its Python workflow.

Component
Role




Positron
Editor and interface for running code


Python interpreter
Executes the Python code


NumPy / pandas
Libraries imported by that interpreter


.py file
Saved source that Git can track

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Goal 3 · Recognize Python data objects
Recognize lists, NumPy arrays, and pandas DataFrames.








Object
Typical use
Familiar R comparison




Python list
Sequence that can mix types
R list


NumPy array
Typed numerical data and arithmetic
Atomic vector or matrix


pandas DataFrame
Rows and named columns
Data frame / tibble



A pandas Series is one labeled column. A DataFrame can contain columns of different types.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Assignment and basic objects
age = 42
group = "treated"
observed = True
values = [4.1, 5.2, None]
Python uses = for assignment and indentation to define blocks. A Python list can contain mixed types; it is not a NumPy array.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Lists and arrays behave differently
values = [1, 2, 3]
values * 2                   # [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
x * 2                        # array([2., 4., 6.])
x.mean()                     # 2.0
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
x * 2                        # 2 4 6
mean(x)                      # 2
Check: which Python object supports the arithmetic you intended?

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Our DataFrame: the starter’s participant visits
text:
Our DataFrame: the starter’s participant visits
Run the starter’s Synthetic data cell, then inspect visit:
visit.shape          # (12, 4)
visit.dtypes         # types of the four columns
visit.head()         # first five participant-visit rows



Column
Meaning




id
Six participants, P01 through P06


arm
Control or treated, three participants each


week
Baseline (0) or follow-up (4)


marker
Numeric outcome, with two missing week-4 values



One row represents one participant at one visit.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Functions, methods, and attributes



Intent
R
Python




Number of rows
nrow(visit)
len(visit)


Column names
names(visit)
visit.columns


Mean of numeric array x
mean(x)
x.mean()




len(visit) calls a function with an argument.
x.mean() calls a method attached to an object.
visit.columns reads an attribute, without parentheses.

Goal 3 check: identify values, x, and visit by their object types.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Goal 4 · Translate one familiar analysis
Translate selection, transformation, and grouped summaries.
Run r-reference.R in R to load the matching data. In both languages:

Keep all week-4 rows, including missing outcomes.
Add a month column from week / 4.
Summarize within randomized arm.
Report total n, observed n, mean, and sample SD.

The output has one row per arm. Missing outcomes contribute to total n.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Column and row selection
visit[["marker"]]                  # a vector
visit["marker"]                    # a one-column data frame
visit[visit$week == 4, ]            # week-4 rows
visit["marker"]                    # a Series
visit[["marker"]]                  # a one-column DataFrame
visit.loc[visit["week"] == 4, :]    # week-4 rows, all columns
loc accepts column labels and a Boolean row condition.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Keep the analysis population intact
week4 <- visit[visit$week == 4, ]
nrow(week4)                         # 6
week4 = visit.loc[visit["week"] == 4].copy()
len(week4)                         # 6
Both keep six rows, including the two missing outcomes.
Dropping missing outcomes now would reduce the total denominator.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Add a derived column
week4$month <- week4$week / 4
week4 = week4.assign(month=week4["week"] / 4)
week4[["id", "week", "month"]]
The new month value is 1 for every retained row.
The transformation adds a column and keeps the same six rows.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
The familiar R grouped summary
library(dplyr)

r_summary <- week4 |>
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_observed = sum(!is.na(marker)),
    mean_marker = mean(marker, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_marker = sd(marker, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = arm
  )
Count all rows for total n. Use observed outcomes for the mean and SD.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
The corresponding pandas summary
summary = week4.groupby("arm", as_index=False).agg(
    n_total=("id", "size"),

Slices: expressions and results
x = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])

x[-1]    # 40

x[1:3] returns 20, 30: the stop position is excluded.

week4.loc[1:3]             # labels 1 through 3, inclusive

loc selects by label and includes the ending label in a slice.
Filtering retains the original index labels. They need not start at 0.

title: Session 11 · Conditions and Functions
text:
Session outline and content

1. Conditions
Begin with unequal-length paired measurements: R can silently recycle values and produce incorrect changes. Use if to check whether calculation may proceed, then repair a vector condition using ifelse() for row labels or any()/all() for a group decision. Treat missing and empty conditions separately before practice.


2. Why functions?
Identify duplicated calculations and state inputs, options, outputs, and edge cases.


3. Function basics
Read an existing function call: package namespace, function name, parameters, supplied arguments, and return value. Connect these to Usage, Arguments, and Value in its help page. Build a summary from a checked calculation, identify required inputs and options, trace a call, and check changed inputs. Extend the helper with an observed count, missing count, and explicit missing-data policy. Use explicit return() calls and invisible() when automatic printing is unwanted. Practice one four-component summary and extract results by name.


4. Scope
Replace hidden global dependencies with explicit arguments.


5. Validation
Use guard clauses and enforce the safe-mean and scalar-center contracts. Trace the first exit for invalid, all-missing, empty, and ordinary inputs.


6. Data-frame functions
Check columns and distinguish quoted-name extraction from bare-name dplyr interfaces.


7. Refactoring and reuse
Compose paired-change helpers and compare against hand-built and original results. Save reusable definitions in R scripts, load them with source(), and verify the report in a fresh session.


8. Exit check
Explain the contract and the evidence that intended behavior was preserved.

3. Function basics · Practice 2
Open help("median", package = "stats"). Identify the package, function name, parameters, and default for na.rm. Use Value to predict the result type and length for stats::median(c(120, NA, 140), na.rm = TRUE). Distinguish the parameter names from the argument values supplied in that call.

State the required input type, length, and output shape. reference_mean <- 130

title: Session 11 guided lab
text:

Add checks to centre_values(): x must be a numeric vector and centre must be one finite number. Reject a character center, a missing center, infinity, and a center of length two. Use && in the order type, shape, value.
Then implement safe_mean(x) with this contract:

Accept a numeric vector containing finite values and missing values (NA/NaN).
Ignore missing observations and return one numeric mean.
Return NA_real_ for an empty or all-missing numeric vector.
Reject nonnumeric input, matrices, and infinite values with useful errors.

Check c(2, 4, NA), numeric(0), c(NA_real_, NA_real_), "4", and c(2, Inf). Do not convert invalid character input silently.

Call it with summarise_column(markers, "marker_a"). Explain why data$column would look for the wrong name. Contrast this interface with the lecture’s summarise_by_arm(data, outcome) and {{ outcome }}.

section: 7. Refactoring and reuse · Practice 5 and integrated task
text:
7. Refactoring and reuse · Practice 5 and integrated task
The starter contains repeated calculations for marker A and marker B.

Write classify_change(change), returning a character vector of the same length. Negative changes are "decrease", zero and positive changes are "no decrease", and missing changes are "missing". Empty input returns character(0). Reject nonnumeric input and matrices.
Write change_summary(baseline, followup) to validate numeric vectors of equal length, reject infinity, compute followup - baseline, and return a data frame with numeric change and character category columns.
Use classify_change() inside it. Document that observations must already be matched by patient and in the same order.
Compare the result for c(10, 8, NA, 12) and c(8, 9, 7, 12) with a hand-built expected table: changes -2, 1, NA, 0 and the corresponding labels.
Replace both repeated blocks with calls to change_summary(). Compare each result with its original using isTRUE(all.equal(...)).
Check zero-length, all-missing, one-pair, unequal-length, and invalid-type inputs. Show expected failures without preventing your report from rendering.

The labels describe direction only. They do not establish clinical benefit or statistical significance. Equal lengths alone cannot verify patient alignment.

Save and reuse the completed helpers
Keep the supplied validated centre_values() in R/centre-values.R. Compare it with your completed version. Move safe_mean(), summarise_column(), classify_change(), and change_summary() into R/functions.R. These files should contain definitions and documentation, not data loading or example calls.
In your saved report, source both files before their first use:
source("R/centre-values.R")
source("R/functions.R")
These paths are relative to the report folder during rendering. In the Console, use here::here("work", "session11", "R", "functions.R") from your personal project. After verifying the saved helpers, remove their duplicate definitions from the report. Restart R and render without manually running helpers first. Submit both R files with the report so someone else can reproduce it.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Learning goals

Implement a within-arm bootstrap for a mean difference.
Report bootstrap SE and an interval, and explain computational stability.
Specify the null and reassignment rule before permuting labels.
Preserve participants, pairs, or clusters when resampling.
Distinguish sampling uncertainty from Monte Carlo variability.
Choose a resampling scheme for independent, paired, or grouped data.

Method

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: The same line of code, twice
text:
The same line of code, twice

sbp <- c(150, 142, 168, 131, 155)

set.seed(1)
sample(sbp, replace = TRUE)   # bootstrap: some values twice, some not at all

[1] 150 131 150 142 155

sample(sbp)                   # permutation: same values, new order

[1] 168 142 131 150 155





With replacement: values may repeat or be omitted.
Without replacement: same values, new order. This changes their pairing with labels, arms, or times.










For length(x) > 1, sample(x) permutes the values. To sample positions in code, prefer sample.int(length(x)).

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Why it works at all
The thing you want is a property of the population: the standard deviation of your estimator across repeated samples from it.

You do not have the population. You have one sample — which is your best available estimate of it.








The plug-in principle. Wherever the formula says population, substitute the empirical distribution of your sample, and compute.






So: resample from your data exactly as nature sampled from the population — same size n, drawn with replacement — and watch how the statistic moves.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Resample, recompute, collect





flowchart LR
  D["<b>your data</b><br/>n = 60"] --> R["<b>resample</b><br/>n = 60,<br/>with replacement"]
  R --> S["<b>recompute</b><br/>the statistic"]
  S --> C["<b>collect</b><br/>one number"]
  C -.->|"B = 2000 times"| R
  C --> H["<b>bootstrap<br/>distribution</b>"]
  style D fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style R fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style S fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff








Three lines of code, and none of them are new. sample() is Session 14, indexing a data frame by a vector of row numbers is Session 4, and replicate() repeats a calculation as in Session 14.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The statistic, as a function
We estimate the Treatment-minus-Placebo mean difference in 12-week SBP. Use the same statistic in the lecture, lab, bootstrap, and permutation test. Welch provides an independent standard-error comparison.

# Difference in mean sbp_12, Treatment minus Placebo.
# Takes a data frame with `arm` and `sbp_12`; returns one number.
mean_diff <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), all(c("arm", "sbp_12") %in% names(data)))
  mean(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Treatment"]) -
    mean(data$sbp_12[data$arm == "Placebo"])
}

obs_mean <- mean_diff(trial)
obs_mean

[1] -12.43333




Statistic first, resampling second. If the function is wrong, 2000 resamples make it wrong 2000 times.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Bootstrap within treatment arms

set.seed(14)
B <- 2000

boot_mean <- replicate(B, {
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial)), trial$arm)
  idx <- unlist(lapply(groups, function(i)
    i[sample.int(length(i), length(i), replace = TRUE)]))
  mean_diff(trial[idx, ])
})

str(boot_mean)

 num [1:2000] -13.63 -5.23 -8.83 -11.9 -10.63 ...

head(round(boot_mean, 1))

[1] -13.6  -5.2  -8.8 -11.9 -10.6 -11.0
