title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
What came back


Figure 1: Bootstrap distribution of the difference in mean SBP at 12 weeks.

The distribution is centered near the observed mean difference. Its spread estimates the sampling uncertainty under this resampling scheme.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The bootstrap standard error
The standard deviation of the resampled statistics is the estimated standard error. That is the whole definition.

se_boot <- sd(boot_mean)
se_boot

[1] 3.487651




mean(boot_mean) - obs_mean    # bootstrap estimate of bias

[1] 0.1196667





This is bias relative to the empirical distribution of the observed sample. It is not the true bias measured against a known population parameter in Session 14.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Percentile and basic intervals

perc <- quantile(boot_mean, c(.025, .975))
basic <- 2 * obs_mean - quantile(boot_mean, c(.975, .025))
rbind(percentile = unname(perc), basic = unname(basic))

                [,1]      [,2]
percentile -19.13333 -5.663333
basic      -19.20333 -5.733333



Percentile: use quantiles of the bootstrap estimates directly.
Basic: reflect those quantiles around the observed estimate.
Both rely on a suitable bootstrap approximation; neither automatically has 95% coverage in small, biased, or irregular problems.

Compare endpoints and assumptions. Do not choose whichever interval gives a preferred conclusion.

Compare the bootstrap and Welch standard errors

c(boot_se = sd(boot_mean),
  welch_se = t.test(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)$stderr)

 boot_se welch_se 
3.487651 3.571884 




Agreement is a useful implementation check. Interval coverage requires a separate evaluation, such as simulation under a known data-generating mechanism.

t(vapply(1501:1503, boot_interval, numeric(2)))

          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] -19.30083 -5.433333
[2,] -19.86833 -6.033333

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Limits of the ordinary bootstrap







Situation
Why extra resamples do not solve it




Very small samples
The empirical distribution may poorly represent the population


Extremes or boundary parameters
The ordinary bootstrap approximation can fail


Heavy tails
Usual finite-variance approximations may fail even though a sampling distribution exists


Dependent rows
Independent row resampling destroys the study’s dependence



A smooth histogram is not proof of validity. Simulation in a relevant known-truth setting can evaluate coverage; the sampling design determines the resampling unit.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The maximum, bootstrapped

set.seed(18)
boot_max <- replicate(B, max(trial$sbp_0[sample(nrow(trial), replace = TRUE)]))

length(unique(boot_max))                # distinct values across 2000 resamples

[1] 7

mean(boot_max == max(trial$sbp_0))      # how often the resample max is THE max

[1] 0.634




The resampled maximum can never exceed the observed maximum, and it equals it when a unique largest observed value is drawn at all — probability 1 − (1 − 1/n)n ≈ 0.63.









The bootstrap distribution of a maximum is a spike at the observed value with a short left tail. It can be a poor approximation to sampling a new maximum from the population. Increasing B cannot fix that mismatch.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: Two packages you should know exist
text:
Two packages you should know exist
Optional package syntax for the same within-arm bootstrap:
# boot: the classical implementation. Statistic takes (data, indices).
library(boot)
b <- boot(trial, statistic = function(data, i) mean_diff(data[i, ]),
          R = 10000, strata = trial$arm)
boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "basic", "bca"))

# rsample: tidymodels. Resamples as a tibble of splits.
library(rsample)
bootstraps(trial, times = 1000, strata = arm)


boot.ci() gives you BCa intervals — bias-corrected and accelerated — which adjust interval endpoints using bias correction and an acceleration term. They still require a suitable resampling scheme and regularity conditions; they do not repair dependence or an unrepresentative sample.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: The null and the reassignment rule
text:
The null and the reassignment rule
In a completely randomized trial with fixed arm sizes, a randomization test of the sharp null of no effect for any participant holds outcomes fixed and reassigns treatment according to the actual randomization scheme.
For independent observational samples, unrestricted label permutation instead needs exchangeability under the null, such as identical group distributions.
Equal means alone do not guarantee exchangeability when variances differ. Blocked or paired randomization requires restricted reassignment.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Shuffle the labels

obs_mean <- mean_diff(trial)

set.seed(19)
P <- 999
perm_stat <- replicate(P, {
  shuffled <- sample(trial$arm)                 # permutation, not a bootstrap
  mean(trial$sbp_12[shuffled == "Treatment"]) -
    mean(trial$sbp_12[shuffled == "Placebo"])
})

c(observed = obs_mean, perm_mean = mean(perm_stat), perm_sd = sd(perm_stat))

    observed    perm_mean      perm_sd 
-12.43333333   0.05789122   3.82457944 




Note what is not shuffled: sbp_12 never moves. Only its label does. Jointly reordering outcome-label rows changes nothing. Breaking their pairing creates the reference distribution; the reassignment rule must match the design.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The null distribution


Figure 2: Permutation null distribution of the mean difference, with the observed value.

Centred at zero by construction. The p-value is the proportion of this histogram at least as extreme as the line.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Exact, or Monte Carlo?
With 4 patients per arm there are only choose(8, 4) = 70 possible label assignments. You can enumerate all of them:

small <- trial[c(1:4, 31:34), c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")]
obs_small <- mean_diff(small)

combos <- combn(8, 4)                    # every way to choose 4 "Treatment"
exact <- apply(combos, 2, function(k) mean(small$sbp_12[k]) -
                                      mean(small$sbp_12[-k]))

ncol(combos)                             # the entire reference set

[1] 70

round(mean(abs(exact) >= abs(obs_small)), 4)    # exact two-sided p-value

[1] 0.0571




With 30 per arm there are choose(60, 30) ≈ 1.2 × 1017. So you sample from them instead — that is all “Monte Carlo permutation” means.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: A permutation p-value is never zero
text:
A permutation p-value is never zero

n_extreme <- sum(abs(perm_stat) >= abs(obs_mean))
n_extreme                                        # out of 999

[1] 0




c(wrong = n_extreme / P,
  right = (n_extreme + 1) / (P + 1))

wrong right 
0.000 0.001 





The observed arrangement is one of the possible arrangements. Counting it in both numerator and denominator is not a fudge to avoid zero — it is the correct count.









With P = 999 and no sampled statistic as extreme, report the adjusted Monte Carlo p-value 0.001 and its limited resolution. Increase P if finer resolution is needed; do not report p = 0.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Interpret a permutation result

A p-value measures incompatibility with the specified null and reassignment scheme.
It does not by itself quantify the effect or remove confounding.
Report the observed mean difference alongside the test result.
This class computes tests; confidence intervals by inverting suitable tests are a further method, not an impossibility.

For an observational comparison, do not interpret a significant label-permutation result as evidence of a causal treatment effect.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Monte Carlo p-value uncertainty

extreme <- sum(abs(perm_stat) >= abs(obs_mean))
c(adjusted_p = (extreme + 1) / (P + 1),
  min_reportable = 1 / (P + 1))

    adjusted_p min_reportable 
         0.001          0.001 

binom.test(extreme, P)$conf.int

[1] 0.000000000 0.003685763
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


The interval describes the tail probability estimated by independent random permutations conditional on the observed data. It is not a confidence interval for the treatment effect. Exact enumeration has no Monte Carlo sampling error.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Practice: which reassignment is allowed?
Treatment was randomized separately within each site. A student permutes all treatment labels across the pooled dataset.
What design feature has been lost? What must remain fixed?

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: Define the statistic for repeated visits
text:
Define the statistic for repeated visits

diff_long <- function(data) {
  mean(data$sbp[data$arm == "Treatment"]) - mean(data$sbp[data$arm == "Placebo"])
}
obs_long <- diff_long(trial_long)
obs_long

[1] -7.1



180 rows. 60 patients. Hold on to that distinction — the rest of this block is about which number is the sample size.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The naive row bootstrap

set.seed(21)
boot_row <- replicate(B, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(trial_long), replace = TRUE)   # 180 rows, independently
  diff_long(trial_long[idx, ])
})

c(estimate = obs_long, se = sd(boot_row))

 estimate        se 
-7.100000  1.878739 

round(quantile(boot_row, c(0.025, 0.975)), 2)

 2.5% 97.5% 
-10.7  -3.4 




Perfectly reasonable code. Runs without complaint. Produces a clean, symmetric histogram. The interval comfortably excludes zero.









It is wrong, and nothing on this slide tells you so.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The cluster bootstrap
Resample patients, and take all of each patient’s rows with them.

ids <- unique(trial_long$id)
rows_by_id <- split(seq_len(nrow(trial_long)), trial_long$id)   # id -> row numbers

set.seed(22)
boot_clu <- replicate(B, {
  picked <- sample(ids, replace = TRUE)              # 60 patients, with repeats
  diff_long(trial_long[unlist(rows_by_id[picked]), ])
})

c(row_se = sd(boot_row), cluster_se = sd(boot_clu),
  ratio = sd(boot_clu) / sd(boot_row))

    row_se cluster_se      ratio 
  1.878739   3.222562   1.715279 




Compare the two estimated SEs. With strong within-person dependence, independent row resampling understates uncertainty in this example.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Side by side


Figure 3: Bootstrap distributions of the same estimate under two resampling schemes.

Same data, same estimate, same statistic function. Only the unit changed.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Dependence limits information
The teaching generator uses a participant intercept with SD 12 and visit noise with SD 4. Within each arm, its known correlation is:

rho <- 12^2 / (12^2 + 4^2)
c(rho = rho, design_effect = 1 + (3 - 1) * rho,
  approximate_se_inflation = sqrt(1 + 2 * rho))

                     rho            design_effect approximate_se_inflation 
                 0.90000                  2.80000                  1.67332 


For equally sized clusters with this correlation structure, the design effect explains why three correlated visits are not three independent participants. This calculation uses the generator’s parameters, not a fitted ICC estimate.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: Permuting at the wrong level, too
text:
Permuting at the wrong level, too
The same mistake, in the other half of the session:

arm_by_id <- trial_long$arm[match(ids, trial_long$id)]

set.seed(32)
p_rows <- replicate(999, {
  s <- sample(trial_long$arm)                    # shuffles visits, not patients
  mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Treatment"]) - mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Placebo"])
})

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: Permute patient assignments, then carry them to visits
text:
Permute patient assignments, then carry them to visits

p_pats <- replicate(999, {
  assigned <- sample(arm_by_id)
  s <- assigned[match(trial_long$id, ids)]      # join by ID, not row order
  mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Treatment"]) - mean(trial_long$sbp[s == "Placebo"])
})

c(p_row_unit = (sum(abs(p_rows) >= abs(obs_long)) + 1) / 1000,
  p_patient_unit = (sum(abs(p_pats) >= abs(obs_long)) + 1) / 1000)

    p_row_unit p_patient_unit 
         0.001          0.034 



Compare the results and their resolution. Randomisation happened to patients, so the permutation must too.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
The resampling unit








Design
Bootstrap or validation unit
Permutation restriction




Independent participants
Participant
Allowed participant assignments


Repeated visits
Participant with all visits
Keep one treatment per participant


Cluster randomized
Clinic or other randomized cluster
Reassign at cluster level


Matched pairs
Pair
Swap labels within pairs when justified


Time series
Dependence-preserving blocks or temporal splits
Requires a justified dependence model



Sampling, randomization, and prediction targets can imply different rules. State the rule before using sample().

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Prediction requires held-out outcomes
The target is error for new participants from a stated population, using predictors available when the prediction will be made.
Training error evaluates data already used to fit the model. Cross-validation instead repeats fitting on training folds and predicting an assessment fold.
We will predict 12-week SBP from baseline variables. A week-12 derived variable would be unavailable at baseline, even if it greatly improved the reported score.

title: Resampling Methods
section: The model interface for this exercise
text:
The model interface for this exercise

cv_data <- trial[, c("id", "arm", "age", "sbp_0", "sbp_12")]
fit_demo <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = cv_data)
head(predict(fit_demo, newdata = cv_data), 3)

       1        2        3 
156.8157 158.8617 154.1750 


lm(response ~ predictors, data = ...) fits a linear regression. predict(fit, newdata = ...) applies its learned coefficients. These predictions are in-sample; Session 16 examines model objects in detail.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Assign and inspect folds

set.seed(1550)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(cv_data)))
table(fold, cv_data$arm)

    
fold Placebo Treatment
   1       6         6
   2       6         6
   3       6         6
   4       5         7
   5       7         5

stopifnot(length(fold) == nrow(cv_data), all(fold %in% 1:5))

Every participant belongs to one assessment fold and appears in training for the other four fits. Balanced counts do not alone establish representative folds.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
One training and assessment split

k <- 1
train <- cv_data[fold != k, ]
assess <- cv_data[fold == k, ]
stopifnot(length(intersect(train$id, assess$id)) == 0L)
fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = train)
head(data.frame(id = assess$id, observed = assess$sbp_12,
                prediction = predict(fit, newdata = assess)), 3)

     id observed prediction
4  P004      163   153.8960
5  P005      140   142.3262
14 P014      139   139.6845


The assessment outcomes are used for scoring, not fitting.

title: Resampling Methods
section: A complete set of held-out predictions
text:
A complete set of held-out predictions

prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(cv_data))
seen <- integer(nrow(cv_data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
  test <- fold == k
  fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm, data = cv_data[!test, ])
  prediction[test] <- predict(fit, newdata = cv_data[test, ])
  seen[test] <- seen[test] + 1L
}
stopifnot(all(seen == 1L), all(is.finite(prediction)))

Preallocate with NA, not zero, so an unfilled prediction is detectable.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Score each participant once

loss <- (cv_data$sbp_12 - prediction)^2
c(cv_rmse = sqrt(mean(loss)),
  training_rmse = sqrt(mean(residuals(fit_demo)^2)))

      cv_rmse training_rmse 
     8.551577      7.930126 

tapply(loss, fold, mean)

        1         2         3         4         5 
114.61935  79.66088  46.29515  70.75535  54.31664 


RMSE has the outcome’s units. Aggregate participant losses before taking the square root. An unweighted average of fold RMSEs is generally a different quantity.

title: Resampling Methods
section: Missing predictors require a learned rule
text:
Missing predictors require a learned rule

cv_missing <- cv_data
cv_missing$sbp_0[c(2, 8, 17, 32, 46, 55)] <- NA_real_
train <- cv_missing[fold != 1, ]
assess <- cv_missing[fold == 1, ]
replacement <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- replacement
assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- replacement

Learn the replacement from training rows; apply the same value to assessment rows. Mean imputation is a teaching example, not a general recommendation for missing data.

title: Resampling Methods
Resampling Methods
text:
Verify the prediction contract

held_out <- cv_predict(cv_missing, fold)
stopifnot(length(held_out) == nrow(cv_missing),
          all(is.finite(held_out)))
sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - held_out)^2))

[1] 8.571046


Also inspect training group sizes and factor levels. A predictor level never seen during training needs a declared handling strategy, not a silent recode.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
A deliberately leaky version

leaky_data <- cv_missing
global_mean <- mean(leaky_data$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
leaky_data$sbp_0[is.na(leaky_data$sbp_0)] <- global_mean
leaky_prediction <- cv_predict(leaky_data, fold)
c(valid = sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - held_out)^2)),
  leaky = sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - leaky_prediction)^2)))

   valid    leaky 
8.571046 8.599058 


The assessment covariates influenced the imputation rule. The scores may be close, and leakage need not improve every realization. Validity follows the information flow, not which score happens to be smaller.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Diagnose leakage before comparing scores







Step
Valid location




Fixed, prespecified unit conversion
Can be applied to all rows


Mean imputation or scaling estimated from data
Training fold


Choose features using outcome associations
Training fold, with selection validated


Select a model or tuning parameter
Inner validation, separate from final evaluation


Compute RMSE
Held-out outcomes after predictions are fixed



A fixed rule is different from a rule estimated using assessment data.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Compare with a simple benchmark

baseline_prediction <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(cv_data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
  baseline_prediction[fold == k] <- mean(cv_data$sbp_12[fold != k])
}
c(training_mean_benchmark =
    sqrt(mean((cv_data$sbp_12 - baseline_prediction)^2)),
  regression = sqrt(mean((cv_data$sbp_12 - prediction)^2)))

training_mean_benchmark              regression 
              15.007163                8.551577 


Use the same folds for each candidate. More predictors need not improve prediction.

title: Resampling Methods
Resampling Methods
text:
Inspect the stratified fold composition

set.seed(1551)
table(make_folds(cv_data$arm), cv_data$arm)

   
    Placebo Treatment
  1       6         6
  2       6         6
  3       6         6
  4       6         6
  5       6         6


Stratification can stabilize composition. It does not repair dependence or make a rare category large enough for every fold.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Repeated cross-validation

cv_rmse_once <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  f <- make_folds(cv_missing$arm)
  p <- cv_predict(cv_missing, f)
  sqrt(mean((cv_missing$sbp_12 - p)^2))
}
scores <- vapply(1561:1570, cv_rmse_once, numeric(1))
summary(scores)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  8.156   8.317   8.544   8.509   8.659   8.897 


Repeated splits describe sensitivity to fold assignment on this dataset. They are not independent new studies; do not treat their SD as a sampling SE or their range as a population confidence interval.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Grouped and temporal validation







Deployment question
Appropriate split idea




Predict a new participant
Keep all visits of a participant together


Predict at a new clinic
Hold out clinics


Predict future outcomes
Train on earlier observations; assess later observations



ids <- unique(trial_long$id)
id_fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(ids)))
row_fold <- id_fold[match(trial_long$id, ids)]
Random row folds answer the wrong question if the same participant appears on both sides.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Selection and final evaluation
Trying many models and reporting the lowest CV error uses the evaluation data to make a selection. The selected score can be optimistic.
Use a prespecified candidate, an untouched test set, or nested cross-validation:

An outer split reserves data for evaluation.
Inner training splits choose features and tuning parameters.
Refit the selected procedure on outer training data; predict outer assessment data.

After evaluation, a final model can be fitted to the intended full training set.

title: Resampling Methods
text:
Lab route and exit check

Bootstrap a treatment-minus-control mean difference within arms.
Compare Monte Carlo and exact permutation calculations.
Build checked folds and held-out predictions with fold-specific imputation.
Compare valid and leaky preprocessing, then repeat the fold assignment.
State how the procedure changes for repeated visits or a new clinic.

Explain: Which uncertainty shrinks with more bootstrap draws? What makes a prediction held out?

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
References

R bootstrap implementation
R bootstrap confidence intervals

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Summary

Bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty from observed data.
Permutation constructs a reference distribution under a specified null.
The resampling unit and reassignment rule must match the study design.
More resamples reduce Monte Carlo variability without adding participants.

Next: regression models, prediction, cross-validation, and a complete course recap in Session 16.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Two resampling targets








Method
Repeated operation
Target




Bootstrap
Sample observational units with replacement
Sampling uncertainty of an estimate


Permutation
Reassign labels under a valid null scheme
Null reference distribution of a statistic



Replacement alone does not determine validity. Specify the target, the unit, and which relationships the repeated operation must preserve.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Exact enumeration: a short demonstration
With 4 patients per arm there are only choose(8, 4) = 70 possible label assignments. You can enumerate all of them:

small <- trial[c(1:4, 31:34), c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")]
obs_small <- mean_diff(small)

combos <- combn(8, 4)                    # every way to choose 4 "Treatment"
exact <- apply(combos, 2, function(k) mean(small$sbp_12[k]) -
                                      mean(small$sbp_12[-k]))

ncol(combos)                             # the entire reference set

[1] 70

round(mean(abs(exact) >= abs(obs_small)), 4)    # exact two-sided p-value

[1] 0.0571




With 30 per arm there are choose(60, 30) ≈ 1.2 × 1017. So you sample from them instead — that is all “Monte Carlo permutation” means.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Guided lab and exit check

Bootstrap the mean difference within treatment arms.
Report SE and intervals, and inspect stability across documented seeds.
Permute treatment labels under the specified randomization scheme.
Preserve participants when there are repeated visits.
Bootstrap paired changes and explain what the estimate does and does not mean.

Explain: What changes when you increase the number of resamples? Which question calls for bootstrap or permutation? Why must both measurements from a participant stay together?

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Why do we need resampling?
We usually have one dataset, but our questions concern what would happen with other samples or other assignments.







Project question
What is hard to observe directly?




How uncertain is our estimated median or mean difference?
The estimate across many new samples


Is this group difference surprising under no effect?
Results under other allowed assignments



Resampling reuses the observed data in a deliberate way to approximate these comparisons. It does not create new independent information.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Two questions, two resampling methods








Method
What we repeat
Main output




Bootstrap
Sample participants with replacement and recompute an estimate
Standard error or confidence interval


Permutation
Reassign labels according to the null and study design
Reference distribution and p-value



Choose the method from the question, then specify the unit and what must stay together. A bootstrap interval describes uncertainty in an estimate; a permutation p-value assesses evidence against a specified null.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
When resampling helps

A useful statistic has no simple standard-error formula, such as a median or a result calculated by a multistep analysis.
A randomized experiment supplies a natural way to construct a null comparison.
A paired or clustered design needs uncertainty estimates that preserve its structure.

For a simple mean difference, a standard t method may already be adequate. Resampling is an additional tool, not a requirement for every analysis.
The design still matters: biased data, dependent rows, and information leakage do not disappear when we repeat the calculation.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: Real-data project: uncertainty in median tumour thickness
text:
Real-data project: uncertainty in median tumour thickness
boot::melanoma contains 205 patients who underwent melanoma surgery in Odense, Denmark. Tumour thickness is recorded in millimetres.
Our teaching analysis: estimate median tumour thickness and its uncertainty for a population represented by this cohort. This is a new analysis of the data, not a claim about the original study’s analysis.
Resample patients with replacement, compute the median each time, and use the distribution to estimate its SE and interval. This avoids deriving a statistic-specific SE formula, but still relies on a suitable sample and bootstrap.

Source: R documentation for the melanoma cohort. This example uses thickness, not censored survival time.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: A bootstrap project in a few lines
text:
A bootstrap project in a few lines

thickness <- boot::melanoma$thickness
stopifnot(length(thickness) == 205L, all(is.finite(thickness)))
set.seed(1500)
boot_median <- replicate(2000,
  median(sample(thickness, replace = TRUE)))
round(c(estimate = median(thickness), SE = sd(boot_median),
        quantile(boot_median, c(.025, .975))), 2)

estimate       SE     2.5%    97.5% 
    1.94     0.19     1.62     2.26 


Report the median, bootstrap SE, and percentile interval in mm. The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the resampling assumptions. It does not show the range containing 95% of individual patients.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Optional: Percentile and basic intervals

perc <- quantile(boot_mean, c(.025, .975))
basic <- 2 * obs_mean - quantile(boot_mean, c(.975, .025))
rbind(percentile = unname(perc), basic = unname(basic))

                [,1]      [,2]
percentile -19.13333 -5.663333
basic      -19.20333 -5.733333



Percentile: use quantiles of the bootstrap estimates directly.
Basic: reflect those quantiles around the observed estimate.
Both rely on a suitable bootstrap approximation; neither automatically has 95% coverage in small, biased, or irregular problems.

Compare endpoints and assumptions. Do not choose whichever interval gives a preferred conclusion.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Real experiment: promotion recommendations
Rosen and Jerdee’s experiment randomly assigned 48 bank supervisors otherwise identical personnel files labelled male or female, 24 of each.



File label
Recommended promotion
Total




Male
21
24


Female
14
24



The observed difference is 21/24−14/24=0.29221/24 - 14/24 = 0.292 (29.2 percentage points). Question: could an assignment difference this large arise if the label had no effect on any supervisor’s decision?

Rosen & Jerdee (1974), via OpenIntro data and study design.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Why permutation fits this project
Under the sharp null, each supervisor’s decision would be unchanged by the file label. Keep the 48 decisions fixed and randomly assign 24 male labels and 24 female labels again.

decision <- c(rep(1, 21), rep(0, 3), rep(1, 14), rep(0, 10))
observed_gap <- 21/24 - 14/24
set.seed(1501)
null_gap <- replicate(9999, {
  male <- sample.int(48, 24)
  mean(decision[male]) - mean(decision[-male])
})
(1 + sum(abs(null_gap) >= abs(observed_gap) - 1e-12)) / 10000

[1] 0.0526


This two-sided p-value measures evidence against the null under the assignment scheme. It does not estimate the size or uncertainty of an effect.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Which bootstrap fits the data?








Approach
What is sampled?
Typical use




Ordinary nonparametric
Observed independent units, with replacement
Median, mean, or another sample statistic


Stratified
Units within each specified group
Preserve treatment-arm sample sizes


Paired or cluster
Whole pairs or clusters
Keep related measurements together


Parametric
New data from a fitted probability model
Use an explicit model for data generation



The parametric bootstrap connects to Session 14, but estimates the generating parameters from the observed data. Its validity depends on that fitted model.

R’s boot documentation describes ordinary, stratified, and parametric resampling.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Paired measurements: bootstrap the change
For the treatment arm, estimate mean 12-week minus baseline SBP. Each participant contributes one paired change.

treated <- trial[trial$arm == "Treatment", ]
change <- treated$sbp_12 - treated$sbp_0
set.seed(1530)
boot_change <- replicate(2000,
  mean(sample(change, length(change), replace = TRUE)))
round(c(mean_change = mean(change), SE = sd(boot_change),
        quantile(boot_change, c(.025, .975))), 2)

mean_change          SE        2.5%       97.5% 
     -13.37        1.62      -16.60      -10.23 


Sampling changes preserves the pairing. Sampling baseline and follow-up values separately would break it. This estimates change within one arm, not a causal treatment effect relative to a control group.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
section: A paired permutation test needs a justified rule
text:
A paired permutation test needs a justified rule
In a randomized matched-pair experiment, one member of each pair receives each treatment. Under the sharp null, swap treatment labels within each pair according to the assignment scheme.
For a difference statistic, a within-pair swap reverses the sign of that pair’s difference. It does not move a person’s outcome into a different pair.
Before-and-after measurements alone do not justify random swapping of time labels. Sign-flipping observational changes requires a suitable null model, such as independent differences symmetric about zero.
The bootstrap can describe uncertainty in a mean change without establishing the randomization assumptions of a paired permutation test.

title: Resampling: Bootstrap and Permutation
text:
Choosing and reporting the analysis







Decision
What to state




Standard method or resampling?
A t method may suffice for a mean; bootstrap can help with less familiar statistics


Estimate uncertainty or test a null?
Report an interval or a justified p-value for the stated question


Which units and restrictions?
Participants, pairs, clusters, and fixed group sizes


How much computation?
Number of resamples, seed, and stability or Monte Carlo precision


What can the result support?
Target population, assumptions, missingness, and limits



More resamples cannot repair an inappropriate unit, biased sample, or invalid reassignment rule. Choose the analysis before inspecting favorable results.

title: Session 14 · Random numbers and simulation
text:
Outline and applied practice

Specify ADEMP — Let each outcome be SBP reduction: baseline minus 12-week SBP, in mmHg. Positive delta means greater mean reduction with treatment. Use independent normal control and treatment groups with SDs 12 and 4. Compare sizes 10/40 and 30/40 and true differences 0 and 6 (four scenarios). Define the estimand as the population mean difference, treatment minus control. Distinguish this target from the estimator and one sample estimate. Write the five ADEMP headings before running the study. Explain why normal reductions are a useful reference scenario, what prior or pilot evidence would support this model in a real project, and one reason to examine a skewed alternative. State the independence assumption and identify the means and SDs as teaching values.
Inspect one replicate — Generate one dataset. Inspect outcome ranges and group summaries to check the generator, allowing for sampling variation. Explain why simulated data cannot establish that real SBP reductions are normal. Compare Welch and pooled results on that same dataset. Verify the estimate direction, result names, and interval ordering. Exercise a failed constant-outcome sample.
Retain each method and replicate — Inspect the supplied run_study(s, B) function and run a pilot with B = 5. Identify where it generates one dataset, applies both methods, and retains results or errors. Check that five replicates produce ten rows. Both methods must use the same dataset in each replicate.
Run reproducible scenarios — Use B = 1000 for this teaching exercise. Assign each scenario a fixed seed and call set.seed() immediately before running that scenario. Insert an unrelated runif() call before the seed and verify that the scenario results stay unchanged. Do not reset the seed inside the replicate loop.
Summarize performance and failures — For each scenario and method report attempts, failures, bias, coverage, rejection rate, and MCSE for rejection. Use sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / B_valid), where B_valid counts successful replicates. Label performance summaries as conditional on success. Interpret rejection rates as type I error when delta = 0 and power when delta = 6.
Interpret the comparison — Compare null calibration, power, coverage, and failure counts across allocations. Draw one rejection-rate comparison with approximate Monte Carlo intervals. Explain why 5.2% from 1,000 replicates need not differ meaningfully from 5%, and why more replicates differ from more patients per trial.
Power for study planning — Use the delta = 6 results to compare Welch power for 10/40 and 30/40 patients. Report rejections, valid trials, power, MCSE, and an approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval. Explain why this interval concerns detection probability rather than the treatment effect. Distinguish power from coverage. Do the results support at least 80% power? Explain what increasing patient numbers changes and what increasing B changes.

title: Session 14 · Random numbers and simulation
section: Warm-up: random draws and the normal distribution
text:
Warm-up: random draws and the normal distribution

Run two successive rnorm(3) calls after set.seed(42). Rerun the entire block. Which results repeat?
Save state_before <- .Random.seed, draw one value, and compare with identical(state_before, .Random.seed). Explain the generator’s changing bookmark.
Insert unused <- runif(1) between the two rnorm(3) calls. Explain why the second output changes even though unused is never used.
Call set.seed(99) immediately before the result you want to reproduce. Verify that earlier random work no longer changes that result. Explain why you should not put the same seed inside every replicate.
Evaluate dnorm(0), pnorm(1.96), qnorm(0.975), and rnorm(8). Match them to density height, left-tail area, cutoff value, and simulated observations. Which two functions reverse each other’s question? Why is dnorm(0) not the probability of observing exactly zero?

title: Session 14 · Random numbers and simulation
text:
Optional extensions

Extend the Welch power comparison to more sample sizes or a smaller effect (for example, 3 mmHg). Keep the test rule fixed and refine promising scenarios with more replicates.
Add dgm = "skewed" to the design using the supplied helper. Explain why it centers errors using the population mean rather than each sample mean. Keep the estimand unchanged.
Report empirical SE, mean model SE, RMSE, mean interval width, and MCSE for bias or coverage.
Plan B from a target MCSE using ceiling(p * (1 - p) / target^2). Try B = 4000 and explain why MCSE is about half its value at B = 1000.
Explore SimDesign::runSimulation() for running a larger study or rsimsum::simsum() for summarising saved results. No package installation is required for the core lab.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Course description
This course introduces statistical computing as part of responsible biostatistical practice. The emphasis is not only on obtaining an answer, but on creating an analysis that another person can inspect, reproduce, verify, and modify.
This is a working introduction to the computing used in statistical practice. By the end, students should be able to take a data file, validate and reshape it, produce effective statistical figures, write and debug R code, and run a simulation study within a reproducible project.
Students will learn R through both base-R and tidyverse approaches. They may use either style when both express the same analysis clearly, although some exercises will target a particular tool for learning purposes. The course also introduces reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto, version control with Git and GitHub, statistical graphics, reliable programming, simulation, resampling, responsible AI-assisted coding, and a short introduction to Python.

What this course is not
This is not a replacement for a statistical-theory or methods course. Means, t-tests, confidence intervals, and related methods provide material to compute with; their full statistical justification belongs elsewhere in the graduate curriculum. This course focuses on implementing, checking, reproducing, and communicating statistical computations.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Prerequisites
Introductory statistics or permission of the instructor is expected. No prior programming experience is required. Session 0 is designed to ensure that every student begins the first class with a working computing environment.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

Organize a statistical analysis as a reproducible project using R, R Markdown or Quarto, relative paths, and version control.
Inspect R objects and predict the consequences of type, coercion, indexing, missingness, and data structure choices.
Import data and perform systematic checks of dimensions, identifiers, column types, ranges, dates, and missing-value encodings.
Manipulate rectangular data using both base-R and tidyverse approaches and select a clear style for a given task.
Reshape and join data while stating the unit of observation, identifying keys, predicting row counts, and checking join relationships.
Construct and critique statistical graphics using base graphics and ggplot2.
Write functions and control-flow code with explicit inputs, outputs, and edge- case behavior.
Diagnose errors, validate inputs, test important behavior, and recognize common numerical-computing problems.
Choose appropriately among vectorized operations, loops, base-R functionals, and purrr mappings.
Design and interpret simulation and resampling studies.
Inspect fitted models, verify predictions and numerical computations, and deliver an analysis with traceable inputs and a documented computing environment.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Course organization

Instructor-managed materials
Course source, examples, slides, and lab starters are distributed through the BIOS6301-materials repository. Students clone it as a separate RStudio project, leave its files unchanged, and click Pull in that project before each class.


Student work
Each student creates an independent private BIOS6301-mywork repository, as explained in Session 2. Keep it beside the course clone. Copy assigned lab and homework starters (and required synthetic data) into its work/ folder. Edit, render, commit, and push your work in this personal project.
The personal repository does not need course materials, instructor history, or an instructor remote. Invite the instructor and TA so they can review your work. No credentials or restricted research data may be committed to either repository.

text:
AI-assisted coding policy

Before Session 9
AI-generated code is not permitted in submitted course work before the completion of Session 9. This period establishes an independent foundation in R, data handling, reproducibility, and visualization. The midterm examination is completed without AI assistance.


After Session 9
After the Positron and AI-assisted coding session, AI coding assistance is permitted but not required for homework and laboratory work unless an assignment is explicitly designated as unaided. GitHub Copilot is a classroom example, not the only supported or permitted tool. No assignment requires students to use an AI tool. AI assistance is not permitted on any examination.
Students using any AI coding tool must:

Understand and be able to explain every submitted line.
Check that suggested code answers the stated statistical question.
Verify data dimensions, inclusion rules, missing-value behavior, grouping, join relationships, and important numerical results.
Correct, test, or reject inappropriate suggestions.
Include the required AI-use disclosure.
Never provide an AI tool with protected health information, restricted research data, credentials, private keys, or confidential material.

These requirements apply regardless of the AI tool or provider used.


Required disclosure
Each submitted assignment after Session 9 should include one of the following:
AI use: None.
or a concise description such as:
AI use: I used GitHub Copilot to suggest the group-summary code. I corrected its
missing-value handling and verified the group counts independently.
Disclosure does not transfer responsibility to the tool. Students remain responsible for the correctness, interpretation, and provenance of their work.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing

Course communication and support
Students should ask for help early when software installation, Git state, file paths, or rendering prevents progress. A useful technical help request includes:

the operating system and relevant software version;
the command or action attempted;
the complete error or warning as text; and
a minimal synthetic example when code is involved.

Screenshots may supplement an error message but should not replace the text of the message.
Students are encouraged to discuss ideas and debugging strategies with classmates, but submitted code and explanations must be their own. When substantial help is received from another person, that collaboration should be acknowledged briefly in the submission.
The early sessions, especially Git, may feel unusually difficult. Installation, paths, and version-control states create friction for experienced analysts as well as beginners. Difficulty during these sessions is not evidence of an inability to program. Read error messages carefully and ask for help before a technical problem blocks the statistical work.

Pseudorandom numbers
R’s random-number functions use a deterministic generator. Its state determines the next draw; a suitable generator gives sequences useful for statistical simulation.

Reproducible randomness is not a contradiction. The same seed, RNG settings, and sequence of random calls reproduce a run in the same computational environment. Changing the calls changes the stream used downstream.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: The state is an ordinary object
text:
The state is an ordinary object

set.seed(42)
length(.Random.seed)

[1] 626

.Random.seed[1:3]

[1]     10403       624 507561766

invisible(rnorm(1))     # one draw ...
.Random.seed[1:3]       # ... and the state has moved

[1]       10403           2 -1577024373




Two consequences that catch people:

Every draw advances the stream. Nothing is reset until you call set.seed() again.
Inserting a chunk changes everything below it. If a result must be reproducible, seed it immediately before it — not once at the top and hope.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Where to put set.seed()







Placement
Consequence




Before the complete study
One reproducible advancing stream


Before a documented independent analysis block
Its output is stable when earlier blocks change


The same seed inside every replicate
Repeats the same random draws: a simulation bug


Arbitrary seeds chosen until results look desirable
Selects results instead of studying performance



For parallel work, use the framework’s documented independent-stream support. parallel::clusterSetRNGStream() supports R clusters; fork-based mclapply() is not a multicore solution on Windows.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
A simulation is an experiment
We create data under known conditions, apply a statistical method, and check how well it works across many simulated datasets.
Before running it, write down:

What question are we asking?
How will we generate the data and analyse each dataset?
How will we judge the results?

ADEMP gives us five headings for this plan.

Optional background: Morris, White & Crowther (2019), “Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods”, Statistics in Medicine, 38:2074–2102.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
ADEMP











You must be able to write down




A
Aims
The question, in one sentence


D
Data-generating mechanism
Exactly how one dataset is produced. Every parameter, every value


E
Estimands
The quantity being estimated — a number that exists before any method touches it


M
Methods
The procedures being compared, including the naive one


P
Performance measures
How you decide which method won, and with what precision






Five headings, and the discipline is that you fill them in before you write any code.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
ADEMP for today








A
Does a two-sample t-test hold its nominal 5% type I error when the arms have different variances and different sizes?


D
yctrl∼N(0,122)y_{\text{ctrl}} \sim N(0, 12^2), nctrln_{\text{ctrl}} patients; ytrt∼N(δ,42)y_{\text{trt}} \sim N(\delta, 4^2), ntrtn_{\text{trt}} patients. Allocations 25/25, 10/40, 40/10


E
δ\delta, the difference in mean SBP change. Null case δ=0\delta = 0; power cases δ=3,6,9,12\delta = 3, 6, 9, 12 mmHg


M
Pooled t-test (var.equal = TRUE) vs Welch (var.equal = FALSE)


P
Rejection rate, bias, empirical SE, coverage, and interval width. Repeat 10,000 times and report simulation uncertainty (explained later)






The SDs 12 and 4 are deliberately chosen teaching scenarios, not estimates from a clinical study. Other variance ratios require separate scenarios.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Estimands — the letter people skip






The estimand is a property of the data-generating mechanism, not of a method. If you cannot write down its true value before running anything, you cannot compute bias.






Two methods can both be “unbiased” — for different estimands. A marginal risk difference and a conditional odds ratio are not the same target, and a simulation that mixes them will report bias that is an artefact of the question, not the method.
In today’s study the estimand is δ\delta, and we know it because we set it. That is the entire reason simulation can measure bias at all.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
The shape of every simulation





flowchart LR
  P["<b>data model</b><br/>shape, dependence, parameters"] --> S["<b>simulate_one()</b><br/>one dataset"]
  S --> A["<b>analyse_one()</b><br/>one row of results"]
  A --> R["<b>replicate</b><br/>× n_sim"]
  R --> T["<b>results</b><br/>one row per replicate"]
  T --> M["<b>performance</b><br/>bias, SE, rejection rate"]
  style S fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style A fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style P fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70








Session 11 gave you functions. Session 13 gave you iteration. This is what they were for.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Generate one dataset

# One SBP trial: y is baseline minus 12-week SBP (mmHg).
# Assumptions: independent patients, normal reductions within each arm.
simulate_trial <- function(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta = 0) {
  stopifnot(n_ctrl >= 2, n_trt >= 2, sd_ctrl > 0, sd_trt > 0)
  data.frame(
    arm = rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), c(n_ctrl, n_trt)),
    y   = c(rnorm(n_ctrl, mean = 0,     sd = sd_ctrl),
            rnorm(n_trt,  mean = delta, sd = sd_trt))
  )
}

set.seed(6301)
head(simulate_trial(3, 3, 12, 4, delta = 8), 3)

   arm         y
1 ctrl -5.667400
2 ctrl 12.457060
3 ctrl  3.299615

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Analyse one dataset

analyse_trial <- function(data, pooled = FALSE) {
  x <- data$y[data$arm == "trt"]
  y <- data$y[data$arm == "ctrl"]
  fit <- t.test(x, y, var.equal = pooled)
  c(est = mean(x) - mean(y), se = fit$stderr,
    p = fit$p.value, lo = fit$conf.int[1], hi = fit$conf.int[2])
}
set.seed(6301)
round(analyse_trial(simulate_trial(20, 20, 12, 4, delta = 8)), 3)

   est     se      p     lo     hi 
 8.171  2.473  0.003  3.096 13.246 


Passing treatment first makes the estimate and interval both treatment minus control. Check this direction before running any replications.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Compare methods on the same dataset
text:
Compare methods on the same dataset

set.seed(1401)
one_data <- simulate_trial(10, 40, 12, 4, delta = 0)
one_pair <- rbind(Welch = analyse_trial(one_data, FALSE),
                 pooled = analyse_trial(one_data, TRUE))
round(one_pair, 3)

         est    se     p     lo    hi
Welch  1.116 2.512 0.666 -4.429 6.661
pooled 1.116 1.883 0.556 -2.670 4.902

stopifnot(one_pair["Welch", "est"] == one_pair["pooled", "est"])

Both tests estimate the same mean difference. Their standard errors, degrees of freedom, intervals, and p-values can differ. Pairing methods within a replicate also supports direct comparisons of their performance.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
One replicate, then ten thousand

run_scenario <- function(n_sim, n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt,
                         delta = 0, pooled = TRUE) {
  out <- replicate(n_sim, {
    d <- simulate_trial(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta)
    analyse_trial(d, pooled = pooled)
  })
  as.data.frame(t(out))          # n_sim rows, one per replicate
}

set.seed(6301)
demo <- run_scenario(5, 20, 20, 12, 4, delta = 8)
round(demo, 3)

    est    se     p     lo     hi

2 2.910 2.843 0.312 -2.845  8.664
3 1.976 2.730 0.474 -3.551  7.502
4 5.212 3.631 0.159 -2.138 12.562

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Save results with the design
bundle <- list(results = res, scenarios = grid, seed = 6301,
               rng = RNGkind(), session = sessionInfo())
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(bundle, "output/simulation.rds")

A results file should identify the parameters and code version that produced it.
Rerun when the generator, analysis, or scenario definition changes.
A file’s existence is not evidence that it matches the current specification.

For expensive studies, run a script once and let the report read the saved results.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: A buggy simulation does not crash
text:
A buggy simulation does not crash

simulate_bad <- function(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta = 0) {
  set.seed(6301)                       # <- the bug
  data.frame(
    arm = rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), c(n_ctrl, n_trt)),
    y   = c(rnorm(n_ctrl, 0, sd_ctrl), rnorm(n_trt, delta, sd_trt))
  )
}

bad <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(500, analyse_trial(simulate_bad(25, 25, 12, 4)))))
c(reject = mean(bad$p < 0.05), bias = mean(bad$est), emp_se = sd(bad$est))

  reject     bias   emp_se 
0.000000 1.082951 0.000000 




No error or warning. The empirical SE is zero and the rejection rate is either zero or one. The reported bias is the error of a single repeated estimate, not necessarily zero.

text:
Failure changes the denominator
Suppose 100 attempts produce 90 valid intervals, of which 86 contain the truth.








Quantity
Calculation
Interpretation




Failure rate

Procedure did not return an interval


Coverage among successful fits

Conditional on success


Successful coverage per attempt

Counts failure as unsuccessful coverage



Report the failure rate and the chosen denominator. Silently applying na.rm = TRUE can hide poor performance in difficult samples.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
What you actually report









Measure
Estimated by
Answers




Bias
θ̂‾−θ\bar{\hat\theta} - \theta
Is the estimator systematically off?


Empirical SE
sd(θ̂)\mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)
How variable is it, run to run?


Coverage
1nsim∑𝟙{θ̂lo≤θ≤θ̂hi}\frac{1}{n_{\text{sim}}}\sum \mathbb{1}\{\hat\theta_{\text{lo}} \le \theta \le \hat\theta_{\text{hi}}\}
Does the 95% CI cover 95% of the time?


Type I error
mean(p<α)\mathrm{mean}(p < \alpha), with θ=0\theta = 0
Does the test hold its size?


Power
mean(p<α)\mathrm{mean}(p < \alpha), with θ≠0\theta \ne 0
Will the study detect a real effect?






Type I error and power are the same computation on data from the same DGM with delta set differently. Nothing else changes.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Monte Carlo error
Every number on the previous slide is itself an estimate, from nsimn_{\text{sim}} draws. It has a standard error.








Quantity
Monte Carlo SE




Bias
EmpSE/nsim\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}


Empirical SE (approximately normal estimates)
EmpSE/2(nsim−1)\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{2(n_{\text{sim}}-1)}


A rejection rate p̂\hat p
p̂(1−p̂)/nsim\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n_{\text{sim}}}






p_hat <- 0.052; n_sim <- 1000
sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_sim)      # MCSE

[1] 0.007021111

p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_sim)

[1] 0.03823862 0.06576138





At nsim=1000n_{\text{sim}} = 1000, an observed 0.052 is consistent with anything from 0.038 to 0.066. That simulation cannot tell 5% from 6.5%.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Sampling SE and Monte Carlo SE
text:
Sampling SE and Monte Carlo SE








Uncertainty
What varies?
What reduces it?




Sampling SE
Estimates across new datasets
More information in each dataset


Monte Carlo SE
A performance summary across repeated simulation runs
More simulation replicates



Increasing the number of simulated datasets does not make an individual study estimate more precise. It makes our assessment of the method more precise.

Coverage and interval width in code

check_ci <- run_scenario(1000, 10, 40, 12, 4, delta = 6, pooled = FALSE)
covered <- check_ci$lo <= 6 & 6 <= check_ci$hi
c(bias = mean(check_ci$est) - 6,
  empirical_se = sd(check_ci$est), mean_model_se = mean(check_ci$se),
  coverage = mean(covered), width = mean(check_ci$hi - check_ci$lo),
  coverage_mcse = sqrt(mean(covered) * (1 - mean(covered)) / nrow(check_ci)))

text:
Bias, variance, and RMSE

error <- check_ci$est - 6
c(bias = mean(error), rmse = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
  mcse_bias = sd(error) / sqrt(length(error)))

RMSE summarizes squared estimation error; coverage evaluates an interval procedure. They answer different questions. A small bias does not imply a calibrated interval.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Plan for the probability you will estimate
text:
Plan for the probability you will estimate

target <- 0.005
ceiling(c(near_null = 0.05 * 0.95, worst_case = 0.25) / target^2)

 near_null worst_case 
      1900      10000 


The conservative bound uses p(1−p)≤0.25p(1-p) \le 0.25 and covers every probability. A design sized for Type I error near 0.05 can give less precise power estimates.
Choose the precision target before inspecting favorable results. Use a pilot to debug and estimate computational cost, then run the planned study.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
The question, restated
Two arms. Different variances — 12 vs 4 mmHg. Different sizes — and it is the combination that does the damage.

The pooled t-test assumes a common variance. It estimates one sps_p from both arms, weighting by degrees of freedom, and gets n1+n2−2n_1 + n_2 - 2 df. Welch estimates each arm’s variance separately and adjusts the df downwards.



t.test() defaults to var.equal = FALSE. The pooled and Welch procedures use different standard-error formulas; neither corrects a wrong sampling unit or a biased dataset.









Four scenarios, δ=0\delta = 0, nsim=10,000n_{\text{sim}} = 10{,}000. If the test is behaving, an individual rejection estimate is typically within about 0.0044 of 0.05. This is an approximate simulation uncertainty range, not a guarantee for every scenario.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Run it

n_sim <- 10000
set.seed(6301)

scenarios <- list(
  list(lab = "25 / 25", nc = 25, nt = 25, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "10 / 40", nc = 10, nt = 40, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "40 / 10", nc = 40, nt = 10, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "10 / 40", nc = 10, nt = 40, pooled = FALSE)
)

type1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(scenarios, function(s) {
  r <- run_scenario(n_sim, s$nc, s$nt, sd_ctrl = 12, sd_trt = 4,
                    delta = 0, pooled = s$pooled)
  data.frame(alloc = s$lab, method = ifelse(s$pooled, "pooled", "Welch"),
             reject = mean(r$p < 0.05), bias = mean(r$est), emp_se = sd(r$est))
}))
type1$mcse <- sqrt(type1$reject * (1 - type1$reject) / n_sim)

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Inspect the null p-value distribution


Figure 1: Null p-values, 10,000 replicates, n = 10 / 40, sd = 12 / 4.

For an exact continuous null p-value, the expected count is 500 per bin. Welch is approximate; discrete valid tests may be conservative rather than uniform. Excess near zero can reveal inflated Type I error.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Interpret the method comparison
Welch uses s12/n1+s22/n2\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2} with approximate degrees of freedom.

In this normal unequal-variance scenario, compare its rejection rate with 0.05 using the reported MCSE.
The pooled test uses a common variance estimate and can be badly calibrated when the smaller group has the larger variance.
This study has not yet measured the cost of Welch under equal variances.

Add an equal-variance scenario before making a claim about that tradeoff.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Power, from the same machinery


Figure 2: Welch power. Total N = 50 in every scenario. sd = 12 (ctrl) / 4 (trt).

Same DGM, same functions, one argument changed: delta. Fifty patients in every scenario — only the allocation differs. Bars show approximate 95% Monte Carlo intervals from 2,000 replicates per scenario.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: What the simulation actually told us
text:
What the simulation actually told us


The pooled test rejected far more than 5% of null datasets when the smaller arm had the larger variance.
Bias estimates were small relative to their Monte Carlo uncertainty in these scenarios.
Welch was better calibrated in the unequal-variance scenarios examined.
With fixed total size and equal per-person costs, the illustrated allocations favor more observations in the noisier arm; real design constraints also matter.




These conclusions apply to the data-generating scenarios we studied. More replicates improve precision within a scenario. They do not establish that its distribution or independence assumptions describe a real trial.









This is the general move: when you do not know whether a method works under your conditions, build your conditions and find out.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
How R makes random numbers
A random-number generator is a recipe that produces numbers that behave like random draws. We use them to simulate data, such as patients’ blood pressures.

set.seed(42)
rnorm(3, mean = 120, sd = 10)  # simulate 3 blood pressures

[1] 133.7096 114.3530 123.6313



R follows a fixed recipe, so we call these pseudorandom numbers.
Think of a long sequence of numbers: each random call moves forward in it.
A seed chooses a starting point. The same starting point and the same calls give the same results.

This lets us share an example and get exactly the same simulated data.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
.Random.seed remembers where R is
R stores its current generator state in .Random.seed, an integer vector. Think of it as a bookmark: set.seed(42) resets it, and random calls update it.


Original code

set.seed(42)
round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1]  1.371 -0.565  0.363

round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1]  0.633  0.404 -0.106


Rerun this block: both outputs repeat.

An unrelated random call inserted

set.seed(42)
round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1]  1.371 -0.565  0.363

unused <- runif(1)  # moves the bookmark
round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1] -1.105  0.539  0.580


The first output matches. The second changes.

Even unused random draws change later results. Calculations such as 2 + 2 do not.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: A seed before each result you want to reproduce
text:
A seed before each result you want to reproduce
Place set.seed() immediately before each simulation or analysis block whose output should stay the same when earlier code changes.


The result we want to reproduce

set.seed(99)
round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1] 0.214 0.480 0.088



Earlier random work can change

unused <- runif(100)
set.seed(99)  # reset just before this result
round(rnorm(3), 3)

[1] 0.214 0.480 0.088



Both blocks give the same result because set.seed(99) resets .Random.seed immediately before rnorm(3).
For a simulation loop: set the seed once before the loop. Resetting the same seed inside every replicate repeats the same draws.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Estimand: the quantity we want to learn
text:
Estimand: the quantity we want to learn
For the same SBP trial, suppose mean reduction is 0 mmHg under control and 6 mmHg under treatment. How much additional reduction does treatment provide?








Term
Meaning
Example in our simulation




Estimand
The true additional mean SBP reduction
δ=6−0=6\delta = 6 - 0 = 6 mmHg


Estimator
The rule applied to sampled patients
Mean reduction in treatment minus mean reduction in control


Estimate
The result from one simulated trial
For example, 7.2 mmHg additional reduction



We set the population means, so we know the truth is 6. New samples give different estimates, but the target stays 6.
If the estimates average 6.3 over many replicates, estimated bias is 6.3−6=0.36.3 - 6 = 0.3 mmHg. One estimate’s error, 7.2−67.2 - 6, is not the bias.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Why simulation results have uncertainty
Monte Carlo means using repeated random draws to answer a question.
Suppose a test really rejects 5% of the time under the null. In 1,000 simulated trials, we expect about 50 rejections, but we will not always get exactly 50.

A run might give 52 rejections: 52 / 1,000 = 5.2%.
A new seed gives new datasets, so the rejection count may change.
This variation from using a finite number of replicates is Monte Carlo uncertainty.

A fixed seed reproduces the same answer. More replicates make the answer less sensitive to the particular random draws.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Two kinds of uncertainty









Sampling uncertainty
Monte Carlo uncertainty




What varies?
A treatment effect estimate across trials
A rejection rate across full simulation runs


Example
Each trial has 50 patients
Each simulation run contains 1,000 trials


What helps?
More patients per trial
More simulated trials per run



Increasing patients per trial changes the study we are evaluating. Increasing replicates helps us evaluate that same study more precisely.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: One calculation for a simulated percentage
text:
One calculation for a simulated percentage
The Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) describes how much a simulated proportion varies across repeated runs of the simulation.
For independent replicates, MCSE=p̂(1−p̂)/B\mathrm{MCSE} = \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/B}, where p̂\hat p is the observed proportion and BB is the number of replicates.

p_hat <- 52 / 1000
n_sim <- 1000
mcse <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_sim)
round(100 * c(rate = p_hat, MCSE = mcse,
              lower = p_hat - 1.96 * mcse,
              upper = p_hat + 1.96 * mcse), 2)

 rate  MCSE lower upper 
 5.20  0.70  3.82  6.58 


The rate is 5.2%, with MCSE 0.70 percentage points and an approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval of 3.82% to 6.58%. This run gives little evidence that the true rejection rate differs from 5%.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Optional: no rejections does not mean zero probability
text:
Optional: no rejections does not mean zero probability

binom.test(0, 1000)$conf.int

[1] 0.000000000 0.003682084
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


Zero rejections out of 1,000 does not establish a true rejection probability of zero. The plug-in MCSE formula gives zero here; a binomial interval exposes the remaining uncertainty.
Use interval estimates near zero or one, and state the number of valid replicates.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: More replicates give a steadier answer
text:
More replicates give a steadier answer
For a rejection probability near 5%:



Replicates
Expected rejections
MCSE (percentage points)




100
5
2.18


1,000
50
0.69


10,000

Four times as many replicates halves the MCSE. More precision costs more computing time.
Start with a small run to check the code. Then choose a larger, fixed number of replicates and report the MCSE with the final result.

Optional: choosing replicates for a target precision

target <- 0.005
ceiling(c(near_null = 0.05 * 0.95, worst_case = 0.25) / target^2)

 near_null worst_case 
      1900      10000 


The conservative bound uses p(1−p)≤0.25p(1-p) \le 0.25 and covers every probability. A design sized for Type I error near 0.05 can give less precise power estimates.
Choose the precision target before inspecting favorable results. Use a pilot to debug and estimate computational cost, then run the planned study.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
ADEMP for an SBP trial
Our simulated trial measures SBP reduction = baseline minus 12-week SBP (mmHg). A larger reduction means a larger drop.


A · Aim: How reliably can we estimate the treatment’s additional mean SBP reduction when group sizes and variability differ?
D · Data: Generate independent normal SBP reductions. Control: mean 0, SD 12. Treatment: mean δ\delta, SD 4. Group sizes: 25/25, 10/40, or 40/10.
E · Estimand: δ=\delta = treatment minus control mean reduction. A value of 6 means an additional 6 mmHg drop with treatment.
M · Methods: Difference in sample means, with Welch or pooled t procedures for the confidence interval and p-value.
P · Performance: Bias, 95% interval coverage, and detection of an effect. When δ=0\delta = 0, check false positives.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Data generation starts with assumptions
A data-generating model describes the population and how we sample from it. We choose this model before choosing an R random-number function.

Outcome: each patient’s SBP reduction, baseline minus 12-week SBP. Values can be positive or negative. A negative value means SBP increased.
Distribution: what shape, spread, and extreme values are plausible within each treatment group?
Structure: are patients independent? Repeated visits or patients within clinics may require a model for their dependence.
Parameters: use previous studies, pilot data, or subject-matter knowledge to choose plausible means and SDs. Explore a range when these are uncertain.

Our means and SDs are invented teaching scenarios, not clinical estimates.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Why use a normal distribution here?
text:
Why use a normal distribution here?
We start with normal SBP reductions as a simple reference scenario. This lets us study unequal group sizes and SDs while keeping the distribution’s shape fixed.
For a real project, examine relevant prior or pilot data: group-specific histograms, Q–Q plots, outliers, and plausible ranges. Rough symmetry and modest tails may support a normal approximation. They do not prove it.
A normal model allows any real value. It may be unsuitable if it generates implausible changes, strong skewness is present, or extreme values are common.
Sensitivity check: repeat the study with skewed errors while preserving the population means and SDs. Report whether the conclusions change.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: From the SBP model to rnorm()
text:
From the SBP model to rnorm()
For one teaching scenario, assume independent reductions within each arm:
Ycontrol∼N(0,122),Ytreatment∼N(6,42).
Y_{\mathrm{control}} \sim N(0,12^2), \qquad
Y_{\mathrm{treatment}} \sim N(6,4^2).

The treatment group’s population mean is 6 mmHg and SD is 4 mmHg. In the formula the second quantity is variance. R’s sd argument takes the SD.

set.seed(1425)
reduction <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 6, sd = 4)
round(reduction, 1)

[1] 3.5 9.0 1.1 7.1 1.9


rnorm() implements our assumption. These five patients need not have a sample mean of exactly 6 or a sample SD of exactly 4.
Before a large run, inspect simulated ranges, plots, and group summaries. That checks the generator’s implementation; real-world plausibility needs evidence.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Power: detecting a specified treatment effect
text:
Power: detecting a specified treatment effect
Suppose treatment truly produces 6 mmHg more mean SBP reduction than control. Our test still asks whether the population mean difference is zero.
Power is the probability that the planned test rejects that null when the specified effect is real. Power of 80% means about 80 of 100 repeated trials would reject it. The remaining 20 would miss the effect (type II error).
To estimate power by simulation:

Specify the effect, distributions, sample sizes, and analysis in advance.
Generate one complete trial under that nonzero effect.
Apply the planned test and record whether p < 0.05.
Repeat independently and calculate the proportion of rejections.

Here we use a two-sided Welch test at 5%. At a true effect of zero, the same calculation estimates type I error instead of power to detect a nonzero effect.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Estimated power for one SBP design
text:
Estimated power for one SBP design
Assume independent normal reductions, 40 patients per arm, SDs 12 and 4, and a true additional reduction of 6 mmHg.

set.seed(1456)
power_run <- run_scenario(2000, 40, 40, 12, 4,
                          delta = 6, pooled = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(power_run) == 2000, all(is.finite(power_run$p)))
detected <- power_run$p < 0.05
power_hat <- mean(detected)
power_mcse <- sqrt(power_hat * (1 - power_hat) / nrow(power_run))
round(c(power = power_hat, MCSE = power_mcse), 3)

power  MCSE 
0.838 0.008 


We detected the effect in 1676 of 2,000 trials. The estimated power is 83.8%, with MCSE 0.82 percentage points.
Each replicate contains 80 patients. The MCSE denominator is 2,000 trials.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Power, coverage, and Monte Carlo uncertainty
text:
Power, coverage, and Monte Carlo uncertainty
For the same true effect of 6 mmHg, each simulated trial gives a p-value and a confidence interval for the treatment effect.







Quantity
What we count or calculate




Power
Fraction of trials rejecting the null effect of zero


Coverage
Fraction of treatment-effect intervals containing the true value 6


MCSE of power
Uncertainty in the power estimate because we simulated a finite number of trials



An interval [2, 10] mmHg covers 6 and excludes 0: it covers and detects. An interval [−2, 14] mmHg covers 6 but includes 0: it covers but does not detect.
The worked design’s approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval for power is 82.2% to 85.4%. These endpoints describe a probability of detection, not a treatment effect in mmHg.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Power across effect sizes and allocations
text:
Power across effect sizes and allocations


Figure 2: Welch power. Total N = 50 in every scenario. sd = 12 (ctrl) / 4 (trt).

Along each curve, the true effect changes. Between curves, the allocation changes while total N stays 50. At effect 0, rejection is type I error; at nonzero effects, it is power. Bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals from 2,000 trials per point.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Power and the number of patients
text:
Power and the number of patients


Figure 3: Welch test at 5%, normal reductions, SDs 12 and 4. Equal group sizes.
More patients increase power in these scenarios. A smaller effect requires more patients to reach the same target. The dashed line marks an illustrative 80% target. Bars describe Monte Carlo uncertainty from 2,000 trials per point.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Simulation for study planning

Choose a meaningful effect: justify the difference worth detecting and examine smaller effects too. Do not substitute the observed effect after a trial.
Specify plausible variability: larger SDs generally reduce power with the other assumptions fixed. Check a range supported by prior information.
Compare sample sizes and allocations: for our mean difference, sampling variance is 122/nctrl+42/ntrt12^2/n_{\mathrm{ctrl}} + 4^2/n_{\mathrm{trt}}. More patients in the noisier control arm can help when total size and per-person costs are fixed.
Keep the test rule fixed: a higher significance threshold can raise power but also permits more false positives. Check null calibration first.
Refine promising designs: use more replicates near the desired power, report MCSE, and assess sensitivity to the model assumptions.

More patients can raise power. More simulation replicates estimate that power more precisely. Neither 80% nor a single simulated crossing is a universal rule.

Make the analysis population explicit

vars <- c("id", "arm", "sbp_0", "age", "sbp_12")
keep <- complete.cases(trial[, vars])
analysis <- trial[keep, vars]
c(available = nrow(trial), analysed = nrow(analysis), excluded = sum(!keep))

title: Practical Statistical Computing
text:
A checkable analysis contract

Input: one row per participant; specified units and factor levels.
Sample: record exclusions and reasons, retaining identifiers.
Fit: a stated formula and fitting procedure.
Output: estimates or predictions with their target and uncertainty.
Evidence: diagnostic checks, held-out evaluation when relevant, and provenance.

An error-free lm() call establishes only that the computation completed.

title: Models, Validation, and Course Review
text:
Read a model formula

f <- sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm
f

sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm


The response is left of ~; the terms on the right specify predictors. An intercept is included by default. In formulas, + adds model terms rather than adding the columns numerically.
Use data = analysis so the intended source of variables is clear.

title: Practical Statistical Computing
text:
Formula operators



Formula fragment
Model terms




x + z
Main effects of x and z


x * z
x + z + x:z


x:z
Interaction term


x + I(x^2)
Linear and literal squared x terms


x - 1
Remove the intercept



The formula ^ has special term-expansion meaning. Use I() when ordinary arithmetic is intended. Include interactions because the scientific question requires them, not simply because the syntax is available.

title: Models, Validation, and Course Review
text:
Factors determine the comparison

analysis$arm <- factor(analysis$arm, levels = c("Control", "Treatment"))
levels(analysis$arm)

[1] "Control"   "Treatment"

contrasts(analysis$arm)

          Treatment
Control           0
Treatment         1


With the treatment contrasts used here, Control is the reference. armTreatment represents the Treatment-versus-Control coefficient conditional on the other terms in this additive model.
Changing the reference changes coefficient interpretation, not the fitted values.

title: Models, Validation, and Course Review
text:
Inspect the design matrix

X <- model.matrix(f, data = analysis)
head(X, 4)

  (Intercept)    sbp_0 age armTreatment
1           1 180.0144  56            0
2           1 160.3498  69            0
3           1 144.7369  62            0
4           1 161.3452  51            0

c(rows = nrow(X), columns = ncol(X), rank = qr(X)$rank)

   rows columns    rank 
     77       4       4 


Factors become numeric contrast columns. Collinear columns can make coefficients unidentifiable even when the formula looks reasonable.

title: Models, Validation, and Course Review
text:
Fit and inspect the object

fit <- lm(f, data = analysis, na.action = na.fail)
class(fit)

[1] "lm"

c(n = nobs(fit), residual_df = df.residual(fit))

          n residual_df 
         77          73 

coef(fit)

 (Intercept)        sbp_0          age armTreatment 
   2.9627981    0.8644030    0.2188276   -6.7356081 


fit is a structured R object, not the printed coefficient table. na.fail prevents the model from silently dropping additional rows after we have defined the analysis sample.

title: Models, Validation, and Course Review
text:
Extract results with model methods

coef(summary(fit))

               Estimate  Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   2.9627981 10.56683207  0.2803866 7.799740e-01
sbp_0         0.8644030  0.05947542 14.5337845 3.044751e-23
age           0.2188276  0.08220370  2.6620164 9.548023e-03

Function

coef(fit)

Fitted values / residuals
