title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Summary

Reproduce the failure before editing the code.
Reduce the data and code until the first broken assumption is visible.
Use the call stack, browser, and breakpoints to inspect state deliberately.
Assertions and small tests preserve a repair after today.
Finite-precision arithmetic requires tolerance-aware reasoning.


Next connection: Session 13 asks how to repeat a correct operation clearly and efficiently.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
message(), print(), or cat()?
All three can communicate with a person. Choose by the purpose of the output:








Function
Purpose
Example




print()
Display an R object
print(summary(model))


cat()
Write text with your formatting
cat("Mean:", 3, "\n")


message()
Report progress or a diagnostic
message("Reading file 2 of 5")



By default, print() and cat() use standard output; message() uses the diagnostic stream (stderr). The stream’s name does not make it an error.
message() also signals an R condition: callers can handle or silence messages separately from results. It is not an instruction to the operating system.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Keep progress separate from results

mean_with_progress <- function(x) {
  message("Computing the mean")
  mean(x)
}
mean_with_progress(c(2, 4))

Computing the mean


[1] 3

suppressMessages(mean_with_progress(c(2, 4)))

[1] 3


Both calls return 3; only the first displays the progress message. suppressMessages() does not silence print() or cat() output.
In a report, a chunk’s message: false can hide progress while retaining results. Use print() freely when inspecting an object during debugging.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: traceback(): see the path after an error
text:
traceback(): see the path after an error
Run the practice example in the R console, then immediately run traceback():
> mean_change(d)
Error in sum(x) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument
> traceback()
3: pooled_mean(x)
2: summarise_change(data$change)
1: mean_change(d)
sum(x) raises the error. In this R 4.5.1 example, pooled_mean(x) is the deepest printed call. Source-line annotations may also appear.
Nothing is paused or opened. This is a printed record, not an interactive debugger. Next, use debugonce(pooled_mean) and run mean_change(d) again.
Only an uncaught error updates the usual console traceback. Errors captured while rendering a report do not; the displayed stack may be from an older error.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: debug() and debugonce(): pause at entry
text:
debug() and debugonce(): pause at entry
For an ordinary R function, think “start browsing when this function is called.” R sets a debugging flag; it does not insert browser() into your source file.
# Restore the original function without a browser() line first.
pooled_mean <- function(x) sum(x) / length(x)
debugonce(pooled_mean)   # mark it; nothing runs yet
mean_change(d)          # next call pauses inside pooled_mean()
# At Browse[...]>: str(x), then n to step, or Q to quit.







Tool
Where / how often it pauses




browser() in the body
At that line whenever execution reaches it


debugonce(f)
At entry on the next call; then step through expressions


debug(f)
On every call, until undebug(f)


IDE breakpoint
At a selected source line



You can inspect x before sum(x) runs. No source edit is needed for debugonce().

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: tryCatch(): choose what an error returns
text:
tryCatch(): choose what an error returns

tryCatch(safe_mean(c(2, 4)),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))

[1] 3

tryCatch(safe_mean("4"),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))

[1] "x must be a numeric vector"



First argument: the expression R tries to evaluate; success returns its value.
error = function(e): a handler called only if an error occurs.
e: the error object; conditionMessage(e) extracts its explanation.

On error, R abandons that expression and returns the handler’s value. Execution continues after tryCatch(); it does not repair the input or resume the failed line.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
R already uses double precision

typeof(1)     # ordinary numeric literal: 64-bit double

[1] "double"

typeof(1L)    # L requests a 32-bit integer

[1] "integer"









Property
Base R double




Precision
About 15–16 significant decimal digits


Largest finite value
About 1.8 × 10308


Smallest positive normal value
About 2.2 × 10-308


Smallest positive subnormal value
About 4.9 × 10-324, with reduced precision



Range is how large or small a value can be. Precision is how finely nearby values can be distinguished. Printing more digits changes neither.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Are these the largest types available?
text:
Are these the largest types available?
No. R’s ordinary numeric vectors already use the 64-bit double format common in many languages. Base R does not provide a wider general-purpose numeric vector.







Need
An option beyond base R’s ordinary types




Exact 64-bit integers
R package bit64


Arbitrarily large integers
R package gmp; Python’s built-in integers


More floating-point precision / range
R package Rmpfr



These require suitable types and arithmetic; installing a package does not upgrade ordinary R numbers. Larger types cost memory and computation.
For likelihoods, change the calculation to the log scale first. A wider fixed-size type only postpones underflow.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: A reprex is a small example someone else can run
text:
A reprex is a small example someone else can run
Reprex = reproducible example. Its purpose is to let another person see the same problem without your files, workspace, or a meeting to explain the setup.
Include:

Tiny synthetic input, written directly in the code.
Every function and package needed to reproduce the problem.
The exact call and actual output, including any error or warning.
The expected result and why you expect it.

Test it in a fresh R session. Remove unrelated code while keeping the problem. Never include private patient data.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: A complete reprex: runs, but gives the wrong answer
text:
A complete reprex: runs, but gives the wrong answer
# Paste this whole block into a fresh R session. No packages needed.
broken_mean <- function(x) {
  sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) / length(x)
}
x <- c(2, NA, 4)
broken_mean(x)
# [1] 2
Question: “I want the mean of observed values: (2 + 4) / 2 = 3. Why does this function return 2?”
The reader can reproduce the problem and see that length(x) counts the missing observation. After the repair, keep this input and expected result as a test.
A reprex is a communication habit. The optional reprex package helps format examples; it is not required for this lab.

These sessions complete the core R programming sequence. Later statistical and topic-specific sessions build on these tools. Each lab includes its own synthetic inputs and supplied prerequisites, so it can run in a fresh session.

title: Session 13 · Iteration and Vectorization
text:
Session outline and content

1. Repeated operations
Start with a function whose behavior is already checked.


2. Loops and allocation
Use for, seq_along(), preallocated results, and bounded while loops.


3. Vectorized operations
Choose vector or matrix operations with the intended missing-value behavior.


4. The apply family
Match list, scalar, and multi-statistic outputs to the correct tool and template.


5. Base R and purrr
Introduce purrr, then compare list and typed mappings and anonymous wrappers.


6. Choosing an implementation
Handle dependent steps and assemble results without repeated growth.


7. Verify, measure, and practice
Check equivalence before timing, repeat measurements, and interpret object-size estimates.

Slides

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
1. Start with a checked operation
The starter supplies the Session 11 helpers, following the contract protected in Session 12, and the same marker table. Run the supplied checks before iterating. one_summary(x) must return a numeric vector named n, mean, and sd. Use observed n; return numeric NA for the mean with no observations and for SD with fewer than two observations. Reject invalid input through safe_mean().

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
2. Loops and allocation
Build a matrix with three rows and one column per marker. Preallocate it with row names n, mean, sd and marker column names. Fill it using seq_along(markers) and markers[[j]]. Preserve a 3-by-0 matrix for zero columns. First practice the simpler scalar case with one safe_mean() result per column.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
3. Vectorized operations
For the supplied numeric matrix, compute one row mean using each of a preallocated loop, apply(..., 1, mean), and rowMeans(). Use the same missing-value rule in all three. Verify numerical equivalence before measuring. Add a character ID column to a copy, inspect as.matrix(), and explain why the mixed data frame is not a safe input for numeric matrix summaries.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
4. Lists and typed outputs

Apply one_summary() with lapply() and vapply() using c(n = 0, mean = 0, sd = 0) as the template. Compare against the loop’s values, names, types, and dimensions.
Check ordinary, all-missing, one-observation, and zero-column cases.
Replace a marker with a character vector. Show that the helper rejects it. Explain why an output template alone cannot detect every invalid input.
Use a named list of unequal-length numeric vectors with lapply() and vapply(..., safe_mean, numeric(1)). Different input lengths do not imply different output lengths when the operation returns one mean.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
5. Base R and optional purrr
Use Map(change_summary, baseline_columns, followup_columns) for the two supplied paired lists. Check list lengths and matching names before mapping, then compare with a preallocated list filled by a loop. Each helper checks its paired vectors.
Optional equivalents: map(markers, one_summary) returns a list; map_dbl(markers, safe_mean) returns one number per marker. map_dbl() cannot hold all three statistics from one_summary() in one element. For paired lists, compare map2() with Map().

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
6. Choose and combine results
Create one data-frame row per marker, including the marker name and three statistics. Collect the rows in a preallocated list and bind once. State the zero-column output schema explicitly. Explain when an ordinary loop is clearer than an independent mapping, especially when the next step uses the previous state.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
7. Verify and measure
Compare the supplied growing and preallocated square-root loops on the same input, checking equality first. Warm up both implementations and record at least five repetitions with system.time(). Do the same for the row-summary implementations. Report input dimensions, R version, repetition count, and observed variation. A zero elapsed time can be below timer resolution; do not claim infinite speedup.
Record object.size() for the input and final outputs. Explain that these are stored object-size estimates, not peak memory measurements. Recommend a solution using correctness, output shape, readability, and your actual measurements.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
Exit evidence
Submit the checked helpers, iteration results, empty/invalid cases, equivalence checks, timing context, and recommendation. No hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, or simulation study design are required in this programming lab.

title: Session 13 guided lab · Repeat checked operations
text:
Optional bounded-loop practice
Starting at x = 1, repeatedly divide by two until x < 0.01, with an explicit maximum iteration count. Record whether the threshold or iteration limit ended the loop. Explain why the next input depends on the previous output.

title: Homework 3: Programming a 12-Week Weight-Management Report
text:
Student instructions and data
Use weight_followup.csv, a synthetic dataset of 200 adults enrolled at five clinics. Each row is one participant. Clinics have different enrollment counts. Eight participants have no week-12 weight because they missed follow-up; all other fields are complete and valid. These data are for programming and descriptive reporting, not for establishing program effectiveness.
Data file: Download weight_followup.csv
Reference MD5: 7858756792f2988f969072865b95558f
Keep the supplied CSV unchanged.



Variable
Meaning




id
Unique participant ID


clinic
Clinic A–E


age
Age in years


sex
Recorded sex


height_cm
Baseline height in centimeters


weight_baseline_kg
Baseline weight in kilograms


weight_week12_kg
Week-12 weight in kilograms


sessions_attended
Number of sessions attended, 0–12



Keep full precision in calculations; round only displayed results. Include code and short explanations in one R Markdown or Quarto report. You may assume inputs use the documented units and are correctly paired. Extensive validation is not required.

Supplied import code
dat <- read.csv("weight_followup.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(head(dat), caption = "First six synthetic participants")
The extra demographic and attendance fields make this a realistic study table; the assignment does not require using every column.

title: Homework 3: Programming a 12-Week Weight-Management Report
text:
Part 1. Participant functions — 20 points

Question 1.1. BMI function — 6 points
Write calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_cm). Convert centimeters to meters inside the function and calculate weight divided by squared height in meters. Use the function to add baseline and week-12 BMI columns. Return unrounded values.
Show some hand calculations of BMI and compare them with your function results to make sure they agree.


Question 1.2. Percentage change — 6 points
Write one function, percent_change(baseline, followup), to calculate the percentage change at follow-up compared with baseline. Use this function to create percentage changes in BMI and weight. Compare the two using == and isTRUE(all.equal(...)). Explain what you find.


Question 1.3. Combine functions with a target parameter — 8 points
The following helper is supplied. It identifies a decrease of at least target percent:
meets_target <- function(pct_change, target = 5) {
  return(pct_change <= -target)
}
Write evaluate_target(baseline, followup, target = 5) by combining percent_change() and meets_target().
Use it to create met_5pct and met_10pct from the weight columns. What would happen if you omitted target = target when calling the helper inside evaluate_target()?

title: Homework 3: Programming a 12-Week Weight-Management Report
Homework 3: Programming a 12-Week Weight-Management Report
text:
Part 3. Clinic iteration — 35 points

Supplied setup
Run this supplied code to keep participants with observed follow-up measurements for Parts 3 and 4.
followup <- dat[!is.na(dat$weight_week12_kg), ]


Question 3.2. Clinic function and preallocated loop — 17 points
Write clinic_summary(x) that takes one clinic’s follow-up data and returns one data-frame row containing the clinic name, participant count, mean baseline BMI, mean percentage weight change, and percentage meeting the 5% target. Use split() to divide followup by clinic. Call your function for each clinic using a preallocated list and a for loop, then combine the rows into one report.


Question 3.3. Reuse with lapply — 8 points
Use lapply() with your clinic_summary() function from Q3.2 to create the clinic report. Compare the report produced by the loop in Q3.2 with the report produced by lapply() here, after aligning their rows and columns. Explain the benefit of reusing the same function in both approaches.


Question 3.4. Explore several targets — 10 points
Use iteration to calculate the percentage meeting 3%, 5%, 7%, and 10% weight-loss targets in each clinic. Produce a numeric matrix with clinics as rows and targets as columns. Label both dimensions. Check that percentages never increase as the target becomes stricter, and explain the check.

title: Homework 3: Programming a 12-Week Weight-Management Report
text:
Part 4. Vectorization and timing — 30 points

Question 4.1. Four implementations — 12 points
For each participant in followup, calculate additional kilograms needed to reach a 7% loss from baseline. Calculate weight_week12_kg - 0.93 * weight_baseline_kg, and replace negative results with zero. For example, a participant starting at 100 kg has a target of 93 kg: at 95 kg they need 2 kg more loss; at 90 kg they need zero.
(a) Loop — 3 points. Write additional_loop(baseline, week12). Preallocate a numeric result vector, use a for loop to calculate each participant’s result, and use if to return zero when no additional loss is needed.
(b) vapply — 3 points. Write additional_vapply(baseline, week12) to perform the same calculation using vapply() over participant indices, returning one number per participant.
(c) Vectorization — 3 points. Write additional_vectorized(baseline, week12) using pmax() or ifelse() to calculate all participants’ results at once. Explain why max() applied to the entire difference vector would not give one result per participant.
(d) apply — 3 points. Write additional_apply(baseline, week12). Combine the two numeric vectors into a matrix and use apply() to calculate one result per row. Explain your choice of MARGIN.
Apply all four functions to the follow-up data and save their results.


Question 4.2. Compare the results — 6 points
Confirm that the four implementations give the same results. Compare the loop result with each other result using both == and isTRUE(all.equal(...)). Explain why tolerance-aware comparison is generally preferable for calculated numeric values, even if exact equality works here.


Question 4.3. Benchmark at a useful scale — 8 points
Repeat the complete follow-up rows 5,000 times. Warm up all implementations, then time each at least five times using system.time(). Include output allocation but exclude data generation and printing. Report row count, median and range of elapsed times, and R version. Explain why replicated rows increase computational work but not the number of independent participants.


Question 4.4. Recommendation — 4 points
Recommend an implementation based on correctness, readability, and your measurements. Explain why performance differences may matter little for the original 200 participants.

title: Iteration and Vectorization
text:
Meet the purrr package
purrr is a tidyverse package for applying a function repeatedly to elements of a vector or list. It offers a consistent interface and named output types.
# Install once in the Console if needed:
install.packages("purrr")

# Load in each new R session:
library(purrr)

map(x, f) applies f to each element of x and returns a list.
map_dbl(x, f) returns one number per element as a double vector.
Put the data first and the function second, as in lapply(x, f).

Next, compare the same calculation using base R and purrr.
